courses.title: Ch 1 · Introduction to Accounting
courses.summary: Meaning, process and branches of accounting, its users, qualitative characteristics and all the basic terms you will use for the rest of the year.
outcomes: Learners can define accounting and its process steps
Learners can identify internal and external users and their needs
Learners can explain reliability, relevance, understandability and comparability
Learners can classify assets, liabilities, capital, expenditure and revenue items

lessons.title: What accounting is and why it exists

scenes.text: Asha starts a tiffin service from home with ₹20,000 of her savings.
By month-end she has bills, UPI receipts and a notebook of who still owes her money.
She cannot tell whether she made a profit — accounting is the tool that answers that question.

steps.title: Definition in your own words
steps.body:
**Accounting** is the process of *identifying, measuring, recording, classifying, summarising, analysing, interpreting and communicating* financial information about an organisation to the people who need it for decisions.

- **Identifying**: deciding which events are financial transactions (a sale is; a friendly phone call is not).
- **Measuring**: expressing them in money (₹).
- **Recording**: writing them in the journal / books of original entry.
- **Classifying**: grouping similar items in ledger accounts.
- **Summarising**: preparing trial balance and financial statements.
- **Analysing and interpreting**: finding meaning (profitability, liquidity).
- **Communicating**: giving reports to users.

steps.title: Book-keeping vs accounting
steps.body:
**Book-keeping** is the routine, clerical part: recording and classifying transactions. **Accounting** starts where book-keeping ends and adds summarising, analysis, interpretation and communication. Book-keeping is the base; accounting is the complete language of business.

- **Branches**: *Financial accounting* (records past transactions, prepares Profit & Loss Account and Balance Sheet), *Cost accounting* (finds cost per unit/product and helps control cost), *Management accounting* (gives information to managers for planning and decisions).

steps.title: Objectives and roles
steps.body:
- Maintain a full and systematic record of transactions.
- Ascertain profit or loss for a period.
- Ascertain the financial position (what is owned and owed) on a date.
- Provide information to users for decisions.

**Roles**: accounting works as the *language of business*, as a *historical record*, as a source of *current economic reality*, as an *information system* (collects, processes and communicates data).

steps.title: Solved example 1: Is it a transaction?
steps.body:
Asha (a) buys rice for ₹1,500 in cash, (b) signs a contract to supply 50 tiffins next month, (c) hires a helper at ₹6,000 per month starting next week.

- Step 1: A transaction must change financial position and be measurable in money now.
- Step 2: (a) cash goes out and stock comes in → **transaction**.
- Step 3: (b) and (c) are only agreements; nothing has been exchanged yet → **not yet transactions** (they will be recorded when goods are supplied / salary becomes due).

steps.title: Solved example 2: Which branch helps?
steps.body: A factory wants to know the cost of one packet of biscuits so it can set a price. → *Cost accounting*. The owner wants next year’s plan for opening a new branch → *Management accounting*. The bank asks for last year’s profit → *Financial accounting*.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating book-keeping and accounting as the same thing.
- Recording non-monetary events (a manager’s skill, staff morale) — accounting records only events measurable in money.
- Thinking an agreement or order is a transaction before goods or money move.

steps.title: Limitations to remember
steps.body: Accounting ignores non-monetary facts, records items at historical cost (so it ignores inflation), involves estimates (depreciation, bad debts) and can be manipulated ("window dressing"). Exams often ask for 3–4 limitations.

activity.prompt: Put the accounting process in order

quiz.q: Which of these is the clerical part of accounting?
quiz.why: Book-keeping is the clerical part, which records and classifies transactions. Analysing and interpreting come after.

quiz.q: A promise to buy goods next month is…
options: not a transaction until goods/money move
quiz.why: A promise to buy later does not change the assets or liabilities now, so it is not recorded as a transaction until goods or money move.

quiz.q: Which branch finds the cost per unit of a product?
quiz.why: Cost accounting finds and controls the cost of a product, such as cost per unit.

quiz.q: Accounting is called the language of business because it…
quiz.why: Accounting is called the language of business because it communicates financial information to its users.

quiz.q: A limitation of accounting is that it…
quiz.why: A limitation of accounting is that it records only what can be measured in money and ignores non-monetary factors, such as staff skill.

sources: NCERT Accountancy Part I (Introduction to Accounting) — topic reference

lessons.title: Users of accounting information and its qualities

scenes.text: A bank manager wants to know if Asha can repay a loan.
Asha’s helper wonders if the business is stable enough to keep her job.
The tax department needs her income figures. Each user needs different information.

steps.title: Internal users
steps.body: People *inside* the business: **owners/proprietors** (profit, growth), **management** (planning, control, decisions), **employees** (job security, bonus, wage negotiations).

steps.title: External users
steps.body:
- **Investors/potential investors**: risk and return.
- **Lenders/banks**: ability to repay loan and interest.
- **Suppliers/creditors**: whether bills will be paid on time.
- **Customers**: continuity of supply.
- **Government and tax authorities**: taxes (income tax, GST), regulation, statistics.
- **Researchers and the public**: studies, social impact.

steps.title: Qualitative characteristics
steps.body:
Information is useful only if it has these qualities:

- **Reliability**: free from error and bias, verifiable, faithfully represents facts.
- **Relevance**: available in time, helps predict or confirm, and actually affects decisions.
- **Understandability**: presented so users with reasonable knowledge can follow it.
- **Comparability**: can be compared across periods (intra-firm) and across firms (inter-firm) because consistent methods are used.

steps.title: Solved example 1: Match user to need
steps.body:
A supplier asks for the balance sheet before giving 60 days’ credit.

- Step 1: Identify user → supplier (external, creditor).
- Step 2: Need → short-term ability to pay (liquidity: current assets vs current liabilities).
- Step 3: So the supplier mainly studies current assets, cash and current liabilities.

steps.title: Solved example 2: Which quality is missing?
steps.body:
A company publishes its 2024 results in December 2026. The figures are correct but too late for investors.

- Step 1: Correct and verified → reliable.
- Step 2: Not available in time to influence decisions → **relevance (timeliness)** is missing.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling employees “external” users — they are internal.
- Mixing up *reliability* (truthful, verifiable) and *relevance* (useful, timely).
- Forgetting that comparability needs **consistent** accounting methods.

activity.prompt: Internal or external user?

quiz.q: A bank granting a loan is mainly interested in…
quiz.why: A bank lending money is mainly interested in the borrower's ability to repay, its solvency.
Employees are part of the organisation, so they are internal users of accounting information.

quiz.q: Information that is free from bias and verifiable is…
quiz.why: Information that is free from bias and can be verified is reliable.

quiz.q: Comparing a firm’s 2025 and 2026 profit requires…
quiz.why: To compare profit across years, the information must be prepared on a consistent basis, which is comparability.
Timeliness is part of relevance, since late information cannot affect decisions.

lessons.title: Basic terms I: assets, liabilities, capital, drawings

scenes.text: Asha buys a scooter for deliveries and owes ₹8,000 to the grocery wholesaler.
She also takes ₹2,000 from the business cash for her sister’s birthday gift.
To record these she needs the exact words accountants use.

steps.title: Business entity and transaction
steps.body: **Entity**: the business is treated as separate from its owner. **Transaction**: an exchange of money or money’s worth between two or more parties that changes financial position (cash or credit).

steps.title: Capital, drawings, liabilities
steps.body:
- **Capital**: amount invested by the owner in the business (cash or assets). It is a liability of the business towards the owner.
- **Drawings**: money or goods withdrawn by the owner for *personal* use. They reduce capital.
- **Liabilities**: obligations payable to outsiders. *Non-current* (long-term) liabilities — e.g., a 5-year bank loan, debentures. *Current* liabilities — payable within a year, e.g., creditors, bills payable, outstanding expenses, short-term loans.

steps.title: Assets
steps.body:
Economic resources owned or controlled that can be measured in money and are expected to give future benefit.

- **Non-current assets**: held for long-term use, not for sale — *tangible* (land, building, machinery, furniture, vehicles) and *intangible* (goodwill, patents, trademarks, software).
- **Current assets**: held for a short time and expected to convert into cash within a year — cash, bank, debtors, bills receivable, stock, prepaid expenses.

steps.title: Solved example 1: Classify items
steps.body:
Classify: Machinery ₹50,000; Creditors ₹12,000; Stock ₹9,000; Patent ₹15,000; Bank loan (5 years) ₹40,000.

- Machinery → non-current tangible asset.
- Patent → non-current intangible asset.
- Stock → current asset.
- Creditors → current liability.
- 5-year bank loan → non-current liability.

steps.title: Solved example 2: Find closing capital
steps.body:
Asha started with capital ₹20,000, earned profit ₹6,500 and withdrew ₹2,000 for personal use.

- Step 1: Closing capital = Opening capital + Profit − Drawings (+ additional capital, if any).
- Step 2: = 20,000 + 6,500 − 2,000.
- Step 3: **Closing capital = ₹24,500.**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating drawings as a business expense — they are a reduction of capital, *not* an expense.
- Calling capital an asset of the business — from the business’s point of view it is owed to the owner.
- Calling goods for personal use “sales”.

activity.prompt: Sort each item

quiz.q: Goods taken by the owner for home use are…
quiz.why: Goods taken by the owner for personal use are drawings, a withdrawal that reduces capital.
A trademark has no physical form, so it is an intangible asset.

quiz.q: Opening capital ₹50,000, profit ₹10,000, drawings ₹4,000. Closing capital?

quiz.why: Outstanding salary is owed and payable soon, so it is a current liability.

quiz.q: Capital, from the business’s view, is…
quiz.why: By the business entity concept, the owner is separate from the business, so capital is a liability of the business to the owner.

lessons.title: Basic terms II: revenue, expense, expenditure, income and more

scenes.text: Asha pays ₹65,000 for the scooter and ₹300 for petrol in the same week.
Her friend says, “Both are expenses.” Asha is not sure.
Accounting separates spending that gives long benefit from spending used up now.

steps.title: Revenue, expense, expenditure
steps.body:
- **Revenue**: amount earned from the normal business activity — sales of goods/services, plus items like commission, interest, rent, royalty received.
- **Expense**: cost incurred to earn revenue during the period — cost of goods sold, wages, rent, salary, advertisement, depreciation.
- **Expenditure**: spending money or incurring a liability to get assets, goods or services. *Capital expenditure* gives benefit for more than one year (scooter, machinery, installation of machine). *Revenue expenditure* gives benefit within the year (petrol, repairs, wages).

steps.title: Income, profit, gain, loss
steps.body:
- **Profit** = Revenue − Expenses for a period.
- **Gain**: profit from incidental events, e.g., selling an old machine above book value.
- **Loss**: excess of expenses over revenue, or money lost without benefit (theft, fire).
- **Income**: increase in owner’s wealth — profit plus gains.

steps.title: Goods, purchases, sales, stock, debtors, creditors
steps.body:
- **Goods**: items the business deals in (for a stationery shop, pens are goods; for a doctor, pens are not).
- **Purchases**: goods bought for resale or for production — cash or credit. *Purchase return* = return outward.
- **Sales**: goods sold — cash or credit. *Sales return* = return inward.
- **Stock (inventory)**: goods unsold on a date (opening and closing stock).
- **Debtors**: persons who owe money to the business (usually for credit sales). **Creditors**: persons to whom the business owes money.
- **Discount**: *trade discount* is a reduction on list price, not recorded in books; *cash discount* is for prompt payment and is recorded.
- **Voucher**: documentary evidence of a transaction (cash memo, invoice, receipt).

steps.title: Solved example 1: Capital or revenue expenditure?
steps.body: (a) Scooter ₹65,000 → *capital* (benefit for years). (b) Petrol ₹300 → *revenue* (used up now). (c) Wages paid to install a new machine ₹2,000 → *capital* (part of the machine’s cost). (d) Repairs to an old machine ₹1,500 → *revenue*.

steps.title: Solved example 2: Profit and cash discount
steps.body:
Goods list price ₹10,000, trade discount 10%, cash discount 2% for paying immediately.

- Step 1: Invoice value = 10,000 − 10% = ₹9,000 (trade discount not recorded).
- Step 2: Cash discount = 2% of 9,000 = ₹180 (recorded).
- Step 3: Cash paid = ₹8,820.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calculating cash discount on the list price instead of the invoice price after trade discount.
- Calling installation charges on a new machine an expense.
- Treating the sale of an old asset as “sales” — it is not sale of goods.

activity.prompt: List price ₹20,000, trade discount 15%, cash discount 2% on immediate payment. How much cash is paid?

quiz.q: Purchase of furniture by a furniture dealer is…
quiz.why: For a furniture dealer, furniture bought for resale is goods, so it is recorded as purchases.
Trade discount is not recorded in the books. Only the net invoice amount is entered.

quiz.q: Sale of old machinery above book value gives…
quiz.why: Selling old machinery above its book value gives a gain, as it is an incidental event, not a normal sale.

quiz.q: Repairs to an old building are…
quiz.why: Repairs to an old building only maintain it, so they are revenue expenditure.
Return inward is goods returned by customers, so it means sales return.

questions.q: Accounting records events that can be…
questions.why: Accounting records only events that can be measured in money, by the money measurement concept.

questions.q: Which is NOT a function in the accounting process?
questions.why: Manufacturing is production. Recording, classifying and summarising are steps of accounting.

questions.q: Tax authorities are…
questions.why: Tax authorities are outside the business, so they are external users.

questions.q: Goodwill is a…
questions.why: Goodwill has no physical form and lasts long, so it is an intangible non-current asset.

questions.q: Bills payable is a…
questions.why: Bills payable are amounts to be paid within a year, so they are a current liability.

questions.q: Opening capital ₹1,00,000; additional capital ₹20,000; profit ₹30,000; drawings ₹12,000. Closing capital?
Assertion (A): Drawings reduce capital. Reason (R): Drawings are business expenses.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Drawings do reduce capital, so A is true. But drawings are personal withdrawals by the owner, not business expenses, so R is false.

questions.q: Information that helps predict future results and is timely is…
questions.why: Information that helps predict future results and is timely is relevant.

questions.q: List price ₹50,000, trade discount 20%, cash discount 5%. Amount paid?
questions.why: Trade discount: 50,000 × 20% = 10,000, so the net price is 40,000. Cash discount: 5% of 40,000 = 2,000. Amount paid = ₹38,000.

questions.q: Wages paid for installing a new machine are debited to…
questions.why: Wages for installing a machine are capital expenditure, so they are added to the cost of Machinery.

questions.q: Case: Ravi, a laptop dealer, buys 10 laptops for resale and 1 laptop for office use. The office laptop is…
questions.why: The office laptop is not bought for resale but for use in the business, so it is a non-current asset.

questions.q: A bank loan repayable after 5 years is…
questions.why: A bank loan repayable after 5 years is a long-term, non-current liability.

questions.q: Which branch helps managers plan and decide?
questions.why: Management accounting provides information that helps managers plan and make decisions.

questions.q: Loss of goods by fire (uninsured) is a…
questions.why: Loss of uninsured goods by fire gives no benefit, so it is a loss.

questions.q: Total revenue ₹4,80,000; total expenses ₹3,65,000; gain on sale of asset ₹15,000. Total income (profit + gain)?
questions.why: Operating profit = 4,80,000 − 3,65,000 = ₹1,15,000. Adding the ₹15,000 gain on sale of the asset gives ₹1,30,000.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Accounting information lacks comparability if methods change every year. Reason (R): Comparability needs consistent methods.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true. Comparability needs consistent methods, so changing methods every year destroys it.

questions.q: A firm’s current assets ₹90,000, current liabilities ₹60,000. A supplier would see working capital of…
questions.why: Working capital = current assets − current liabilities = 90,000 − 60,000 = ₹30,000.

courses.title: Ch 2 · Theory Base of Accounting
courses.summary: GAAP and all basic accounting concepts, double vs single entry, cash vs accrual basis, Accounting Standards, Ind AS and the basics of GST with input tax credit.
outcomes: Learners can explain each basic accounting concept with an example
Learners can compute profit on cash and accrual basis
Learners can describe AS, Ind AS and IFRS
Learners can compute CGST, SGST, IGST and net GST after input tax credit

lessons.title: GAAP and the first six accounting concepts

scenes.text: Kabir and Zoya run identical shops but each records things his or her own way.
Their profits cannot be compared — one values stock at cost, the other at market price.
Generally Accepted Accounting Principles (GAAP) give everyone the same rules.

steps.title: What GAAP means
steps.body: **GAAP** are the rules, concepts and conventions that accountants follow so that financial statements are uniform, reliable and comparable. They come from experience, professional bodies (in India, the ICAI) and law. The underlying ideas are called **basic accounting concepts**.

steps.title: Concepts 1–3
steps.body:
- **Business entity**: business and owner are separate. Owner’s capital is a liability of the business; drawings are recorded as reduction in capital.
- **Money measurement**: only events measurable in money are recorded, in one currency unit (₹). Quantities like “10 machines” are converted to money.
- **Going concern**: the business is assumed to continue for the foreseeable future. That is why fixed assets are shown at cost less depreciation, not at what they would fetch if sold today.

steps.title: Concepts 4–6
steps.body:
- **Accounting period**: life of a business is divided into periods (usually 1 year; in India 1 April – 31 March) so results can be measured regularly.
- **Cost concept (historical cost)**: assets are recorded at the price paid to acquire them, including installation and transport, and are not revalued for market changes.
- **Dual aspect**: every transaction has two equal effects — the basis of double entry and of the equation **Assets = Liabilities + Capital**.

steps.title: Solved example 1: Cost concept
steps.body:
Machine bought for ₹2,00,000; freight ₹10,000; installation ₹15,000. Market value at year-end ₹2,60,000.

- Step 1: Cost = 2,00,000 + 10,000 + 15,000 = ₹2,25,000.
- Step 2: Cost concept → record at **₹2,25,000**, not ₹2,60,000.

steps.title: Solved example 2: Dual aspect
steps.body:
Owner starts business with cash ₹80,000 and buys goods ₹30,000 on credit.

- Step 1: Cash (asset) +80,000; Capital +80,000.
- Step 2: Stock (asset) +30,000; Creditors (liability) +30,000.
- Step 3: Assets 1,10,000 = Liabilities 30,000 + Capital 80,000 ✔

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying the going concern concept means the business *will* never close — it is an assumption, used until there is evidence otherwise.
- Revaluing land each year to market price under historical cost.
- Forgetting that business entity applies to sole proprietors too, not only companies.

activity.prompt: Match the concept with the example
pairs: Owner’s personal electricity bill is not a business expense
Assets shown at cost less depreciation

quiz.q: Which concept is the basis of double entry?
quiz.why: The dual aspect concept says every transaction has two equal effects, which is the basis of double entry.

quiz.q: Fixed assets are not shown at realisable value because of…
quiz.why: Under the going concern concept, the business will continue, so fixed assets are held for use, not shown at what they would fetch if sold.

quiz.q: Machine ₹1,00,000 + transport ₹5,000 + installation ₹3,000 is recorded at…
quiz.why: Cost of a machine includes all costs to bring it to working condition: 1,00,000 + 5,000 + 3,000 = ₹1,08,000.

quiz.q: The financial year in India usually runs…
quiz.why: The financial year in India usually runs from 1 April to 31 March.

quiz.q: Recording owner’s capital as a liability follows…
quiz.why: By the business entity concept, the owner is separate from the business, so capital is a liability of the business.

lessons.title: More concepts: revenue recognition to objectivity

story.title: When is a sale a sale?

scenes.text: In March, Zoya receives an order and an advance of ₹5,000; the goods will be sent in April.
Should she show the ₹5,000 as March revenue?
Revenue recognition and matching give the answer.

steps.title: Revenue recognition and matching
steps.body:
- **Revenue recognition (realisation)**: revenue is recognised when it is earned — i.e., when goods are sold/services rendered and the right to receive is established — whether or not cash is received. An advance received is *not* revenue yet; it is a liability.
- **Matching**: expenses of a period are matched with revenues of the same period. So outstanding expenses are added and prepaid expenses deducted; cost of goods *sold* (not purchased) is matched with sales.

steps.title: Full disclosure, consistency, conservatism
steps.body:
- **Full disclosure**: all material facts are disclosed in statements and notes (e.g., contingent liabilities, accounting policies).
- **Consistency**: same methods are used year after year (e.g., depreciation method); any change is disclosed with its effect.
- **Conservatism (prudence)**: “anticipate no profit, but provide for all possible losses”. Stock valued at cost or market price, whichever is lower; provision for doubtful debts is made.

steps.title: Materiality and objectivity
steps.body:
- **Materiality**: items that would influence a user’s decision must be shown separately; trivial items can be treated simply (a ₹50 stapler can be written off as an expense although it lasts years).
- **Objectivity**: records are supported by verifiable evidence (vouchers, invoices) and are free from personal bias.

steps.title: Solved example 1: Matching
steps.body:
Rent ₹12,000 is paid for 12 months on 1 October 2025; books close 31 March 2026.

- Step 1: Rent relating to the year = 6 months = ₹6,000.
- Step 2: Prepaid rent = ₹6,000 (current asset).
- Step 3: Only ₹6,000 is charged to Profit & Loss — matching.

steps.title: Solved example 2: Conservatism
steps.body:
Closing stock cost ₹40,000; market price ₹36,000.

- Step 1: Lower of cost or market = ₹36,000.
- Step 2: Stock is shown at **₹36,000**; the ₹4,000 fall is recognised now. If market were ₹45,000, stock would stay at ₹40,000 (no unrealised profit).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating advance from customers as revenue.
- Charging the whole year’s payment as expense when part relates to next year.
- Thinking conservatism allows creating secret reserves by understating profit on purpose — that breaks reliability.

statements.s: An advance received for goods to be supplied next year is revenue of this year.
statements.why: It is a liability until goods are delivered.

statements.s: Closing stock is valued at lower of cost or market price due to conservatism.
statements.why: Provide for losses, not anticipated profits.

statements.s: Changing depreciation method every year follows consistency.
A ₹30 pencil sharpener may be charged as an expense due to materiality.
Objectivity requires evidence like invoices.

quiz.q: Provision for doubtful debts is created because of…
quiz.why: Conservatism says to provide for all possible losses, so a provision for doubtful debts is created.

quiz.q: Disclosing contingent liabilities in notes follows…
quiz.why: Disclosing contingent liabilities in the notes follows full disclosure, which requires all material facts to be disclosed.

quiz.q: Cost of goods sold, not purchases, is matched with sales due to…
quiz.why: By the matching concept, expenses of earning revenue, like the cost of goods sold, are matched with that revenue.

quiz.q: Stock cost ₹25,000, market ₹28,000. Value under conservatism?
quiz.why: Under conservatism, stock is valued at the lower of cost and market value, which is ₹25,000.

quiz.q: Revenue from a credit sale is recognised…
quiz.why: Revenue from a credit sale is recognised when the sale is made, not when cash is received.

story.title: Cash in hand vs money earned

scenes.text: Dr. Mehta records fees only when patients pay.
A factory next door records sales when invoices are raised, even if unpaid.
They are using different bases of accounting.

steps.title: Double entry vs single entry
steps.body:
- **Double entry system**: both aspects of every transaction are recorded (debit and credit). It is complete, scientific, allows a trial balance, detects some errors and is accepted by law.
- **Single entry system**: incomplete — usually only cash and personal accounts are kept. Cheap and simple but cannot give a reliable profit or trial balance.

steps.title: Cash basis vs accrual basis
steps.body:
- **Cash basis**: income and expenses are recorded only when cash is received or paid. Simple; used by some professionals and non-profit bodies.
- **Accrual basis**: income is recorded when earned and expenses when incurred, whether paid or not. Gives a true profit and is required for companies in India.

steps.title: Solved example 1: Profit on each basis
steps.body:
Year’s fees earned ₹5,00,000, of which ₹60,000 is still unpaid. Fees for last year received this year ₹20,000. Expenses incurred ₹2,00,000, of which ₹15,000 outstanding; last year’s expenses paid this year ₹10,000.

- Accrual: Income 5,00,000 − Expenses 2,00,000 = **₹3,00,000**.
- Cash: Receipts = (5,00,000 − 60,000) + 20,000 = 4,60,000; Payments = (2,00,000 − 15,000) + 10,000 = 1,95,000; Profit = **₹2,65,000**.

steps.title: Solved example 2: Which basis?
steps.body: Salary for March ₹30,000 is paid on 5 April. Under accrual, it is March’s expense (outstanding salary at 31 March). Under cash basis, it appears in April.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Adding last year’s collections to this year’s accrual income.
- Thinking accrual means “credit only” — it covers cash and credit transactions.
- Believing single entry is a separate legal system; it is just incomplete double entry.

activity.prompt: Fees earned this year ₹3,00,000 (₹40,000 unpaid). Expenses incurred ₹1,20,000 (₹10,000 unpaid). Profit on CASH basis (no old items)?

quiz.q: Which basis records income when earned?
quiz.why: Under the accrual basis, income is recorded when it is earned and expenses when they are incurred, whether or not cash moves.

quiz.q: Trial balance can be prepared under…
quiz.why: A trial balance needs both aspects of each transaction, so it is prepared under double entry.

quiz.q: Under cash basis, outstanding expenses are…
quiz.why: Under the cash basis only cash actually paid is recorded, so outstanding expenses are ignored.
Companies in India must follow the accrual basis.

quiz.q: A limitation of single entry is…
quiz.why: Single entry is incomplete, so a trial balance cannot be prepared from it.

lessons.title: Accounting Standards, Ind AS and IFRS

scenes.text: An Indian software firm wants foreign investors.
Investors ask: “Are your accounts prepared like global ones?”
India’s Ind AS, converged with IFRS, help answer “yes”.

steps.title: What accounting standards are
steps.body:
**Accounting Standards (AS)** are written policy documents that set out how particular transactions are to be recognised, measured, presented and disclosed. In India the **Accounting Standards Board (ASB)** was set up by the ICAI in **1977** to formulate them.

- Benefits: uniformity, comparability, reliability, reduce choice of methods, help auditors and prevent manipulation.
- Limitations: can be rigid, may limit professional judgement, cannot override law.

steps.title: Ind AS and IFRS
steps.body:
- **IFRS** are issued by the International Accounting Standards Board (IASB) and used in many countries.
- **Ind AS** are Indian standards *converged* with IFRS, notified by the Ministry of Corporate Affairs (2015), applying in phases to listed and large companies. Smaller entities continue with AS.
- Ind AS are numbered similarly to IFRS (e.g., Ind AS 1 Presentation of Financial Statements).

steps.title: Solved example 1: Why standards help
steps.body: Firm A depreciates at 10% straight line, firm B at 25% reducing balance with no disclosure. Investors cannot compare. A standard on depreciation requires disclosure of method and rates → comparability is restored.

steps.title: Solved example 2: Identify the body
steps.body: Q: Who formulates AS in India? → ASB of ICAI. Who notifies Ind AS for companies? → Ministry of Corporate Affairs (Government of India), on recommendation of the National Financial Reporting Authority (NFRA) and ICAI.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying Ind AS are *identical* to IFRS — they are converged, with some carve-outs.
- Thinking standards replace concepts — they are built on the concepts.
- Confusing ICAI (professional body) with the Government.

cards.back: Accounting Standards Board of ICAI, formed 1977
Indian standards converged with IFRS, notified by MCA

quiz.q: ASB in India was set up in…
quiz.why: The Accounting Standards Board was set up by ICAI in 1977.
Ind AS are converged with IFRS, with some carve-outs for India.
IFRS are issued by the International Accounting Standards Board (IASB).

quiz.q: A main benefit of standards is…
quiz.why: A main benefit of standards is comparability, since similar items are treated alike.

quiz.q: If a standard conflicts with a law…
quiz.why: A law overrides an accounting standard, so if they conflict, the law prevails.

scenes.text: A shopkeeper in Lucknow sells a fan to a customer in Lucknow and another to a buyer in Delhi.
The first bill shows CGST + SGST; the second shows IGST.
Let us understand why.

steps.title: What GST is
steps.body:
**GST** is a comprehensive, destination-based, multi-stage indirect tax on the supply of goods and services, in force in India from **1 July 2017** (101st Constitutional Amendment). It replaced many indirect taxes such as excise duty, service tax, VAT and entry tax.

- **CGST** (Central) + **SGST** (State) on intra-state supply; **UTGST** instead of SGST in Union Territories without legislature.
- **IGST** on inter-state supply and imports; collected by the Centre and shared.
- **GST Council** chaired by the Union Finance Minister recommends rates and rules.

steps.title: Input Tax Credit (ITC)
steps.body:
A registered business can set off the GST it paid on purchases (*input tax*) against GST collected on sales (*output tax*). Only the value added is taxed at each stage, removing the cascading “tax on tax” effect.

- Order of set-off for IGST credit: first against IGST, then CGST, then SGST.
- CGST credit cannot be used against SGST and vice versa.

steps.title: Solved example 1: Intra-state bill
steps.body:
Goods ₹10,000 sold within UP; GST 18%.

- Step 1: CGST 9% = ₹900; SGST 9% = ₹900.
- Step 2: Invoice total = 10,000 + 900 + 900 = **₹11,800**.

steps.title: Solved example 2: Net GST payable
steps.body:
A trader buys goods ₹50,000 + IGST 12% (₹6,000) and sells within the state for ₹80,000 + 12% GST (CGST ₹4,800, SGST ₹4,800).

- Step 1: Output tax: CGST 4,800, SGST 4,800.
- Step 2: Use IGST credit 6,000 → first against CGST 4,800 (CGST now 0), balance 1,200 against SGST.
- Step 3: SGST payable = 4,800 − 1,200 = **₹3,600**; CGST payable = **0**.

steps.title: Characteristics and advantages
steps.body: Destination based, comprehensive, dual structure, uses online GSTN portal, rates in slabs, threshold exemption for small suppliers. Advantages: removes cascading, common national market, easier compliance, better transparency, boosts competitiveness of exports.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Charging IGST on a sale within the same state.
- Using CGST credit to pay SGST.
- Treating GST paid on purchases as cost when ITC is available.

activity.prompt: Goods worth ₹25,000 are sold within the state at 12% GST. What is the total invoice value?

quiz.why: An inter-state supply attracts IGST, which is collected by the Centre.
GST came into force on 1 July 2017.
Input tax credit (ITC) removes the cascading effect of tax on tax.
At 18% on an intra-state sale, the tax is split equally: CGST 9% and SGST 9%. SGST = 9% of 5,000 = ₹450.

quiz.q: IGST credit is first used against…
quiz.why: IGST credit is used first against IGST, then against CGST and then against SGST.

questions.q: “Anticipate no profit but provide for all losses” is…
questions.why: Anticipating no profit but providing for all losses is conservatism, or prudence.

questions.q: The assumption that a business will continue is…
questions.why: The going concern assumption says that the business will continue for a long time.

questions.q: Assets = Liabilities + Capital follows…
questions.why: Assets = Liabilities + Capital follows from the dual aspect concept.

questions.q: A machine bought for ₹3,00,000 + ₹20,000 installation; market value now ₹3,50,000. Book value at purchase?
questions.why: The book value at purchase is the historical cost, including installation: 3,00,000 + 20,000 = ₹3,20,000. The later market value is not recorded.

questions.q: Accounting Standards Board of ICAI was constituted in…
questions.why: The Accounting Standards Board of ICAI was formed in 1977.

questions.q: Under accrual basis, outstanding salary is…
options: treated as expense of the year
questions.why: Under the accrual basis, outstanding salary is an expense incurred in the year, so it is recorded as an expense of the year.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Advance received from a customer is not revenue. Reason (R): Revenue is recognised when earned.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true. Revenue is recognised only when it is earned, so an advance received before delivery is not yet revenue.

questions.q: Stock: cost ₹60,000, net realisable value ₹55,000. Value shown?
questions.why: Stock is shown at the lower of cost (₹60,000) and net realisable value (₹55,000), which is ₹55,000.

questions.q: Fees earned ₹4,00,000 (₹50,000 unpaid); expenses ₹1,80,000 (₹20,000 unpaid). Cash-basis profit?
questions.why: Cash basis counts only cash: received 4,00,000 − 50,000 = 3,50,000, and paid 1,80,000 − 20,000 = 1,60,000. Profit = ₹1,90,000.

questions.q: Inter-state sale ₹40,000 at 18% GST. Tax and type?
questions.why: An inter-state supply attracts IGST. 18% of 40,000 = ₹7,200 IGST.

questions.q: Case: A trader has IGST credit ₹9,000; output CGST ₹5,000 and SGST ₹5,000. Net SGST payable?
questions.why: IGST credit of 9,000 first offsets CGST of 5,000, leaving 4,000. This offsets SGST of 5,000, so net SGST payable = ₹1,000.

questions.q: Which is NOT replaced by GST?
questions.why: Income tax is a direct tax and is not replaced by GST. GST replaced indirect taxes like service tax, VAT and most central excise.

questions.q: Changing stock valuation method every year violates…
questions.why: Changing the stock valuation method every year violates the consistency concept.

questions.q: Showing accounting policies in notes reflects…
questions.why: Disclosing accounting policies in the notes reflects the full disclosure principle.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Ind AS are identical to IFRS. Reason (R): Ind AS are converged with IFRS.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Ind AS are converged with IFRS but have some carve-outs, so they are not identical. A is false and R is true.

questions.q: Rent ₹24,000 paid for one year on 1 January 2026; year ends 31 March 2026. Prepaid rent?
questions.why: The rent paid is for 12 months from 1 January 2026. Three months (Jan–Mar) fall in this year, so 9 months are prepaid: 24,000 × 9/12 = ₹18,000.

questions.q: Which concept explains recording a ₹40 calculator as an expense?
questions.why: By the materiality concept, a trivial item like a ₹40 calculator is recorded as an expense, even though it lasts for years.

courses.title: Ch 3 · Recording of Transactions – I
courses.summary: Source documents and vouchers, the accounting equation, rules of debit and credit, journal entries (with discounts, GST and special cases) and ledger posting and balancing.
outcomes: Learners can identify source documents and prepare vouchers
Learners can show the effect of transactions on the accounting equation
Learners can apply modern and traditional rules of debit and credit
Learners can journalise transactions and post and balance ledger accounts

lessons.title: Business transactions, source documents and vouchers

scenes.text: Nikhil’s stationery shop sells pens on credit to a school and gets a cash memo for paper bought.
His accountant refuses to record a payment that has no bill.
Every entry needs proof — a source document.

steps.title: Source documents
steps.body: A **source document** is the written proof of a transaction: *cash memo* (cash sale), *invoice/bill* (credit sale, sent by seller), *receipt* (acknowledges cash received), *pay-in-slip* (cash/cheque deposited into bank), *cheque*, *debit note* (sent by buyer when returning goods — debits the supplier), *credit note* (sent by seller when goods are returned — credits the buyer).

steps.title: Accounting vouchers
steps.body:
A **voucher** is prepared from source documents and authorised before entry.

- *Cash vouchers*: debit voucher (cash paid), credit voucher (cash received).
- *Non-cash (transfer) vouchers*: credit purchases, depreciation, etc.
- *Compound vouchers*: one debit with many credits or vice versa.
- Contents: name of firm, date, voucher number, accounts debited and credited, amount, narration, signatures of preparer and authoriser.

steps.title: Solved example 1: Which document?
steps.body: (a) Goods sold for cash ₹800 → cash memo. (b) Goods sold on credit to Ravi ₹5,000 → invoice. (c) Ravi returns goods ₹500 → Ravi sends a *debit note*; we issue a *credit note*. (d) Cash ₹10,000 deposited in bank → pay-in-slip.

steps.title: Solved example 2: Debit or credit voucher?
steps.body: Rent paid in cash ₹4,000 → *debit voucher* (Rent A/c debited, cash paid). Commission received in cash ₹1,200 → *credit voucher* (Commission A/c credited).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing up debit note and credit note: the **buyer** sends the debit note when returning goods.
- Recording a transaction without an authorised voucher.
- Thinking a voucher is the same as a source document — the voucher is prepared *on the basis of* it.

activity.prompt: Match the document to the transaction

quiz.q: A debit note is sent by…
options: buyer to seller when returning goods
quiz.why: A debit note is sent by the buyer to the seller when goods are returned, showing that the seller's account is debited.

quiz.q: Cash deposited into bank is proved by…
quiz.why: The pay-in-slip counterfoil is the proof that cash was deposited into the bank.

quiz.q: A voucher recording one debit and three credits is…
quiz.why: A voucher with one debit and several credits, or the reverse, is a compound voucher, since many accounts are on one side.
Depreciation involves no movement of cash, so it is recorded through a non-cash (transfer) voucher.
An invoice is the bill issued by the seller for a credit sale of goods.

scenes.text: Nikhil’s teacher says, “Whatever happens in your shop, Assets always equal Liabilities plus Capital.”
Nikhil tests it with every transaction in his notebook.
It holds every time — because of dual aspect.

steps.title: The equation
steps.body: **Assets = Liabilities + Capital**  (A = L + C), or **Capital = Assets − Liabilities**. Revenue increases capital; expenses and drawings decrease capital. Every transaction keeps the equation balanced: it may increase both sides, decrease both sides, or change items within one side.

steps.title: Solved example 1: Building the equation
steps.body:
1. Started business with cash ₹1,00,000 → Cash +1,00,000 = Capital +1,00,000.
2. Bought furniture for cash ₹20,000 → Cash −20,000, Furniture +20,000 (one side).
3. Bought goods on credit from Raj ₹30,000 → Stock +30,000 = Creditors +30,000.
4. Sold goods costing ₹10,000 for ₹14,000 cash → Cash +14,000, Stock −10,000 = Capital +4,000 (profit).
5. Paid rent ₹2,000 → Cash −2,000 = Capital −2,000.
6. Withdrew cash ₹3,000 for personal use → Cash −3,000 = Capital −3,000.

**Final**: Cash 89,000 + Furniture 20,000 + Stock 20,000 = **₹1,29,000**; Creditors 30,000 + Capital 99,000 = **₹1,29,000** ✔

steps.title: Solved example 2: Find the missing figure
steps.body: Assets ₹3,40,000; liabilities ₹95,000. Capital = 3,40,000 − 95,000 = **₹2,45,000**. If during the year capital rose to ₹2,80,000 with additional capital ₹10,000 and drawings ₹15,000 → Profit = 2,80,000 − 2,45,000 − 10,000 + 15,000 = **₹40,000**.

steps.title: Effect patterns
steps.body:
- Asset ↑, Asset ↓ (buy furniture for cash)
- Asset ↑, Liability ↑ (credit purchase)
- Asset ↑, Capital ↑ (capital introduced, profit on sale)
- Asset ↓, Liability ↓ (pay creditor)
- Asset ↓, Capital ↓ (expenses, drawings)
- Liability ↑, Capital ↓ (outstanding expense)

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Recording a sale at selling price on the stock side — stock falls by *cost*, the profit goes to capital.
- Forgetting that drawings reduce capital, not liabilities.
- Treating an outstanding expense as an asset.

activity.prompt: Started with cash ₹50,000; bought goods on credit ₹20,000; sold goods costing ₹8,000 for ₹11,000 cash. What is the capital now?

quiz.why: Paying a creditor reduces cash (an asset) and also reduces the creditors (a liability), so both fall.
From A = L + C, liabilities = assets − capital = 5,00,000 − 3,60,000 = ₹1,40,000.

quiz.q: Purchase of machinery on credit affects…
quiz.why: Buying machinery on credit increases an asset (machinery) and a liability (creditor), so assets and liabilities are affected.

quiz.q: Goods costing ₹6,000 sold for ₹9,000 on credit. Capital changes by…
quiz.why: Profit = sale price − cost = 9,000 − 6,000 = ₹3,000, so capital increases by ₹3,000. The sale is on credit, but profit still arises.
Outstanding salary is an expense incurred but not yet paid, so a liability is created and capital falls.

scenes.text: Nikhil opens a ledger and sees two columns: Dr and Cr.
Which account goes on which side?
Two sets of rules tell him — modern and traditional.

steps.title: Modern (accounting equation) approach
steps.body:
Accounts are classified as Assets, Liabilities, Capital, Revenues/Gains, Expenses/Losses.

- **Assets**: increase → debit; decrease → credit.
- **Expenses/Losses**: increase → debit; decrease → credit.
- **Liabilities**: increase → credit; decrease → debit.
- **Capital**: increase → credit; decrease (drawings) → debit.
- **Revenues/Gains**: increase → credit; decrease → debit.

Memory aid: *DEAD CLIC* — Debit: Expenses, Assets, Drawings; Credit: Liabilities, Income, Capital.

steps.title: Traditional (golden) rules
steps.body:
- **Personal accounts** (persons, firms, banks, capital, drawings): Debit the receiver, credit the giver.
- **Real accounts** (assets, cash, goods): Debit what comes in, credit what goes out.
- **Nominal accounts** (expenses, incomes, losses, gains): Debit all expenses and losses, credit all incomes and gains.

Personal accounts include natural (Ravi), artificial (ABC Ltd, SBI) and representative (Outstanding salary, Prepaid rent).

steps.title: Solved example 1: Apply both rules
steps.body:
Bought furniture from Sharma Furnitures on credit ₹15,000.

- Modern: Furniture (asset ↑) Dr; Sharma (liability ↑) Cr.
- Traditional: Furniture (real, comes in) Dr; Sharma (personal, giver) Cr. Same answer.

steps.title: Solved example 2: Analyse
steps.body: Paid wages ₹3,000 in cash → Wages (expense ↑) Dr ₹3,000; Cash (asset ↓) Cr ₹3,000. Received interest ₹800 → Cash Dr ₹800; Interest received (revenue ↑) Cr ₹800.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Debiting capital when the owner introduces money — capital increases, so it is **credited**.
- Treating outstanding salary as nominal — it is a representative *personal* account (liability).
- Forgetting that drawings are debited (they reduce capital).

activity.prompt: An INCREASE in this account is recorded on which side?

quiz.q: An increase in a liability is…
quiz.why: By the rules of debit and credit, an increase in a liability is credited.

quiz.q: “Debit the receiver, credit the giver” applies to…
quiz.why: The rule 'debit the receiver, credit the giver' applies to personal accounts.
Prepaid insurance represents the insurer who owes the benefit of insurance, so it is a representative personal account.
Discount received is a gain, and gains and incomes are credited.

quiz.q: Goods purchased for cash: credit side account?
quiz.why: When goods are bought for cash, Purchases is debited and Cash, which goes out, is credited.

scenes.text: In March, Nikhil records every transaction date-wise in his journal.
Each entry has a debit, a credit and a narration.
Later these will be posted to the ledger.

steps.title: Format of the journal
steps.body: Columns: **Date | Particulars | L.F. (ledger folio) | Debit ₹ | Credit ₹**. The account debited is written first with “Dr.”, the account credited on the next line starting with “To”, then a narration in brackets (“Being …”). A **compound entry** has more than one debit or credit. An **opening entry** brings forward assets and liabilities: Assets A/c Dr; To Liabilities A/c; To Capital A/c.

steps.title: Solved example 1: Journalise (March 2026)
steps.body:
- 1: Started business with cash ₹2,00,000 → Cash A/c Dr 2,00,000; To Capital A/c 2,00,000.
- 3: Deposited into bank ₹1,20,000 → Bank A/c Dr; To Cash A/c 1,20,000.
- 5: Purchased goods from Kiran on credit ₹40,000 → Purchases A/c Dr; To Kiran 40,000.
- 8: Sold goods to Meena on credit ₹25,000 → Meena Dr; To Sales A/c 25,000.
- 12: Paid Kiran by cheque ₹39,200 in full settlement → Kiran Dr 40,000; To Bank A/c 39,200; To Discount Received A/c 800.
- 15: Goods ₹2,000 taken for personal use → Drawings A/c Dr 2,000; To Purchases A/c 2,000.
- 20: Goods ₹3,000 distributed as free samples → Advertisement A/c Dr; To Purchases A/c 3,000.
- 31: Salary outstanding ₹6,000 → Salary A/c Dr; To Outstanding Salary A/c 6,000.

steps.title: Solved example 2: Purchase with trade discount and GST
steps.body:
Bought goods list price ₹50,000, trade discount 10%, CGST 6% and SGST 6%, on credit from Vimal.

- Step 1: Net price = 45,000. CGST = 2,700; SGST = 2,700.
- Step 2: Purchases A/c Dr 45,000; Input CGST A/c Dr 2,700; Input SGST A/c Dr 2,700; To Vimal 50,400.

steps.title: Special entries to know
steps.body:
- Goods lost by fire ₹5,000, insurance claim admitted ₹3,000 → Loss by Fire A/c Dr 2,000; Insurance Claim (Insurance Co.) A/c Dr 3,000; To Purchases A/c 5,000.
- Bad debts: Bad Debts A/c Dr; To Debtor.
- Interest on capital: Interest on Capital A/c Dr; To Capital A/c.
- Depreciation: Depreciation A/c Dr; To Asset A/c.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing “Goods A/c” — use **Purchases A/c** or **Sales A/c**.
- Recording trade discount in the journal.
- Crediting Stock A/c for goods withdrawn — credit **Purchases A/c**.
- Forgetting the narration or the word “To” on the credit line.

activity.prompt: Complete the journal entry: “Paid rent ₹5,000 by cheque.”

quiz.q: Goods withdrawn by the owner are credited to…
quiz.why: Goods taken by the owner reduce purchases, so Purchases A/c is credited and Drawings A/c debited.

quiz.q: Paid ₹19,600 to Raju in full settlement of ₹20,000. Discount is…
quiz.why: Paying less than the amount due in full settlement gives a gain. The ₹400 saved is credited as Discount Received.

quiz.q: Goods given as free samples are debited to…
quiz.why: Goods given as free samples are a promotional expense, so they are debited to Advertisement.
The opening entry debits the assets and credits liabilities and capital: Assets Dr; To Liabilities; To Capital.
L.F. stands for Ledger Folio, the page number of the ledger account.

scenes.text: The journal is date-wise; the boss asks “How much do we owe Kiran?”
Nikhil has to scan the whole journal.
A ledger account for Kiran would show the answer at once.

steps.title: Ledger and its format
steps.body:
The **ledger** is the principal book: it contains all accounts. Each account (T-format) has a Debit side (left) and a Credit side (right) with columns *Date | Particulars | J.F. | Amount*.

**Posting rule**: for the account debited in the journal, write on its *debit side* “To <the account credited>”. For the account credited, write on its *credit side* “By <the account debited>”.

steps.title: Balancing an account
steps.body:
Total both sides. Put the difference on the *smaller* side as **“By Balance c/d”** (if debit total is bigger) or **“To Balance c/d”**, make totals equal, then bring it down on the opposite side next period as “To/By Balance b/d”.

- Asset, expense and debtor accounts usually show **debit balances**; liability, capital, income and creditor accounts show **credit balances**.
- Nominal accounts are not balanced but **closed** by transfer to Trading/Profit & Loss Account.

steps.title: Solved example 1: Cash account
steps.body:
Cash introduced ₹2,00,000; deposited in bank ₹1,20,000; cash sales ₹18,000; rent paid ₹5,000.

- Debit side: To Capital 2,00,000; To Sales 18,000 → total 2,18,000.
- Credit side: By Bank 1,20,000; By Rent 5,000 → 1,25,000.
- Difference 93,000 → “By Balance c/d 93,000”. Next period: “To Balance b/d 93,000” (debit balance).

steps.title: Solved example 2: Creditor account
steps.body: Purchased from Kiran on credit ₹40,000 (Kiran credited: “By Purchases 40,000”). Paid by cheque ₹39,200 and discount ₹800 (debit side: “To Bank 39,200; To Discount Received 800”). Totals 40,000 each → **nil balance**, Kiran fully paid.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing the same account name in posting (in Cash A/c write “To Capital”, not “To Cash”).
- Putting balance c/d on the bigger side.
- Balancing nominal accounts instead of closing them.

activity.prompt: Bank A/c: deposits ₹1,20,000 and ₹15,000; cheques issued ₹39,200 and ₹22,000. Closing (debit) balance?

quiz.q: When Cash A/c is debited for capital, the posting in Cash A/c reads…
quiz.why: Cash A/c is debited, so the other side account is named on the debit side with 'To', as in 'To Capital'.
The balance c/d is written on the smaller side, so that the totals of both sides become equal.
A debtor owes money to the business, so the account normally shows a debit balance.
At year-end nominal accounts are closed by transferring them to the Trading and Profit & Loss accounts.

quiz.q: J.F. column in the ledger gives…
quiz.why: The J.F. column in a ledger gives the journal page number of the entry.

questions.q: Debit note is prepared by…
questions.why: A debit note is prepared by the buyer when returning goods to the seller.

questions.q: A = L + C is based on…
questions.why: A = L + C is based on the dual aspect concept.

questions.q: Increase in expense is…
questions.why: An increase in an expense is debited.

questions.q: Assets ₹6,40,000; Liabilities ₹2,15,000. Capital?
questions.why: Capital = assets − liabilities = 6,40,000 − 2,15,000 = ₹4,25,000.

questions.q: Goods ₹4,000 taken by proprietor: entry?
questions.why: Goods taken by the owner reduce purchases and increase drawings: Drawings Dr; To Purchases.

questions.q: Outstanding wages are a…
questions.why: Outstanding wages represent the workers to whom the amount is due, so it is a representative personal account.

questions.q: Paid ₹29,400 to Sohan in full settlement of ₹30,000. Discount received?
questions.why: Discount received = amount due − amount paid = 30,000 − 29,400 = ₹600.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Trade discount is not recorded in books. Reason (R): Only the net price is the transaction value.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true. Only the net price after trade discount is the real transaction value, so trade discount is not recorded.

questions.q: Goods costing ₹20,000 destroyed by fire; insurer admits ₹14,000. Loss by fire debited?
questions.why: The insurer admits ₹14,000, so only the unrecovered part, 20,000 − 14,000 = ₹6,000, is debited as loss by fire.

questions.q: Capital at start ₹2,00,000, at end ₹2,60,000; additional capital ₹30,000; drawings ₹18,000. Profit?
questions.why: Profit = closing capital − opening capital − additional capital + drawings = 2,60,000 − 2,00,000 − 30,000 + 18,000 = ₹48,000.

questions.q: Case: Bought goods list price ₹80,000, trade discount 5%, IGST 12% on credit from Mohit. Amount credited to Mohit?
questions.why: Net price after 5% trade discount = 80,000 − 4,000 = 76,000. IGST at 12% = 9,120. Mohit is credited with 76,000 + 9,120 = ₹85,120.

questions.q: In the ledger, credit side entries begin with…
questions.why: In a ledger account, entries on the credit side begin with 'By'.

questions.q: Which account normally shows a credit balance?
questions.why: Capital is a source of funds owed to the owner, so it normally has a credit balance.

questions.q: Started with cash ₹80,000; bought goods ₹30,000 on credit; sold goods costing ₹20,000 for ₹26,000 cash; paid creditor ₹10,000. Total assets now?
A compound journal entry has…
options: more than one debit or credit
questions.why: A compound journal entry has more than one debit or more than one credit, for similar transactions on the same date.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Drawings A/c is debited when the owner withdraws cash. Reason (R): Drawings reduce capital.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true. When the owner withdraws cash, capital decreases, and a decrease in capital is a debit, so Drawings A/c is debited.

questions.q: Interest on capital allowed is credited to…
questions.why: Interest on capital allowed to the owner is added to capital, so Capital A/c is credited.

courses.title: Ch 4 · Recording of Transactions – II
courses.summary: Special purpose books: simple and double-column cash book, contra entries, petty cash (imprest), purchases, sales and return books, and the journal proper.
outcomes: Learners can prepare simple and double-column cash books
Learners can record contra entries and recognise an overdraft
Learners can maintain an analytical petty cash book
Learners can prepare purchases, sales and return books and post them

lessons.title: Special purpose books and the simple cash book

story.title: Too many entries for one journal

scenes.text: Nikhil’s shop now has 200 transactions a month.
Writing each in the journal and posting each one separately takes hours.
Accountants split the journal into special purpose (subsidiary) books.

steps.title: Why subdivide the journal
steps.body: Repetitive transactions of the same type are recorded in separate books: **Cash book** (all cash and bank receipts/payments), **Purchases book** (credit purchases of goods), **Purchases return book**, **Sales book** (credit sales of goods), **Sales return book**, **Journal proper** (everything else). Benefits: division of work, specialisation, saves time in posting (totals posted periodically), easier reference and checking.

steps.title: Simple (single-column) cash book
steps.body:
It is a journal *and* a ledger: left (Dr) side for receipts, right (Cr) side for payments. Columns on each side: Date, Particulars, Receipt/Voucher No., L.F., Amount. It always shows a **debit balance or nil** (cash paid cannot exceed cash available).

- Posting: an item on the debit side of the cash book is posted to the *credit* side of the respective ledger account (“By Cash”), and vice versa.

steps.title: Solved example 1: Simple cash book
steps.body:
April 2026: 1 Cash in hand ₹12,000; 4 Cash sales ₹8,500; 7 Paid wages ₹1,800; 10 Received from Sonu ₹4,000; 15 Purchased goods for cash ₹6,000; 22 Paid rent ₹3,000.

- Dr side: Balance b/d 12,000 + Sales 8,500 + Sonu 4,000 = 24,500.
- Cr side: Wages 1,800 + Purchases 6,000 + Rent 3,000 = 10,800.
- **Balance c/d = ₹13,700** (debit balance).

steps.title: Solved example 2: Posting
steps.body: In the cash book above, “To Sonu ₹4,000” on the debit side → Sonu’s account is credited “By Cash 4,000”. “By Rent 3,000” → Rent A/c debited “To Cash 3,000”. No separate Cash A/c is opened in the ledger.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Showing a credit balance in a simple cash book (impossible).
- Recording credit sales in the cash book — they go to the sales book.
- Opening a separate Cash A/c in the ledger when a cash book is kept.

activity.prompt: Opening cash ₹5,000; cash sales ₹7,200; paid salary ₹4,500; bought stationery ₹600; received commission ₹900. Closing cash?

quiz.q: Credit sales of goods are recorded in…
quiz.why: Credit sales of goods are recorded in the sales book.

quiz.q: A simple cash book can show…
quiz.why: A simple cash book can show only a debit balance or nil, because cash payments cannot exceed cash available.
The cash book serves as both a journal (original entry) and a ledger (cash account).

quiz.q: Purchase of furniture on credit is recorded in…
quiz.why: Furniture is not goods for resale, so its credit purchase is recorded in the journal proper, not in the purchases book.

quiz.q: An entry on the debit side of the cash book is posted to the ledger on the…
quiz.why: A debit-side entry in the cash book is posted to the credit side of the other ledger account.

lessons.title: Cash book with bank column and contra entries

story.title: Cash and bank side by side

scenes.text: Nikhil now deposits most takings in the bank and pays suppliers by cheque or UPI.
He wants one book to show both cash in hand and money in bank.
A double-column cash book does that.

steps.title: Double-column cash book
steps.body: Each side has two amount columns: **Cash** and **Bank**. Receipts by cheque/online deposited same day → Bank column (Dr). Payments by cheque/online → Bank column (Cr). The bank column can show a **credit balance** = bank overdraft.

steps.title: Contra entries
steps.body:
A transaction affecting both cash and bank is entered on both sides and marked **“C”** in the L.F. column; it is *not* posted to the ledger.

- Cash deposited into bank: Dr side Bank column “To Cash”; Cr side Cash column “By Bank”.
- Cash withdrawn from bank for office: Dr side Cash column “To Bank”; Cr side Bank column “By Cash”.
- Cheque received and deposited the same day: Bank column directly. If deposited later: first cash column (as cheque in hand), then contra entry.

steps.title: Solved example 1: Double-column cash book
steps.body:
1 May: Cash ₹10,000, Bank ₹40,000. 3: Deposited cash ₹6,000 (C). 6: Paid Arjun by cheque ₹12,000. 10: Cash sales ₹9,000. 15: Withdrew from bank for office ₹5,000 (C). 20: Received cheque from Neha ₹8,000 and deposited same day. 25: Paid electricity bill online ₹2,500.

- Cash: Dr 10,000 + 9,000 + 5,000 = 24,000; Cr 6,000 → **Cash balance ₹18,000**.
- Bank: Dr 40,000 + 6,000 + 8,000 = 54,000; Cr 12,000 + 5,000 + 2,500 = 19,500 → **Bank balance ₹34,500**.

steps.title: Solved example 2: Overdraft
steps.body: Bank balance ₹5,000; cheques issued ₹12,000; no deposits. Bank column Cr total exceeds Dr by ₹7,000 → balance c/d written on the **debit** side; shown as **bank overdraft ₹7,000** (liability).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Posting contra entries to the ledger (they cancel out inside the cash book).
- Recording a cheque received but not yet deposited in the bank column.
- Forgetting that a credit balance in the bank column means overdraft, not an error.

statements.s: Cash deposited into bank is a contra entry.
statements.why: Both sides of the cash book are affected.

statements.s: A bank column can never show a credit balance.
statements.why: A credit balance is an overdraft.

statements.s: Contra entries are posted to the ledger.
Online payment of rent goes to the bank column, credit side.

quiz.q: “C” in the L.F. column of a cash book means…
quiz.why: 'C' in the L.F. column of a cash book marks a contra entry, in which cash and bank columns are both affected.

quiz.q: Withdrawal of cash from bank for office use: debit side column?
quiz.why: Withdrawal of cash from the bank for office use increases cash, so it is entered on the debit side in the cash column. It is a contra entry.

quiz.q: Credit balance in the bank column indicates…
quiz.why: A credit balance in the bank column means the bank has paid more than was deposited, so it shows a bank overdraft.

quiz.q: Cheque received and deposited the same day is entered in…
quiz.why: A cheque received and deposited the same day is entered on the debit side in the bank column.

quiz.q: Cash ₹3,000 deposited: cash balance changes by…
quiz.why: Depositing ₹3,000 cash in the bank reduces the cash balance by ₹3,000.

scenes.text: The office spends small amounts daily: courier, tea for guests, auto fares.
The chief cashier cannot record ₹40 items all day.
A petty cashier gets a fixed “imprest” to manage these.

steps.title: Imprest system
steps.body:
The chief cashier gives the petty cashier a fixed amount (**imprest**), say ₹5,000, at the start of a period. At the end, the petty cashier submits vouchers for the amount spent and is **reimbursed exactly that amount**, so the imprest is restored.

- *Analytical* petty cash book: receipts column on the left, then Date, Particulars, Voucher No., Total payment, and separate columns for Postage, Stationery, Conveyance, Cartage, Refreshment, Sundries, etc.
- Totals of each column are posted to the respective expense accounts periodically.

steps.title: Solved example 1: Analytical petty cash book
steps.body:
Imprest ₹4,000 on 1 June. Payments: postage ₹350, stationery ₹620, taxi fare ₹480, cartage ₹300, tea for staff ₹250, courier ₹200, repairs to chair ₹400.

- Postage 350 + 200 = **550**; Stationery **620**; Conveyance **480**; Cartage **300**; Refreshment **250**; Sundries (repairs) **400**.
- Total spent = **₹2,600**; balance ₹1,400; reimbursement ₹2,600 restores imprest to ₹4,000.

steps.title: Solved example 2: Advantages
steps.body: Saves the chief cashier’s time, gives control (fixed limit, vouchers checked), reduces risk of fraud on small payments, and provides analysis of small expenses.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Reimbursing a round sum instead of exactly the amount spent.
- Paying large items (e.g., purchase of a ₹20,000 computer) through petty cash.
- Posting each tiny payment to the ledger instead of column totals.

activity.prompt: Imprest ₹3,000. Petty expenses: ₹420, ₹380, ₹675, ₹250, ₹125. What amount is reimbursed at period end?

quiz.q: Under imprest system, the petty cashier is reimbursed…
quiz.why: Under the imprest system, the petty cashier is reimbursed exactly the amount spent, which restores the imprest.

quiz.q: Petty cash book is best for…
quiz.why: The petty cash book records small routine expenses like postage and stationery.

quiz.q: Column totals of the petty cash book are posted to…
quiz.why: The column totals of the petty cash book are debited to the respective expense accounts.
Amount spent = imprest − balance left = 5,000 − 1,250 = ₹3,750, so that is the reimbursement.

quiz.q: An analytical petty cash book has separate columns for…
quiz.why: An analytical petty cash book has a separate column for each type of expense.

scenes.text: Nikhil buys notebooks on credit from three wholesalers and sells to five schools on credit.
Some notebooks come back damaged.
Each kind of entry has its own book.

steps.title: Purchases book and purchases return book
steps.body:
- **Purchases (invoice/purchase day) book**: records *credit purchases of goods only*. Columns: Date | Invoice No. | Name of supplier (Particulars) | L.F. | Amount (net of trade discount; GST shown separately). Periodic total → debited to Purchases A/c; each supplier credited.
- **Purchases return (return outwards) book**: goods returned to suppliers on credit; source document: *debit note*. Total credited to Purchases Return A/c; each supplier debited.

steps.title: Sales book and sales return book
steps.body:
- **Sales book**: *credit sales of goods only*. Total credited to Sales A/c; each customer debited.
- **Sales return (return inwards) book**: goods returned by customers; source: *credit note* issued. Total debited to Sales Return A/c; each customer credited.

steps.title: Solved example 1: Purchases book
steps.body:
June: (a) Bought from Om Traders 100 registers @ ₹60, trade discount 10%; (b) from Lal & Co. 50 pens boxes @ ₹200 less 5%; (c) bought a computer on credit from Tech Mart ₹40,000.

- (a) 6,000 − 600 = **5,400**; (b) 10,000 − 500 = **9,500**; total purchases book **₹14,900**.
- (c) is an asset purchase → **journal proper**, not purchases book.
- Ledger: Purchases A/c Dr 14,900; Om Traders Cr 5,400; Lal & Co. Cr 9,500.

steps.title: Solved example 2: With GST
steps.body: Credit sale to Riya Stores: goods ₹20,000 + CGST 9% + SGST 9%. Sales book shows Goods 20,000, CGST 1,800, SGST 1,800, Total 23,600. Posting: Riya Stores Dr 23,600; Sales A/c Cr 20,000; Output CGST Cr 1,800; Output SGST Cr 1,800.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Putting cash purchases or asset purchases in the purchases book.
- Recording the gross (list) price instead of the price after trade discount.
- Debiting Sales A/c for returns instead of Sales Return A/c (both are fine in books, but exams expect the return book totals to go to the Return A/c).

activity.prompt: Which book records it?

items.text: Goods bought on credit from Om
Goods sold on credit to Riya
Goods bought on credit from Lal & Co.

quiz.q: Total of the purchases return book is credited to…
quiz.why: The total of the purchases return book is credited to Purchases Return A/c.

quiz.q: Credit purchase of furniture by a stationery shop goes to…
quiz.why: Furniture bought by a stationery shop is not goods for resale, so it goes to the journal proper.

quiz.q: Sales return book is prepared from…
quiz.why: The sales return book is prepared from credit notes issued to customers (debit notes received from them).

quiz.q: 100 units @ ₹50, trade discount 20%. Entry in sales book?
quiz.why: Gross value = 100 × ₹50 = ₹5,000. Trade discount is not recorded in the books, so the sales book shows the net amount 5,000 − 1,000 = ₹4,000.

quiz.q: Each customer in the sales book is…
quiz.why: Each customer in the sales book owes money to the business, so the customer's account is debited.

lessons.title: Journal proper and posting from subsidiary books

scenes.text: Some entries fit no special book: depreciation, a credit purchase of machinery, a bad debt.
They go into the journal proper.
Then all books are posted to the ledger.

steps.title: Entries in the journal proper
steps.body:
- Opening entry and closing entries.
- Credit purchase/sale of assets.
- Adjustment entries: outstanding/prepaid expenses, accrued income, depreciation, interest on capital, interest on drawings.
- Rectification entries.
- Transfer entries; bad debts; goods withdrawn by owner; goods lost by fire; dishonour of cheques where needed.

steps.title: Solved example 1: Journal proper
steps.body: (a) Bought machinery from Ajay Engineering on credit ₹60,000 → Machinery A/c Dr; To Ajay Engineering 60,000. (b) Mohan, a debtor for ₹5,000, became insolvent and paid 60 paise per rupee → Cash A/c Dr 3,000; Bad Debts A/c Dr 2,000; To Mohan 5,000. (c) Charged depreciation ₹6,000 → Depreciation A/c Dr; To Machinery A/c 6,000.

steps.title: Solved example 2: Posting summary
steps.body: Sales book total ₹48,000 → Sales A/c (Cr) “By Sundry Debtors 48,000”. Purchases book total ₹30,000 → Purchases A/c (Dr) “To Sundry Creditors 30,000”. Individual customers/suppliers are posted daily.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Recording an insolvent debtor’s full amount as bad debt when part was received.
- Using purchases book for machinery bought on credit.
- Forgetting to post the periodic totals of subsidiary books.

activity.prompt: Debtor Mohan owes ₹8,000. He pays 50 paise per rupee. Complete:
activity.text: Cash A/c Dr ___; Bad Debts A/c Dr ___; To Mohan 8,000

quiz.q: Credit purchase of an asset goes to…
quiz.why: Credit purchase of an asset is not a purchase of goods, so it is recorded in the journal proper.
The debtor pays 40% of ₹10,000, so 60% is not recovered, which is ₹6,000 bad debts.
Closing entries are not routine business transactions, so they are made in the journal proper.

quiz.q: Total of sales book is posted to…
quiz.why: The total of the sales book is posted to the credit side of Sales A/c.
Depreciation entry is Depreciation A/c Dr; To Asset A/c. The asset is credited because its value falls.

questions.q: Which book records only credit purchases of goods?
questions.why: The purchases book records only credit purchases of goods.

questions.q: Contra entries affect…
questions.why: Contra entries affect both the cash and bank columns of the cash book.

questions.q: Petty cash book usually follows…
questions.why: The petty cash book usually follows the imprest system.

questions.q: Credit sale of old furniture is entered in…
questions.why: Old furniture is not goods for resale, so its credit sale goes to the journal proper.

questions.q: A credit balance in the bank column means…
questions.why: A credit balance in the bank column means the bank has paid out more than the amount deposited, so it is an overdraft.

questions.q: Opening cash ₹8,000; cash sales ₹15,000; deposited in bank ₹12,000; paid wages ₹2,500. Closing cash?
Imprest ₹6,000; spent ₹4,350. Amount reimbursed?
questions.why: The petty cashier is reimbursed the amount spent, ₹4,350.

questions.q: Assertion (A): A simple cash book cannot have a credit balance. Reason (R): Payments of cash cannot exceed cash available.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true. A simple cash book cannot show a credit balance, since cash payments cannot exceed cash available.

questions.q: Goods returned by a customer are recorded in…
questions.why: Goods returned by a customer are sales returns (return inwards), recorded in the sales return book.

questions.q: 200 items @ ₹45 less 10% trade discount + IGST 12%. Amount in supplier’s account?
questions.why: 200 × 45 = 9,000. Less 10% trade discount (900) gives 8,100. IGST at 12% = 972. Total = ₹9,072.

questions.q: Case: Cash ₹20,000, bank ₹50,000. Deposited ₹15,000; withdrew ₹4,000 for office; cheques issued ₹30,000. Bank balance?
questions.why: Bank balance = 50,000 + 15,000 deposited − 4,000 withdrawn − 30,000 cheques = ₹31,000.

questions.q: The source document for the purchases return book is…
questions.why: The purchases return book is prepared from the debit notes sent to suppliers.

questions.q: Which is NOT an advantage of subsidiary books?
questions.why: Subsidiary books save time, divide work and make reference easier, but they do not remove the need for a ledger.

questions.q: Debtor ₹12,000 becomes insolvent; 35 paise per rupee received. Bad debts?
questions.why: The debtor pays 35 paise per rupee, so 65% is lost: 65% of ₹12,000 = ₹7,800 bad debts.

questions.q: Case: Same month — cash withdrawn ₹10,000 from bank for personal use. This is…
questions.why: Cash taken from the bank for personal use is drawings, not a business contra entry. The entry is Drawings Dr; To Bank.

questions.q: The total of the purchases book is posted to…
questions.why: The total of the purchases book is posted to the debit of Purchases A/c.

courses.title: Ch 5 · Bank Reconciliation Statement
courses.summary: Why the cash book and bank statement differ, and how to prepare a BRS from favourable and overdraft balances, including the amended cash book method.
outcomes: Learners can list timing differences and errors
Learners can prepare a BRS starting from either book
Learners can handle overdraft balances
Learners can prepare an amended cash book and then a BRS

lessons.title: Why cash book and passbook differ

scenes.text: On 31 March Nikhil’s cash book shows ₹52,000 in bank, but the bank statement shows ₹47,500.
Has someone stolen ₹4,500?
Usually not — the difference comes from timing and a few errors.

steps.title: Two records of one account
steps.body: The business keeps the *bank column of the cash book*; the bank keeps the customer’s account and sends a **bank statement / passbook**. A deposit is a *debit* in our cash book but a *credit* in the bank’s books (the bank owes us). So a **favourable balance** is a debit balance in the cash book and a credit balance in the passbook. An **overdraft** is the reverse.

steps.title: Causes of difference
steps.body:
**Timing differences**
- Cheques issued but not yet presented for payment.
- Cheques deposited but not yet collected (credited) by the bank.
- Amounts credited by bank but not known to us: interest allowed, direct deposits by customers, dividends collected.
- Amounts debited by bank not known to us: bank charges, interest on overdraft, direct payments (insurance, EMI standing instructions), cheques dishonoured.

**Errors**: by the business (wrong amount, wrong side, wrong casting) or by the bank.

steps.title: Solved example 1: Identify the effect
steps.body: Cheque issued ₹6,000 to a supplier on 28 March, presented on 3 April. On 31 March: cash book already reduced by 6,000; passbook not yet. → **Passbook balance is ₹6,000 more** than cash book.

steps.title: Solved example 2: Another
steps.body: Bank charged ₹250 for SMS alerts and debit card fee, not recorded in cash book. → Passbook shows **₹250 less** than cash book.

steps.title: Need for BRS
steps.body: A **Bank Reconciliation Statement** explains the difference on a date. It helps detect errors and frauds, ensures recording of bank-originated items, and confirms the correct balance for the balance sheet. It is a *statement*, not an account, and is prepared periodically (e.g., monthly).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking a deposit is a debit in the passbook — for the bank it is a credit.
- Treating BRS as part of the double-entry books.
- Forgetting dishonoured cheques reduce the bank balance.

activity.prompt: Starting from a FAVOURABLE cash book balance, is the item ADDED or LESS to reach the passbook balance?

items.text: Insurance premium paid by bank on standing order

quiz.q: A favourable balance in the passbook is a…
quiz.why: A favourable balance in the passbook is a credit balance, since the bank owes the customer.

quiz.q: Cheques deposited but not collected make the passbook balance…
quiz.why: Cheques deposited but not yet collected have not been credited by the bank, so the passbook balance is lower than the cash book.
A BRS is a statement that explains the difference between the cash book and passbook balances. It is not a ledger account.

quiz.q: Interest on overdraft charged by bank: passbook overdraft is…
quiz.why: Interest on overdraft is debited by the bank, so the passbook overdraft is larger.
A cheque issued but not yet presented is a timing difference, which will be removed when the bank pays it.

lessons.title: Preparing BRS from a favourable balance

scenes.text: Nikhil lists every item causing the difference.
He starts from the cash book balance and adds or subtracts each.
The final figure must equal the passbook balance.

steps.title: Method
steps.body:
Format: *Bank Reconciliation Statement as on 31 March 2026* with columns “Plus items (+)” and “Minus items (−)”.

1. Start: Balance as per cash book (Dr).
2. Add items that make passbook higher: cheques issued not presented; credits by bank not in cash book (interest, direct deposits, collections); errors that understated the cash book.
3. Less items that make passbook lower: cheques deposited not collected; debits by bank not in cash book (charges, direct payments, dishonoured cheques); errors that overstated it.
4. Result = Balance as per passbook.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
Cash book balance ₹52,000 (Dr). (a) Cheques issued not presented ₹9,500. (b) Cheques deposited not collected ₹14,000. (c) Interest credited ₹600. (d) Bank charges ₹350. (e) Direct deposit by a customer ₹2,000. (f) Insurance premium paid by bank ₹2,250.

- Plus: 9,500 + 600 + 2,000 = 12,100.
- Less: 14,000 + 350 + 2,250 = 16,600.
- Passbook balance = 52,000 + 12,100 − 16,600 = **₹47,500** ✔

steps.title: Solved example 2: Starting from the passbook
steps.body:
Passbook balance ₹30,000 (Cr). Cheques issued not presented ₹4,000; cheques deposited not collected ₹2,500; bank charges ₹200.

- Reverse the signs: Less cheques not presented 4,000; Add cheques not collected 2,500; Add bank charges 200.
- Cash book balance = 30,000 − 4,000 + 2,500 + 200 = **₹28,700**.

steps.title: Errors
steps.body:
- A cheque of ₹1,800 received was recorded as ₹1,080 in the cash book → cash book understated by 720 → **add** 720.
- Payment side of cash book overcast by ₹100 → cash book balance understated → **add** 100.
- Bank wrongly debited our account ₹500 → passbook lower → **less** 500 (from cash book side).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the same signs when starting from the passbook — every sign reverses.
- Including items that appear in *both* records (they cause no difference).
- Treating “cheques issued” and “cheques deposited” the same way.

activity.prompt: Cash book balance ₹25,000 (Dr). Cheques issued not presented ₹3,500; cheques deposited not credited ₹6,000; bank charges ₹150; interest credited ₹400. Passbook balance?

quiz.q: Starting from cash book (Dr), cheques issued but not presented are…
quiz.why: Cheques issued but not yet presented have reduced the cash book but not the passbook, so they are added to the cash book balance to get the passbook balance.
