quiz.q: Starting from passbook (Cr), bank charges are…
quiz.why: Bank charges are debited in the passbook but not yet in the cash book. Starting from the passbook, they are added to find the cash book balance.

quiz.q: Cheque received ₹2,300 recorded as ₹3,200 in cash book. From cash book balance you…
quiz.why: The cash book shows ₹900 too much (3,200 instead of 2,300), so it is overstated and ₹900 is deducted.

quiz.q: Items recorded in both books are…
quiz.why: Items recorded in both books cause no difference, so they are ignored in a BRS.

quiz.q: Cash book ₹10,000; only difference: cheque deposited ₹3,000 not collected. Passbook?
quiz.why: The cheque of ₹3,000 is not yet credited by the bank, so the passbook balance is 10,000 − 3,000 = ₹7,000.

lessons.title: BRS when there is an overdraft

scenes.text: Riya’s firm uses an overdraft facility; its cash book shows a *credit* balance of ₹18,000.
Her BRS must start with a minus figure.
Same logic — just read the signs carefully.

steps.title: Treat overdraft as a negative
steps.body:
Simplest approach: write the overdraft as **minus** (or in the minus column), apply the same add/less rules as for a favourable balance, and the result will be negative = overdraft as per passbook.

Starting from overdraft as per cash book:
- **Add** (reduces overdraft): cheques issued but not presented; credits by bank not in cash book.
- **Less** (increases overdraft): cheques deposited not collected; bank charges; interest on overdraft; direct payments.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
Overdraft as per cash book ₹18,000. Cheques issued not presented ₹5,000. Cheques deposited not collected ₹7,500. Interest on overdraft ₹900. Dividend collected by bank ₹1,200.

- Start −18,000.
- Add 5,000 + 1,200 = +6,200 → −11,800.
- Less 7,500 + 900 = −8,400 → −20,200.
- **Overdraft as per passbook ₹20,200**.

steps.title: Solved example 2: From passbook overdraft
steps.body:
Overdraft as per passbook ₹12,000. Cheques issued not presented ₹3,000; cheques deposited not credited ₹4,500; bank charges ₹300.

- Start −12,000. Cheques not presented: passbook overdraft is smaller than cash book’s → **less** 3,000 → −15,000.
- Deposits not credited: passbook overdraft bigger → **add** 4,500 → −10,500.
- Bank charges not in cash book → **add** 300 → −10,200.
- **Overdraft as per cash book ₹10,200.**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Starting with a positive figure when the balance is an overdraft.
- Getting a positive result and still calling it overdraft — if the final figure turns positive, it is a favourable balance.
- Forgetting interest on overdraft (a bank debit).

activity.prompt: Overdraft as per cash book ₹10,000. Cheques issued not presented ₹4,000; bank charges ₹500 not recorded. Overdraft as per passbook (enter as positive amount)?

quiz.q: Overdraft as per cash book is a…
quiz.why: An overdraft per cash book is a credit balance, as the bank has given us money.

quiz.q: Starting from cash book overdraft, interest on overdraft is…
quiz.why: Interest on overdraft raises the overdraft, so it is deducted (the negative balance becomes larger).

quiz.q: Starting from cash book overdraft ₹5,000, cheques issued not presented ₹7,000 → passbook shows…
quiz.why: Overdraft −5,000 plus cheques issued not presented 7,000 gives +2,000, so the passbook shows a favourable balance of ₹2,000.
An overdraft in the passbook is a debit balance, since the customer owes the bank.
An easy way for overdraft BRS is to treat the overdraft as a negative balance, and use signs consistently.

lessons.title: Amended cash book and then BRS

scenes.text: Exam question: “Prepare an amended cash book and then a BRS.”
First, record in the cash book everything the bank did that we missed, and correct our own errors.
Then only timing items remain for the BRS.

steps.title: Two-stage method
steps.body:
**Stage 1 – Amended cash book** (bank column): post items that the business should record — bank charges, interest credited/debited, direct deposits/payments, dishonoured cheques, own errors. Find the *corrected* balance (this goes to the balance sheet).

**Stage 2 – BRS**: start with the amended balance and adjust only for items that the *bank* has not yet recorded (cheques not presented, cheques not collected) and bank errors.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
Cash book Dr ₹40,000. Bank charges ₹300; interest credited ₹800; direct payment of electricity ₹1,500; customer’s cheque ₹2,000 dishonoured (not in cash book); cheques issued not presented ₹6,000; cheques deposited not collected ₹4,200.

- Amended cash book: 40,000 + 800 − 300 − 1,500 − 2,000 = **₹37,000**.
- BRS: 37,000 + 6,000 − 4,200 = **₹38,800** = passbook balance.

steps.title: Solved example 2: Error in own book
steps.body: Cash book Dr ₹15,000 includes a cheque deposited ₹5,600 that was recorded as ₹6,500. Amended balance = 15,000 − 900 = **₹14,100**. This error does not appear again in the BRS because it is now corrected.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Adjusting the same item in both the amended cash book and the BRS.
- Putting cheques not presented into the amended cash book (the business already recorded them correctly).
- Using the unamended balance in the balance sheet.

activity.prompt: Order the steps for “amended cash book + BRS”
items: Take the unadjusted cash book balance
Record bank-originated items missing from the cash book
Correct errors in the cash book
Find the amended cash book balance
Start the BRS with the amended balance
Adjust for cheques not presented/not collected and bank errors

quiz.q: Bank charges in a two-stage question are adjusted in…
quiz.why: Bank charges must be recorded by the business, so they are adjusted in the amended cash book, not just shown in the BRS.

quiz.q: Cheques issued not presented are adjusted in…
quiz.why: Cheques issued but not presented are timing differences caused by the bank, so they are shown only in the BRS.

quiz.q: The balance shown in the balance sheet is…
quiz.why: The balance sheet shows the bank balance as per the amended cash book, which is the correct figure.

quiz.q: Cash book Dr ₹20,000; interest credited ₹500; bank charges ₹100. Amended balance?
quiz.why: Amended balance = 20,000 + 500 interest − 100 charges = ₹20,400.

quiz.q: A dishonoured cheque not recorded: in the amended cash book it is…
quiz.why: A dishonoured cheque reduces the bank balance, so in the amended cash book it is credited.

questions.q: A favourable cash book balance is a…
questions.why: A favourable balance as per the cash book is a debit balance.

questions.q: BRS is prepared by…
questions.why: The account holder (the business) prepares the BRS.

questions.q: Interest allowed by bank not in cash book (from cash book balance):
questions.why: Interest allowed by the bank is not yet in the cash book, so starting from the cash book balance it is added.

questions.q: Cheque dishonoured not recorded (from cash book balance):
questions.why: A dishonoured cheque not yet recorded lowers the passbook balance, so starting from the cash book balance it is deducted (less).

questions.q: Which is NOT a cause of difference?
questions.why: Cash sales do not touch the bank account, so they are not a cause of difference.

questions.q: Cash book Dr ₹30,000; cheques issued not presented ₹5,000; cheques deposited not credited ₹8,000. Passbook?
questions.why: Passbook = 30,000 + 5,000 (issued not presented) − 8,000 (deposited not credited) = ₹27,000.

questions.q: Passbook Cr ₹45,000; cheques issued not presented ₹6,000; bank charges ₹400. Cash book balance?
questions.why: Cash book = passbook 45,000 − 6,000 (issued not presented) + 400 (bank charges) = ₹39,400.

questions.q: Assertion (A): A deposit is credited in the passbook. Reason (R): For the bank, the customer’s deposit is a liability.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true. A deposit is a liability of the bank to the customer, so the bank credits it in the passbook.

questions.q: Overdraft per cash book ₹20,000; cheques deposited not credited ₹3,000; interest on OD ₹600. Overdraft per passbook?
questions.why: The bank's overdraft is higher than ours: 20,000 + 3,000 (cheques not credited) + 600 (interest) = ₹23,600.

questions.q: Cheque received ₹4,700 recorded in cash book as ₹7,400. Starting with cash book Dr ₹50,000 (only item):
questions.why: The cash book shows 7,400 instead of 4,700, which is ₹2,700 too much. Deducting gives 50,000 − 2,700 = ₹47,300.

questions.q: Case: Amended cash book requires cash book Dr ₹25,000 + interest ₹300 − charges ₹150 − direct EMI ₹5,000. Amended balance?
Case (continued): cheques issued not presented ₹2,000 and cheques deposited not collected ₹3,500. Passbook balance?
questions.why: Passbook = 20,150 + 2,000 (issued not presented) − 3,500 (deposited not collected) = ₹18,650.

questions.q: Payment side of the cash book undercast by ₹200 (from cash book balance):
questions.why: The payment side is undercast by ₹200, so the cash book balance is overstated, and 200 is deducted.

questions.q: A bank statement shows a debit balance. It means…
questions.why: A debit balance in a bank statement means the customer owes the bank, so it is an overdraft.

questions.q: Overdraft per cash book ₹8,000; cheques issued not presented ₹10,000. Passbook shows…
questions.why: Overdraft −8,000 plus cheques not presented 10,000 gives +2,000, so the passbook shows a favourable balance of ₹2,000.

questions.q: The main purpose of BRS is to…
options: explain the difference between two balances
questions.why: The main purpose of a BRS is to explain the difference between the cash book and passbook balances.

school-c11-accountancy-b.title: Class 11 Accountancy (Part B)
school-c11-accountancy-b.description: Every chapter of Class 11 Financial Accounting, from the accounting equation to final accounts, with solved entries, ledgers and chapter tests.

courses.title: Ch 6 · Trial Balance and Rectification of Errors
courses.summary: Preparing a trial balance, classifying errors, using a suspense account, rectifying errors before and after final accounts and finding their effect on profit.
outcomes: Learners can prepare a trial balance by the balance method
Learners can classify errors and say whether TB is affected
Learners can pass rectification entries with and without suspense account
Learners can compute corrected profit

scenes.text: At year-end Nikhil lists every ledger balance in two columns.
Debits total ₹4,85,000 and credits ₹4,85,000 — they agree!
Does that mean there are no errors at all? Not necessarily.

steps.title: What a trial balance is
steps.body:
A **trial balance** is a *statement* of the debit and credit balances (or totals) of all ledger accounts on a date, prepared to check the arithmetical accuracy of posting and balancing. Because every debit has an equal credit, totals should agree.

- Objectives: check arithmetical accuracy, help locate errors, summary for preparing financial statements.
- Methods: **balance method** (most common), totals method, totals-cum-balances method.

steps.title: Which side?
steps.body:
**Debit balances**: assets (cash, bank, machinery, debtors, stock opening, bills receivable), expenses and losses (purchases, wages, rent, salaries, carriage inwards/outwards, bad debts, discount allowed), drawings, sales return.

**Credit balances**: capital, liabilities (creditors, bills payable, loans, bank overdraft), incomes and gains (sales, commission received, discount received, interest received), purchases return, provisions (doubtful debts, depreciation).

steps.title: Solved example 2: Find the missing capital
steps.body: Debit total ₹6,72,000; credit items excluding capital ₹4,10,000. Capital = 6,72,000 − 4,10,000 = **₹2,62,000**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Putting closing stock in the trial balance when it is an adjustment (only *opening* stock normally appears, unless adjusted purchases are given).
- Placing purchases return on the debit side or sales return on the credit side.
- Thinking an agreed trial balance proves the books are error-free.

activity.prompt: Debit or credit balance in the trial balance?

quiz.why: A trial balance is a statement of the debit and credit balances of ledger accounts, not an account.
Discount received is a gain, so its balance is shown on the credit side.

quiz.q: Most common method of preparing TB is…
quiz.why: The most common method of preparing a trial balance is the balance method, which lists each ledger balance.

options: arithmetical accuracy only to an extent
quiz.why: Agreement of the trial balance shows arithmetical accuracy only to an extent, since some errors do not affect it.
Drawings reduce capital, so they have a debit balance and appear on the debit side.

scenes.text: Nikhil’s helper forgot to record a credit sale completely.
The trial balance still agreed.
Some errors show up in the trial balance; others hide.

steps.title: Classification
steps.body:
- **Errors of commission**: wrong recording, posting, casting (totalling), carrying forward or balancing — e.g., posting ₹540 as ₹450, posting to the wrong side, undercasting the sales book.
- **Errors of omission**: *complete* omission (transaction not recorded at all — TB not affected) or *partial* omission (posted to one account only — TB affected).
- **Errors of principle**: violating accounting principles, e.g., treating capital expenditure as revenue (machine purchase debited to Purchases A/c).
- **Compensating errors**: two or more errors that cancel each other (Ram’s A/c debited ₹100 short and Shyam’s A/c debited ₹100 excess).

steps.title: Affects TB or not?
steps.body:
**Not disclosed by TB** (one-sided errors are absent): complete omission, error of principle, compensating errors, recording wrong amount in a book of original entry, posting to the wrong account but on the correct side.

**Disclosed by TB** (one-sided errors): wrong casting of a subsidiary book, posting wrong amount, posting to the wrong side, partial omission, wrong balancing, omitting a balance from TB.

steps.title: Solved example 1: Classify
steps.body: (a) Furniture purchase ₹8,000 debited to Purchases A/c → principle, TB agrees. (b) Sales book overcast by ₹1,000 → commission, one-sided, TB disagrees. (c) Credit sale to Rohit ₹3,000 not recorded at all → complete omission, TB agrees. (d) Cash paid to Sita ₹500 debited to Gita → commission (wrong account, correct side), TB agrees.

steps.title: Solved example 2: Effect on TB
steps.body: Wages ₹2,500 posted to the credit side of Wages A/c → debit total short by 2,500 and credit total up by 2,500 → **difference ₹5,000** (credit excess).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying posting to the wrong side causes a difference of the amount only — it is **double** the amount.
- Classifying “posting to the wrong person on the correct side” as affecting TB.
- Calling a complete omission a partial one.

activity.prompt: Will the trial balance disagree?

items.text: Credit purchase not recorded at all
Rent posted to credit side of Rent A/c
Cash paid to Mohan not posted to his account

quiz.q: Purchase of machinery debited to Purchases A/c is an error of…
quiz.why: Debiting machinery purchase to Purchases A/c treats capital expenditure as revenue, which is an error of principle.

quiz.q: Posting ₹700 to the wrong side causes a TB difference of…
quiz.why: Posting ₹700 on the wrong side makes the debit and credit totals differ by twice the amount, ₹1,400.
A complete omission leaves both the debit and credit missing, so it does not affect the trial balance.

quiz.q: Errors that cancel each other are…
quiz.why: Errors that cancel each other's effect on the trial balance are compensating errors.
Undercasting of the purchases book affects only Purchases A/c, so it is a one-sided error.

scenes.text: The trial balance differs by ₹1,800 and final accounts are due tomorrow.
The accountant puts ₹1,800 into a Suspense Account so statements can be prepared.
When errors are found, the suspense account is cleared.

steps.title: Rectification before the trial balance
steps.body: If an error is found before the TB: two-sided errors are corrected by a journal entry; one-sided errors are corrected by a note/entry in the affected account only (e.g., “By error in casting 500”).

steps.title: Suspense account
steps.body: If the TB disagrees and errors cannot be located, the difference is put in a **Suspense A/c** (debit side if debits are short, credit side if credits are short). Later, each one-sided error is rectified by a journal entry using Suspense A/c as the other side. When all are found, Suspense A/c closes. Two-sided errors never touch Suspense A/c.

steps.title: Solved example 1: Work out the difference, then rectify
steps.body:
Errors found after the TB disagreed:

- (a) Purchases book undercast ₹1,000 → debit side short by 1,000.
- (b) Goods ₹600 returned by Kamal posted to the *debit* side of his account (should be credit) → debit side 600 too high and credit side 600 too low.
- (c) Wages ₹1,200 not posted to Wages A/c → debit side short by 1,200.

**Step 1 – Net difference**: debit side −1,000 + 600 − 1,200 = −1,600; credit side −600. Debits are short by 1,600 − 600 = **₹1,000** → Suspense A/c shown on the **debit** side ₹1,000.

**Step 2 – Entries**: (a) Purchases A/c Dr 1,000; To Suspense 1,000. (b) Suspense A/c Dr 1,200; To Kamal 1,200. (c) Wages A/c Dr 1,200; To Suspense 1,200.

**Step 3 – Suspense A/c**: Dr: Difference in TB 1,000 + Kamal 1,200 = 2,200. Cr: Purchases 1,000 + Wages 1,200 = 2,200. It closes ✔

steps.title: Solved example 2: Mixed one-sided and two-sided errors
steps.body:
- (a) Sales book undercast ₹700 → credit side short 700.
- (b) Cash paid to Arun ₹1,800 posted to his account as ₹600 → debit side short 1,200.
- (c) Repairs ₹3,000 debited to Machinery A/c → two-sided error, TB not affected.

**Step 1**: Debits short 1,200, credits short 700 → debits short by **₹500** → Suspense A/c debit ₹500.

**Step 2**: (a) Suspense Dr 700; To Sales 700. (b) Arun Dr 1,200; To Suspense 1,200. (c) Repairs Dr 3,000; To Machinery 3,000 (no suspense).

**Step 3 – Suspense A/c**: Dr: Difference 500 + Sales 700 = 1,200; Cr: Arun 1,200 → closes ✔. Tip: if your Suspense A/c does not close, recheck the side of each error.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using Suspense A/c for two-sided errors (e.g., error of principle).
- Rectifying a wrong-side posting with only the original amount instead of double.
- Not preparing the Suspense A/c to check that it closes.

activity.prompt: Rent ₹2,000 posted to the credit side of Rent A/c (TB disagreed). Rectification:
activity.text: Rent A/c Dr ___; To Suspense A/c ___

quiz.why: A suspense account is used for one-sided errors, which make the trial balance disagree.
Furniture debited to Purchases is a two-sided error, so no suspense is needed: Furniture Dr; To Purchases.

quiz.q: TB debit total short by ₹600. Suspense appears on…
quiz.why: If the debit total is short by ₹600, the difference is placed in suspense on the debit side to equalise the totals.
Sales are overstated by ₹400, so Sales is debited and Suspense is credited: Sales Dr; To Suspense.

quiz.q: Salary ₹1,500 posted to Wages A/c. Rectification uses suspense?
quiz.why: Salary posted to Wages is the right side but the wrong account, so it is two-sided, and no suspense is needed.

lessons.title: Rectification after final accounts and effect on profit

scenes.text: In May, after accounts are closed, Nikhil discovers that ₹5,000 of repairs was debited to Machinery A/c last year.
Last year’s profit was overstated.
Nominal-account corrections now go through Profit & Loss Adjustment A/c.

steps.title: Effect of errors on profit
steps.body:
- Revenue expense debited to an asset (or capital expenditure debited to expense) changes profit.
- An item over-debited to an expense, or under-credited to income, **understates** profit; and vice versa.
- Errors between personal/real accounts only (e.g., wrong debtor) do **not** affect profit.

steps.title: After final accounts
steps.body:
In the next period, nominal accounts of the old year are closed, so corrections affecting them are made through **Profit & Loss Adjustment A/c** (balance transferred to Capital A/c).

- Example: Last year’s sales of ₹2,000 to Ravi not recorded → Ravi Dr 2,000; To P&L Adjustment A/c 2,000.

steps.title: Solved example 1: Net effect on profit
steps.body:
Profit before rectification ₹80,000. Errors: (a) Repairs ₹5,000 debited to Machinery; (b) Purchases book undercast ₹1,200; (c) Commission received ₹800 credited to Rent Received (both incomes).

- (a) Expense omitted → profit overstated → −5,000.
- (b) Purchases understated → profit overstated → −1,200.
- (c) Both are incomes → no effect.
- **Corrected profit = ₹73,800**.

steps.title: Solved example 2: Wages for installation
steps.body: Wages ₹4,000 for installing a new machine debited to Wages A/c → rectify: Machinery A/c Dr 4,000; To Wages A/c 4,000. Profit was **understated** by ₹4,000; corrected profit increases.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Changing profit for errors between two personal accounts.
- Forgetting that undercasting an expense overstates profit.
- Using nominal accounts directly in next-year rectification instead of P&L Adjustment A/c.

activity.prompt: Profit ₹60,000. Errors: furniture ₹6,000 debited to Purchases; sales return ₹1,000 not recorded in Sales Return A/c (debtor credited correctly). Corrected profit?

quiz.q: Machinery purchase debited to Purchases understates profit?
quiz.why: Machinery debited to Purchases overstates expenses, so profit is understated.

quiz.q: Cash received from Rahul credited to Rohit affects profit?
quiz.why: Posting to the wrong personal account does not change any income or expense, so profit is unaffected.

quiz.q: After closing books, nominal account corrections go through…
quiz.why: After the books are closed, corrections affecting nominal accounts are routed through the P&L Adjustment Account.

quiz.q: Sales book overcast by ₹900: profit was…
quiz.why: If the sales book is overcast, sales are too high, so profit is overstated by ₹900.

quiz.q: Rent paid ₹3,000 debited to Landlord’s personal A/c: profit is…
quiz.why: Rent debited to the landlord's personal account leaves the expense out, so profit is overstated by ₹3,000.

questions.q: Trial balance checks…
questions.why: The trial balance checks the arithmetical accuracy of the books, that is, whether total debits equal total credits.

questions.q: Sales return appears on the…
questions.why: Sales return reduces sales and has a debit balance, so it appears on the debit side.

questions.q: Which error is NOT disclosed by TB?
questions.why: An error of principle is two-sided, with equal debit and credit, so the trial balance does not disclose it.

questions.q: A difference in TB is temporarily placed in…
questions.why: A difference in the trial balance is temporarily placed in the Suspense A/c.

questions.q: Credit sale ₹4,000 to Mohan recorded in purchases book. Rectification:
options: Mohan Dr 8,000; To Purchases 4,000; To Sales 4,000
questions.why: Mohan was wrongly credited ₹4,000 instead of being debited. Correcting needs: Mohan Dr 8,000; To Purchases 4,000; To Sales 4,000.

questions.q: Posting ₹960 as ₹690 to the debit of an account; TB difference?
questions.why: The debit was posted as ₹690 instead of ₹960, so the debit side is short by ₹270.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Agreement of TB is not a conclusive proof of accuracy. Reason (R): Some errors do not affect the TB.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true. Some errors do not affect the trial balance, so its agreement is not conclusive proof of accuracy.

questions.q: Debit total ₹5,40,000; credits except capital ₹3,10,000. Capital?
questions.why: Capital = debit total − other credits = 5,40,000 − 3,10,000 = ₹2,30,000.

questions.q: Purchase of furniture ₹12,000 debited to Purchases. Profit effect?
questions.why: Furniture debited to Purchases overstates expenses by ₹12,000, so profit is understated by ₹12,000.

questions.q: Profit ₹1,00,000; repairs ₹7,000 debited to Building; sales book undercast ₹2,000. Corrected profit?
questions.why: Repairs wrongly debited to Building: profit was overstated by 7,000. Sales undercast: profit was understated by 2,000. Corrected profit = 1,00,000 − 7,000 + 2,000 = ₹95,000.

questions.q: Compensating errors are…
questions.why: Compensating errors are errors whose effects cancel each other, so the trial balance still agrees.

questions.q: Case: Discount allowed ₹300 posted to the credit side of Discount A/c. Rectification?
questions.why: Discount allowed should be debited. It was credited, so the correction needs double the amount: Discount Dr 600; To Suspense 600.

questions.q: Next year: last year’s repairs ₹5,000 were debited to Machinery A/c. Entry?
questions.why: After the books are closed, nominal accounts cannot be used, so P&L Adjustment Dr; To Machinery ₹5,000.

questions.q: Which balance is shown on the credit side of TB?
questions.why: A provision for depreciation is a credit balance. Prepaid rent, bad debts and carriage outwards are debits.

questions.q: Errors: Purchases book undercast ₹1,000; commission received ₹400 not posted. Difference on TB?
options: Debit short 1,000; credit short 400 → net debit short ₹600
questions.why: Purchases undercast makes the debit side short by 1,000. Commission not posted makes the credit side short by 400. Net: debit short by ₹600.

questions.q: Goods taken by owner ₹2,000 not recorded at all is an error of…
questions.why: Goods taken by the owner not recorded at all is a complete omission, since both the debit and the credit are missing.

courses.title: Ch 7 · Depreciation, Provisions and Reserves
courses.summary: Depreciation concepts and factors, straight line and written down value methods, two recording methods, disposal of assets, and the difference between provisions and reserves.
outcomes: Learners can compute depreciation by SLM and WDV including part years
Learners can record depreciation with and without a provision account
Learners can calculate profit or loss on disposal of assets
Learners can distinguish provisions, revenue reserves and capital reserves

story.title: The delivery van that loses value

scenes.text: Nikhil buys a van for ₹5,00,000. After five years of deliveries it is worth about ₹1,00,000.
The ₹4,00,000 fall happened slowly while it earned revenue.
Charging this fall year by year is depreciation.

steps.title: Meaning
steps.body: **Depreciation** is the systematic allocation of the depreciable cost of a tangible fixed asset over its useful life. It is a *decline in the book value* due to use, passage of time or obsolescence. It is a *non-cash* expense. For intangible assets it is called **amortisation**; for natural resources (mines, quarries) **depletion**.

steps.title: Causes and need
steps.body:
**Causes**: wear and tear due to use; expiry of legal rights (lease, patent); obsolescence (new technology); abnormal factors (accident, flood).

**Need**: correct profit (matching cost with revenue), true and fair balance sheet, legal and tax requirements, and helps *retain funds* for replacement (since profit available for drawings is reduced).

steps.title: Factors in calculating depreciation
steps.body:
- **Cost of asset** (including freight, installation, transit insurance).
- **Estimated useful life** (years or units/hours).
- **Estimated net residual (scrap) value**.
- **Depreciable cost** = Cost − Residual value.

steps.title: Solved example 1: Depreciable cost
steps.body:
Machine price ₹1,80,000; freight ₹8,000; installation ₹12,000; scrap value after 8 years ₹20,000.

- Cost = 2,00,000.
- Depreciable cost = 2,00,000 − 20,000 = **₹1,80,000**.
- Annual depreciation (straight line) = 1,80,000 ÷ 8 = **₹22,500**.

steps.title: Solved example 2: Name the term
steps.body: A coal mine’s value falls as coal is extracted → *depletion*. A ₹10 lakh patent written off over 10 years → *amortisation*. A computer → *depreciation*.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying depreciation creates cash or is a source of funds — it only reduces profit available for withdrawal.
- Ignoring installation costs.
- Charging depreciation on land (land normally is not depreciated) or on current assets.

activity.prompt: Match the term
pairs: Expected scrap value at end of life

quiz.why: Depreciation is a non-cash expense, as no cash is paid out when it is charged.

quiz.q: Cost ₹1,50,000; scrap ₹10,000; life 7 years. SLM depreciation?
quiz.why: SLM depreciation = (cost − scrap) ÷ life = (1,50,000 − 10,000) ÷ 7 = ₹20,000.
Writing off an intangible asset like a patent is called amortisation.

quiz.q: Which is NOT a cause of depreciation?
quiz.why: A rise in market price is not a cause of depreciation. Wear and tear, expiry of lease and obsolescence are.
Depreciation is charged to match the cost of using an asset with the revenue it helps earn, so it follows the matching concept.

lessons.title: Straight line and written down value methods

story.title: Two ways to spread the cost

scenes.text: Nikhil’s accountant asks: equal charge every year, or bigger charge early?
Straight line gives the same amount; written down value gives a falling amount.
Indian income-tax rules use WDV; companies may use either.

steps.title: Straight Line Method (SLM)
steps.body:
Also called *fixed instalment / original cost method*.

**Annual depreciation = (Cost − Residual value) ÷ Useful life**, or **Rate % × Cost**.

- Rate = Annual depreciation ÷ Cost × 100.
- Merits: simple; asset can be written down to scrap value. Demerits: ignores higher repairs in later years (total charge rises over time), ignores pattern of use.

steps.title: Written Down Value (WDV) Method
steps.body:
Also called *reducing / diminishing balance method*. A fixed rate is applied on the **opening book value** each year.

- Depreciation falls every year; repairs rise → total charge is more even.
- Book value never becomes zero.
- Accepted by income-tax law.

steps.title: Solved example 1: SLM with part year
SLM vs WDV at a glance
steps.body:
- Basis: cost (SLM) vs opening book value (WDV).
- Amount: same every year vs decreasing.
- Book value: can reach zero/scrap vs never zero.
- Suitable: patents, leases, assets with steady use (SLM) vs plant, vehicles with rising repairs (WDV).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Applying WDV rate on the original cost every year.
- Forgetting to count months for an asset bought mid-year.
- Deducting residual value before applying a WDV rate (the rate already reflects it).

activity.prompt: Cost ₹1,00,000, WDV rate 20%. What is the depreciation for Year 3?

quiz.q: Under WDV, depreciation each year is…
quiz.why: Under WDV, depreciation is a fixed percentage of the reducing book value, so it decreases each year.

quiz.q: Cost ₹80,000; scrap ₹8,000; life 6 years. SLM rate on cost?
quiz.why: Annual depreciation = (80,000 − 8,000) ÷ 6 = 12,000. As a percentage of cost, 12,000 ÷ 80,000 = 15%.

quiz.q: Asset ₹60,000 bought 1 July; 10% SLM; year ends 31 March. First year depreciation?
quiz.why: Annual depreciation 6,000 for 9 months (1 July to 31 March) = ₹4,500.

quiz.q: Income tax in India generally uses…
quiz.why: The Income Tax Act generally uses the WDV method on blocks of assets.
Under WDV the rate is applied to a reducing balance, so the book value never becomes zero.

story.title: Where does depreciation sit in the ledger?

scenes.text: One firm reduces the Machinery A/c every year; another keeps machinery at cost and builds up a separate provision.
Both are correct — they just present it differently.
Let us record both.

steps.title: Method 1: Charging to asset account
steps.body:
- Depreciation A/c Dr; To Asset A/c.
- Depreciation A/c is closed: P&L A/c Dr; To Depreciation A/c.
- Asset shown in balance sheet at *written down value*.

steps.title: Method 2: Provision for depreciation (accumulated depreciation) account
steps.body:
- Depreciation A/c Dr; To Provision for Depreciation A/c.
- P&L A/c Dr; To Depreciation A/c.
- Asset stays at **original cost**; provision accumulates (credit balance). Balance sheet shows Cost − Accumulated depreciation.
- On sale: Provision for Depreciation A/c Dr; To Asset A/c (transfer accumulated amount on the sold asset).

steps.title: Solved example 1: Method 1 ledger
steps.body:
Machinery bought 1 April 2024 ₹1,00,000; SLM 10%.

- 2024-25: Machinery A/c: To Bank 1,00,000; By Depreciation 10,000; By Balance c/d 90,000.
- 2025-26: To Balance b/d 90,000; By Depreciation 10,000; By Balance c/d **80,000**.

steps.title: Solved example 2: Method 2
steps.body: Same machine. Machinery A/c stays at **1,00,000**. Provision for Depreciation A/c: 2024-25 By Depreciation 10,000 → balance 10,000; 2025-26 By Depreciation 10,000 → balance **20,000**. Balance sheet 31-3-2026: Machinery 1,00,000 less Provision 20,000 = 80,000.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Crediting the asset account when the question says a provision account is maintained.
- Closing Provision for Depreciation A/c to P&L — it is carried forward; only Depreciation A/c is closed.
- Forgetting to transfer accumulated depreciation of a sold asset.

statements.s: Under the provision method, the asset account shows original cost.
Provision for depreciation has a debit balance.
Depreciation A/c is transferred to P&L A/c every year.
Under method 1, the balance sheet shows the asset at cost.

quiz.q: Entry for depreciation under the provision method credits…
quiz.why: Under the provision method, depreciation is credited to Provision for Depreciation A/c, which keeps accumulated depreciation.

quiz.q: Under method 1, asset in balance sheet is at…
quiz.why: Under the method where depreciation is credited to the asset account, the asset is shown at its written down value.

quiz.q: Asset ₹50,000; accumulated depreciation ₹18,000. Net book value?
quiz.why: Net book value = cost − accumulated depreciation = 50,000 − 18,000 = ₹32,000.

quiz.q: Depreciation A/c is closed by transfer to…
quiz.why: Depreciation is an expense, so Depreciation A/c is closed by transfer to the Profit & Loss A/c.
Accumulated depreciation is deducted from the asset's cost in the balance sheet.

lessons.title: Disposal of an asset: profit or loss on sale

scenes.text: Nikhil sells the old van for ₹1,30,000 when its book value is ₹1,10,000.
Is the extra ₹20,000 “sales”?
No — it is a profit on sale of asset, found through the asset account or an Asset Disposal account.

steps.title: Steps
steps.body:
1. Find book value on the date of sale = Cost − depreciation up to the date of sale (charge depreciation for the part year).
2. Compare with sale price: Sale price > BV → **profit**; < BV → **loss**.
3. Entries: Bank A/c Dr; To Asset A/c (sale proceeds). Loss: P&L A/c Dr; To Asset A/c. Profit: Asset A/c Dr; To P&L A/c.
4. With provision method, an **Asset Disposal A/c** is often opened: transfer cost (Dr), accumulated depreciation (Cr), sale proceeds (Cr); balance = profit or loss.

steps.title: Solved example 2: WDV, part of machinery sold
Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting depreciation for the part year up to the date of sale.
- Crediting sale proceeds to Sales A/c.
- Calculating WDV of the sold machine together with the remaining one.

activity.prompt: Asset cost ₹60,000; accumulated depreciation ₹22,000 at sale; sold for ₹41,000. Profit on sale?

quiz.q: Sale proceeds of an old machine are credited to…
quiz.why: Sale proceeds of an old machine are credited to the Machinery A/c or the Asset Disposal A/c, not to Sales.
Sold for ₹40,000 against a book value of ₹45,000, so there is a loss of ₹5,000.

quiz.q: Profit on sale of asset is transferred to…
quiz.why: A profit on sale of an asset is a gain, so it is credited to the Profit & Loss A/c.

quiz.q: Asset Disposal A/c is debited with…
quiz.why: Asset Disposal A/c is debited with the original cost of the asset sold.

quiz.q: Before computing profit on sale mid-year, you must…
options: charge depreciation up to sale date
quiz.why: When an asset is sold mid-year, depreciation is first charged up to the date of sale, so the book value is correct.

scenes.text: Nikhil expects 5% of his debtors may never pay.
He also wants to keep part of his profit inside the business for expansion.
The first is a provision; the second is a reserve.

steps.title: Provisions
steps.body:
A **provision** is an amount charged against profit to provide for a *known liability or expected loss* whose amount cannot be determined accurately: provision for doubtful debts, depreciation, repairs and renewals, taxation, discount on debtors.

- Created by debiting P&L A/c; it is a *charge* against profit (made even if there is a loss).
- Shown as a deduction from the asset (doubtful debts from debtors) or as a liability (taxation).

steps.title: Reserves
steps.body:
A **reserve** is an *appropriation* of profit retained to strengthen the financial position or meet future contingencies. Made only when there is profit. Shown under *Reserves and Surplus* (owner’s equity).

- **Revenue reserves**: from operating profits — *general reserve* (no specific purpose) and *specific reserves* (dividend equalisation, debenture redemption, investment fluctuation, workmen compensation).
- **Capital reserves**: from capital profits — e.g., profit on sale of fixed assets, profit on revaluation, premium on issue of shares; normally not available for dividends.
- **Secret reserve**: hidden by understating assets/overstating liabilities (not permitted for companies beyond what law allows).

steps.title: Solved example 1: Provision for doubtful debts
steps.body:
Debtors ₹2,00,000; bad debts written off ₹5,000; create 5% provision.

- Debtors after bad debts = 1,95,000.
- Provision = 5% × 1,95,000 = ₹9,750.
- P&L debit = 5,000 + 9,750 = **₹14,750** (if no old provision). Balance sheet: Debtors 1,95,000 − 9,750 = **₹1,85,250**.

steps.title: Solved example 2: Provision or reserve?
steps.body: (a) ₹50,000 set aside for income tax payable → *provision*. (b) ₹1,00,000 kept aside from profit for future expansion → *general reserve*. (c) Profit on sale of land ₹2,00,000 → *capital reserve*.

steps.title: Provision vs reserve
steps.body:
- Nature: charge against profit vs appropriation of profit.
- Purpose: known liability/loss vs strengthening finances.
- Presentation: deducted from asset or shown as liability vs under reserves & surplus.
- Profit needed? No (provision) vs Yes (reserve).
- Dividend: provisions never distributed; revenue reserves can be.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calculating provision on debtors *before* deducting further bad debts.
- Calling provision for tax a reserve.
- Saying a reserve can be created when there is a loss.

activity.prompt: Provision, revenue reserve or capital reserve?

quiz.why: A provision is a charge against profit, made for a known liability or a likely loss.

quiz.q: A reserve can be created only if there is…
quiz.why: A reserve is an appropriation of profit, so it can be created only if there is profit.

quiz.q: Profit on sale of fixed asset usually goes to…
quiz.why: A profit on sale of a fixed asset is a capital profit, so it normally goes to a capital reserve.

quiz.q: Debtors ₹80,000; further bad debts ₹2,000; provision 5%. New provision?
quiz.why: Debtors after further bad debts = 80,000 − 2,000 = 78,000. Provision at 5% = ₹3,900.
Secret reserves are created by understating assets (or overstating liabilities), which hides profit.

questions.q: Depreciation on intangible assets is called…
questions.why: Writing off the cost of intangible assets is called amortisation.

questions.q: Depreciation is calculated on…
questions.why: Depreciation is charged on tangible fixed assets, which wear out with use.

questions.q: Under SLM, depreciation is…
questions.why: Under the straight line method, depreciation is the same amount every year.

questions.q: Cost ₹2,50,000, scrap ₹10,000, life 8 years. SLM depreciation?
Asset ₹1,00,000, WDV 10%. Book value after 2 years?
questions.why: Book value after 2 years = 1,00,000 × 0.9 × 0.9 = ₹81,000.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Provision is a charge against profit. Reason (R): It is made even when there is a loss.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true. A provision is a charge against profit and must be made even if there is a loss.

questions.q: Asset ₹90,000 bought 1 Oct 2025; 10% SLM; year ends 31 March. Depreciation 2025-26?
questions.why: Annual SLM depreciation = 10% of ₹90,000 = ₹9,000. The asset is used for 6 months (1 Oct to 31 Mar), so depreciation = 9,000 × 6/12 = ₹4,500.

questions.q: Cost ₹1,60,000; accumulated depreciation ₹64,000; sold for ₹90,000. Result?
questions.why: Book value = 1,60,000 − 64,000 = 96,000. Sold for 90,000, so there is a loss of ₹6,000.

questions.q: Which is a capital reserve?
questions.why: A profit on revaluation of assets is a capital profit, so it goes to a capital reserve.

questions.q: Provision for depreciation account has a…
questions.why: The provision for depreciation account has a credit balance, since it records accumulated depreciation.

questions.q: Case: A van ₹3,00,000 (1 April 2024), 20% WDV. Sold 30 Sept 2025 for ₹2,00,000. Profit/loss?
questions.why: Year 1 depreciation = 20% of 3,00,000 = 60,000, so WDV = 2,40,000. For the half-year to 30 Sept, 20% × 6/12 × 2,40,000 = 24,000, so book value = 2,16,000. Sold for 2,00,000, so there is a loss of ₹16,000.

questions.q: Debtors ₹1,20,000; bad debts ₹4,000 to be written off; 5% provision. Net debtors shown?
questions.why: Debtors after bad debts = 1,16,000. Provision at 5% = 5,800. Net debtors = 1,16,000 − 5,800 = ₹1,10,200.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Depreciation is a source of funds. Reason (R): Depreciation is a non-cash expense.
questions.why: Depreciation is a non-cash expense, so R is true. But depreciation is not a source of funds, as it only retains cash from profit, so A is false.

questions.q: The most suitable method for patents is…
questions.why: A patent has a fixed legal life, so the straight line method is most suitable.

questions.q: Machine ₹50,000 on 1 April; SLM 10%; on 1 October, another ₹20,000 added. Depreciation for the year?
An amount set aside for income tax payable is a…
questions.why: An amount set aside for income tax payable is a provision, as the liability is known but its exact amount is not.

courses.title: Ch 8 · Financial Statements – I
courses.summary: Capital vs revenue items, Trading Account and gross profit, Profit and Loss Account and operating profit, Balance Sheet grouping and marshalling, closing and opening entries.
outcomes: Learners can classify capital and revenue items
Learners can prepare a Trading Account and compute COGS and GP
Learners can prepare a P&L Account and compute operating profit
Learners can prepare a Balance Sheet in liquidity or permanence order

lessons.title: Financial statements and capital vs revenue items

scenes.text: On 31 March Nikhil’s trial balance is ready.
His bank asks for “final accounts”: a Trading and Profit & Loss Account and a Balance Sheet.
First he must separate capital items from revenue items.

steps.title: What financial statements are
steps.body: **Financial statements** summarise the results of a period and the position on a date. For a sole proprietor: **Trading and Profit and Loss Account** (income statement for the year ended …) and **Balance Sheet** (position statement as at …). Objectives: show profit or loss, show financial position, give information to users, help planning and comparison.

steps.title: Capital and revenue
steps.body:
- **Capital expenditure**: acquires/improves fixed assets or increases earning capacity; benefit > 1 year → Balance Sheet (e.g., machinery, installation, legal charges on buying land).
- **Revenue expenditure**: maintains earning capacity; benefit within the year → Trading/P&L (wages, rent, repairs, depreciation).
- **Deferred revenue expenditure**: large revenue spending with benefit over a few years (heavy advertising campaign) — written off over 3–5 years.
- **Capital receipts** (capital introduced, loans, sale of fixed assets) vs **revenue receipts** (sales, commission, interest).

steps.title: Solved example 1: Classify
steps.body: (a) ₹50,000 paid for a second-hand machine and ₹6,000 for its overhaul before use → *capital* ₹56,000. (b) Annual whitewashing ₹4,000 → *revenue*. (c) ₹2,00,000 on an advertising campaign expected to benefit 4 years → *deferred revenue*. (d) Loan of ₹1,00,000 from bank → *capital receipt*.

steps.title: Solved example 2: Why it matters
steps.body: If (a) were charged to P&L, profit would be understated by ₹56,000 and assets understated by the same amount — both statements would mislead users.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating repairs to an old asset as capital.
- Treating sale proceeds of an old asset as revenue receipt.
- Forgetting that a Balance Sheet is *as at* a date, while P&L is *for the year ended*.

activity.prompt: Capital or revenue?

quiz.q: Legal charges paid on purchase of land are…
quiz.why: Legal charges paid on the purchase of land are part of its cost, so they are capital expenditure.
A Balance Sheet shows the financial position as at a particular date.

quiz.q: Heavy advertising with benefit over 3 years is…
quiz.why: Heavy advertising whose benefit lasts three years is deferred revenue expenditure, written off over those years.

quiz.q: Sale of old machinery is a…
quiz.why: Sale of old machinery is the sale of a fixed asset, so the receipt is a capital receipt. Any profit is a gain.

quiz.q: Wages paid to workers producing goods go to…
quiz.why: Wages paid to workers who produce goods are a direct expense, so they go to the Trading A/c.

story.title: How much did the goods earn?

scenes.text: Nikhil sold notebooks worth ₹6,00,000 this year.
They cost him ₹4,20,000 including freight.
The difference — gross profit — comes from the Trading Account.

steps.title: Format and items
steps.body:
**Trading Account for the year ended 31 March 2026**

- *Debit*: Opening stock; Purchases less returns; Direct expenses — carriage/freight inwards, wages, wages & salaries (if combined, treat as direct), factory rent, power and fuel, octroi, import duty, dock charges, royalty on production, gas & water.
- *Credit*: Sales less returns; Closing stock.
- Balance: Credit > Debit → **Gross Profit** (transferred to P&L credit side); else Gross Loss.

steps.title: Cost of goods sold
steps.body:
**COGS = Opening stock + Net purchases + Direct expenses − Closing stock**

**Gross profit = Net sales − COGS**. Gross profit ratio = GP ÷ Net sales × 100.

steps.title: Solved example 1: Trading Account
steps.body:
Opening stock 40,000; Purchases 3,80,000; Purchases return 10,000; Wages 25,000; Carriage inwards 5,000; Sales 6,10,000; Sales return 10,000; Closing stock 60,000.

- Net purchases 3,70,000; Net sales 6,00,000.
- Debit: 40,000 + 3,70,000 + 25,000 + 5,000 = 4,40,000.
- Credit: 6,00,000 + 60,000 = 6,60,000.
- **Gross profit = ₹2,20,000**; COGS = 4,40,000 − 60,000 = 3,80,000; GP ratio = 36.67%.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Putting carriage *outwards* in the Trading Account (it is a selling expense → P&L).
- Taking closing stock from the trial balance as well as from adjustments (it appears once).
- Forgetting to deduct returns.

activity.prompt: Opening stock ₹20,000; net purchases ₹1,50,000; wages ₹10,000; closing stock ₹30,000; net sales ₹2,10,000. Gross profit?

quiz.why: Carriage inwards is a direct expense, so it is debited to the Trading A/c.

options: Trading A/c credit and Balance Sheet
quiz.why: Closing stock given as an adjustment appears twice: on the credit side of the Trading A/c and as an asset in the Balance Sheet.

options: opening stock + purchases + direct expenses − closing stock
quiz.why: Cost of goods sold = opening stock + net purchases + direct expenses − closing stock.
Factory rent is a production expense, so it is a direct expense and goes to the Trading A/c.

lessons.title: Profit and Loss Account and operating profit

scenes.text: Gross profit ₹2,20,000 looks great, but Nikhil also pays rent for the shop, salaries and advertising.
After these, what is left is net profit.
The Profit and Loss Account works this out.

steps.title: Items in P&L
steps.body:
- *Debit*: Gross loss (if any); office and administrative expenses (salaries, office rent, printing & stationery, telephone, insurance, audit fees, legal charges); selling and distribution expenses (carriage outwards, advertisement, commission paid, discount allowed, bad debts, delivery van expenses); financial expenses (interest on loan); depreciation; losses (loss by fire, loss on sale of asset).
- *Credit*: Gross profit; other incomes (commission/rent/interest/dividend received, discount received); gains.
- Balance = **Net profit** (credit > debit) → added to Capital in the Balance Sheet; or Net loss → deducted.

steps.title: Operating profit
steps.body: **Operating profit = Net profit + Non-operating expenses/losses − Non-operating incomes/gains**. It shows profit from the main business activity. Non-operating items: interest on investments, dividend received, profit/loss on sale of fixed assets, loss by fire.

steps.title: Solved example 1: P&L Account
steps.body:
GP 2,20,000; Salaries 60,000; Rent 24,000; Advertisement 15,000; Carriage outwards 6,000; Interest on loan 8,000; Commission received 9,000; Loss on sale of furniture 3,000.

- Debit: 60,000 + 24,000 + 15,000 + 6,000 + 8,000 + 3,000 = 1,16,000.
- Credit: 2,20,000 + 9,000 = 2,29,000.
- **Net profit = ₹1,13,000**.

steps.title: Solved example 2: Operating profit
steps.body: From above: NP 1,13,000 + interest on loan 8,000 (financial, non-operating) + loss on sale 3,000 − commission received 9,000 (assume non-operating) = **₹1,15,000**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Putting drawings in the P&L Account (they go to the Balance Sheet, deducted from capital).
- Putting income-tax of a sole proprietor as business expense — it is the owner’s personal tax → drawings.
- Mixing capital receipts into P&L.

activity.prompt: Where does it go?

quiz.why: Discount allowed is a selling expense, so it is shown on the debit side of the Profit & Loss A/c.
Net profit belongs to the owner, so it is added to capital.

quiz.q: Proprietor’s income tax paid from business is…
quiz.why: The proprietor's personal income tax paid from the business is drawings, not a business expense.
An uninsured loss by fire is an abnormal loss, so it is debited to the Profit & Loss A/c.
Operating profit excludes non-operating incomes, such as dividends, as they are not from the main business.

scenes.text: The Balance Sheet is like a photograph taken on 31 March.
Items must be grouped (current, non-current) and arranged in an order.
Liquidity order or permanence order — accountants choose one.

steps.title: Grouping
steps.body:
**Assets**: Non-current — fixed assets (tangible: land, building, plant, furniture, vehicles; intangible: goodwill, patents), long-term investments. Current — stock, debtors (less provision), bills receivable, short-term investments, prepaid expenses, accrued income, bank, cash.

**Liabilities**: Owner’s capital (opening + additional capital + net profit + interest on capital − drawings − interest on drawings − net loss); Non-current — long-term loans; Current — creditors, bills payable, bank overdraft, outstanding expenses, income received in advance.

steps.title: Marshalling
steps.body:
- **Order of liquidity**: assets from most liquid (cash) to least (goodwill); liabilities from most urgent (creditors, bills payable) to capital. Common for sole proprietors.
- **Order of permanence**: reverse — assets from goodwill/land down to cash; liabilities from capital to current liabilities. Companies present in a vertical format under Schedule III of the Companies Act, 2013.

steps.title: Solved example 1: Capital in the balance sheet
steps.body:
Capital 1 April ₹3,00,000; additional capital ₹50,000; net profit ₹1,13,000; drawings ₹40,000.

- Closing capital = 3,00,000 + 50,000 + 1,13,000 − 40,000 = **₹4,23,000**.

steps.title: Solved example 2: Balance Sheet totals
steps.body: Liabilities: Capital 4,23,000; Bank loan 1,00,000; Creditors 77,000 → total 6,00,000. Assets: Building 2,50,000; Furniture 50,000; Stock 60,000; Debtors 1,40,000; Bank 85,000; Cash 15,000 → total **₹6,00,000** ✔

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Showing debtors without deducting the provision for doubtful debts.
- Writing “To/By” in a Balance Sheet — it is a statement, not an account.
- Showing drawings as an asset.

activity.prompt: Arrange assets in ORDER OF LIQUIDITY (most liquid first)

quiz.why: A bank overdraft is repayable on demand, so it is a current liability.

quiz.q: Order of permanence starts assets with…
quiz.why: In the order of permanence, the most permanent assets, like goodwill and land, come first.
Prepaid insurance is a benefit still to be received, so it is shown as a current asset.
A Balance Sheet is a statement, not an account, so it does not use 'To' and 'By'.

scenes.text: Before the new year, every expense and income account must reach zero.
They are transferred to Trading and P&L by closing entries.
Assets and liabilities are carried forward by an opening entry next year.

steps.title: Closing entries
steps.body:
1. Opening stock, purchases, direct expenses → Trading A/c Dr; To Opening Stock, To Purchases, To Wages, To Carriage inwards.
2. Returns: Purchases Return A/c Dr; To Purchases A/c (or to Trading). Sales A/c Dr; To Sales Return A/c.
3. Sales and closing stock → Sales A/c Dr; Closing Stock A/c Dr; To Trading A/c.
4. Gross profit → Trading A/c Dr; To P&L A/c.
5. Indirect expenses → P&L A/c Dr; To Salaries, Rent, …
6. Incomes → Commission Received A/c Dr; To P&L A/c.
7. Net profit → P&L A/c Dr; To Capital A/c. Drawings → Capital A/c Dr; To Drawings A/c.

steps.title: Solved example 1: Closing entry for GP and NP
Solved example 2: Opening entry
steps.body: Next year: Building A/c Dr 2,50,000; Furniture Dr 50,000; Stock Dr 60,000; Debtors Dr 1,40,000; Bank Dr 85,000; Cash Dr 15,000; To Bank Loan 1,00,000; To Creditors 77,000; To Capital 4,23,000.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Passing closing entries for asset and liability accounts (they are carried forward).
- Transferring drawings to P&L instead of Capital.
- Forgetting the closing stock entry (Closing Stock A/c Dr; To Trading A/c).

activity.prompt: Complete the closing entry for net profit ₹90,000
answers: Profit and Loss|Profit & Loss|P&L|Profit and loss

quiz.q: Which accounts are closed at year-end?
quiz.why: Nominal accounts (expenses and incomes) are closed at year-end by transfer to the Trading and Profit & Loss accounts.

quiz.q: Closing stock entry: Closing Stock A/c Dr; To…
quiz.why: For closing stock: Closing Stock A/c Dr; To Trading A/c, so Trading is credited.

quiz.q: Drawings are closed by transfer to…
quiz.why: Drawings reduce capital, so the Drawings A/c is closed by transfer to Capital A/c.
The opening entry debits the assets, which are brought forward from the last year.
Net loss reduces capital, so it is transferred by Capital A/c Dr; To Profit & Loss A/c.

questions.q: Trading Account shows…
questions.why: The Trading Account shows gross profit or gross loss.

questions.q: Carriage outwards goes to…
questions.why: Carriage outwards is a selling expense, so it is debited to the Profit & Loss A/c.

questions.q: A Balance Sheet is prepared…
questions.why: A Balance Sheet is prepared on a particular date to show the financial position.

questions.q: Opening stock ₹30,000; purchases ₹2,00,000; wages ₹20,000; closing stock ₹40,000. COGS?
Net sales ₹3,00,000; COGS ₹2,10,000. GP?
questions.why: Gross profit = net sales − COGS = 3,00,000 − 2,10,000 = ₹90,000.

questions.q: Capital ₹5,00,000; NP ₹1,20,000; drawings ₹60,000; additional capital ₹40,000. Closing capital?
Assertion (A): Drawings are not shown in P&L A/c. Reason (R): Drawings are not business expenses.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true. Drawings are not business expenses, so they are not shown in the Profit & Loss A/c.

questions.q: Which is deferred revenue expenditure?
questions.why: A large advertising campaign whose benefit lasts four years is deferred revenue expenditure, written off over the years.

questions.q: Net sales ₹8,00,000; GP 25% on cost. GP amount?
questions.why: GP is 25% on cost, so it is 25/125 = 20% on sales. GP = 20% of 8,00,000 = ₹1,60,000.

questions.q: Case: Opening stock ₹50,000; net purchases ₹4,00,000; direct expenses ₹30,000; net sales ₹5,50,000; GP 20% on sales. Closing stock?
In order of liquidity, the first asset is…
questions.why: In the order of liquidity, the most liquid asset comes first, which is cash in hand.

questions.q: NP ₹1,00,000 includes dividend received ₹8,000 and loss on sale of asset ₹5,000. Operating profit?
questions.why: Operating profit = NP − non-operating income + non-operating loss = 1,00,000 − 8,000 + 5,000 = ₹97,000.

questions.q: Closing entry for sales: Sales A/c Dr; To…
questions.why: The closing entry for sales is Sales A/c Dr; To Trading A/c, so Trading is credited.

questions.q: Legal charges on purchase of building are…
questions.why: Legal charges on the purchase of a building are part of its cost, so they are added to Building.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Closing stock is shown in Trading A/c and Balance Sheet. Reason (R): It is given as an adjustment outside the trial balance.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true. Closing stock is given as an adjustment outside the trial balance, so it appears in both the Trading A/c and the Balance Sheet.

questions.q: Total assets ₹7,50,000; creditors ₹80,000; bank loan ₹1,20,000. Capital?
questions.why: Capital = assets − outside liabilities = 7,50,000 − (80,000 + 1,20,000) = ₹5,50,000.

courses.title: Ch 9 · Financial Statements – II
courses.summary: Preparing final accounts with adjustments: closing stock, outstanding and prepaid expenses, accrued and advance incomes, depreciation, bad debts and provisions, interest, manager’s commission, abnormal losses and goods used, ending with a full solved problem.
outcomes: Learners can show the two-fold effect of every adjustment
Learners can compute bad debts, PDD and provision for discount
Learners can compute manager’s commission before/after charging
Learners can prepare complete final accounts with adjustments

lessons.title: Why adjustments: closing stock, outstanding and prepaid expenses

scenes.text: March salary of ₹20,000 will be paid on 7 April.
Insurance of ₹12,000 paid in January covers January–December.
To get a true profit, Nikhil must adjust both (accrual + matching).

steps.title: Principle of adjustments
steps.body: Every adjustment given *outside* the trial balance has a **two-fold effect**: once in Trading/P&L and once in the Balance Sheet. Items *inside* the trial balance appear only once.

steps.title: Main expense adjustments
steps.body:
- **Closing stock**: Trading A/c (Cr) and Balance Sheet (current asset).
- **Outstanding expense**: add to the expense in Trading/P&L; show as current liability. Entry: Expense A/c Dr; To Outstanding Expense A/c.
- **Prepaid expense**: deduct from the expense; show as current asset. Entry: Prepaid Expense A/c Dr; To Expense A/c.

steps.title: Solved example 1: Outstanding salary
steps.body:
TB salaries ₹2,20,000 (11 months paid); March salary ₹20,000 outstanding.

- P&L Dr: Salaries 2,20,000 + 20,000 = **₹2,40,000**.
- Balance Sheet liabilities: Outstanding salary **₹20,000**.

steps.title: Solved example 2: Prepaid insurance
steps.body:
Insurance ₹12,000 paid on 1 January 2026 for one year; year ends 31 March 2026.

- Expired 3 months = 3,000; prepaid 9 months = **₹9,000**.
- P&L Dr: Insurance 12,000 − 9,000 = **₹3,000**. Balance Sheet assets: Prepaid insurance ₹9,000.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Showing an adjustment in only one place.
- Showing a TB item (e.g., prepaid rent already in TB) again in P&L — TB items appear only once.
- Showing outstanding *wages* in P&L — wages go to the Trading A/c.

activity.prompt: Rent paid as per TB ₹33,000 for 11 months. Monthly rent ₹3,000. What amount of rent is debited to P&L?

quiz.why: An outstanding expense is owed, so it is shown as a current liability.
A prepaid expense belongs to the next year, so it is deducted from the expense of this year.
Adjustments outside the trial balance appear twice, once in the Trading or P&L A/c and once in the Balance Sheet.

quiz.q: Outstanding wages are added to wages in…
quiz.why: Wages are a direct expense, so outstanding wages are added to wages in the Trading A/c.

quiz.q: Closing stock given in TB (adjusted purchases) appears…
quiz.why: Closing stock that is already in the trial balance is shown only in the Balance Sheet, since it has already been adjusted in purchases.

lessons.title: Accrued income, income received in advance, depreciation and interest

story.title: Money earned but not yet received

scenes.text: Nikhil sub-lets part of his shop for ₹2,000 a month; March rent is still unpaid.
A coaching client paid ₹15,000 in March for April–June sessions.
Both must be adjusted.

steps.title: Income adjustments
steps.body:
- **Accrued income** (earned, not received): add to income in P&L; show as current asset. Entry: Accrued Income A/c Dr; To Income A/c.
- **Income received in advance** (received, not earned): deduct from income; show as current liability. Entry: Income A/c Dr; To Income Received in Advance A/c.

steps.title: Depreciation and interest
steps.body:
- **Depreciation**: P&L Dr; deduct from asset in Balance Sheet.
- **Interest on capital** (allowed): P&L Dr; add to capital.
- **Interest on drawings** (charged): P&L Cr; deduct from capital.
- **Interest on loan outstanding**: add to interest in P&L; add to loan/show as outstanding liability.

steps.title: Solved example 1: Rent receivable
steps.body:
TB Rent received ₹22,000 (11 months). March rent ₹2,000 accrued.

- P&L Cr: 22,000 + 2,000 = **₹24,000**. Balance Sheet asset: Accrued rent ₹2,000.

steps.title: Solved example 2: Interest on capital and drawings
steps.body:
Capital ₹4,00,000; interest on capital 6% p.a.; drawings ₹30,000; interest on drawings ₹900.

- Interest on capital = 24,000 → P&L Dr; add to capital.
- Interest on drawings 900 → P&L Cr; deduct from capital.
- Capital in BS (before NP) = 4,00,000 + 24,000 − 30,000 − 900 = 3,93,100, then add NP.

steps.title: Solved example 3: Interest on loan
steps.body: Loan ₹1,00,000 at 9% taken on 1 July 2025; TB shows interest paid ₹4,500. Interest for 9 months = 6,750 → outstanding 2,250. P&L Dr: **₹6,750**; BS: Loan 1,00,000 + outstanding interest 2,250.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Adding income received in advance to income.
- Charging interest on capital for the full year when capital was introduced mid-year.
- Forgetting to deduct depreciation from the asset in the Balance Sheet.

activity.prompt: Match the adjustment with its Balance Sheet treatment

quiz.why: Accrued income is earned but not yet received, so it is an asset.
Income received in advance is not yet earned, so it is deducted from income.
Interest on drawings is charged to the owner, so it is income for the business and is credited to the P&L A/c.

quiz.q: Capital ₹2,00,000; IOC 5%. Amount debited to P&L?
quiz.why: Interest on capital = 5% of 2,00,000 = ₹10,000, which is debited to the Profit & Loss A/c.

quiz.q: Commission TB ₹18,000 includes ₹3,000 for next year. Credited to P&L?
quiz.why: The commission of ₹3,000 for next year is deducted: 18,000 − 3,000 = ₹15,000 is credited to the P&L A/c.

lessons.title: Bad debts and provisions on debtors

story.title: The customers who may not pay

scenes.text: A customer who owed ₹4,000 has shut his shop and vanished.
Nikhil also fears 5% of the remaining debtors may not pay.
He writes off the bad debt and creates a provision.

steps.title: Three steps
steps.body:
1. **Further bad debts** (given in adjustments): add to bad debts in P&L; deduct from debtors.
2. **New provision for doubtful debts (PDD)** = % × (Debtors − further bad debts).
3. **Provision for discount on debtors** = % × (Debtors − further bad debts − new PDD).

steps.title: P&L treatment with old provision
steps.body:
Charge to P&L = Bad debts (TB) + Further bad debts + New PDD − Old PDD.

- If the result is positive → debit P&L. If negative → credit P&L (excess provision written back).
- Balance Sheet: Debtors − further bad debts − new PDD − provision for discount.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
TB: Debtors ₹1,04,000; Bad debts ₹3,000; Old PDD ₹5,000. Adjustments: further bad debts ₹4,000; PDD 5%; provision for discount 2%.

- Debtors after bad debts = 1,00,000.
- New PDD = 5,000. Net charge = 3,000 + 4,000 + 5,000 − 5,000 = **₹7,000** (P&L Dr).
- Provision for discount = 2% × (1,00,000 − 5,000) = **₹1,900** (P&L Dr).
- BS: 1,04,000 − 4,000 − 5,000 − 1,900 = **₹93,100**.

steps.title: Solved example 2: Write-back
steps.body:
TB: Debtors ₹60,000; Bad debts ₹1,000; Old PDD ₹4,500. New PDD 5% on debtors (no further bad debts).

- New PDD = 3,000. Charge = 1,000 + 3,000 − 4,500 = **−₹500** → **credit P&L ₹500**.
- BS: Debtors 60,000 − 3,000 = ₹57,000.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calculating the new provision on debtors before deducting further bad debts.
- Computing discount provision without deducting the new PDD.
- Deducting old provision in the Balance Sheet — only the **new** provision is deducted there.

activity.prompt: Debtors ₹82,000; further bad debts ₹2,000; PDD 5%. TB bad debts ₹1,500; old PDD ₹3,000. Net amount debited to P&L?

quiz.q: Provision for doubtful debts is calculated on…
quiz.why: The provision for doubtful debts is calculated on debtors after deducting further bad debts.

quiz.q: Old PDD in the Balance Sheet is…
quiz.why: The old provision is replaced by the new one, so only the new provision is deducted from debtors in the Balance Sheet.

quiz.q: If old PDD exceeds the required amount, the excess is…
quiz.why: If the old provision is more than needed, the excess is written back and credited to the P&L A/c.

quiz.q: Debtors ₹50,000; new PDD ₹2,500; discount 2%. Provision for discount?
quiz.why: Provision for discount is on debtors after bad debts and provision: 50,000 − 2,500 = 47,500. 2% of 47,500 = ₹950.
Further bad debts are written off and deducted from debtors in the Balance Sheet.

lessons.title: Manager’s commission, abnormal loss and goods used

scenes.text: Nikhil’s manager gets 10% commission on net profit *after* charging the commission.
Goods worth ₹20,000 were burnt; the insurer accepted ₹15,000.
₹3,000 of goods were given as free samples.

steps.title: Manager’s commission
steps.body:
- On net profit **before** charging commission: Commission = NP × r/100.
- On net profit **after** charging commission: Commission = NP (before commission) × r/(100 + r).
- P&L Dr; Balance Sheet: Outstanding commission (liability).

steps.title: Abnormal loss and goods used
steps.body:
- **Goods lost by fire/theft**: Trading A/c Cr with the full cost (to remove from goods available); P&L Dr with the loss not covered by insurance; Balance Sheet asset: insurance claim receivable.
- **Goods taken by proprietor**: deduct from purchases (Trading Dr side); add to drawings (deduct from capital).
- **Goods distributed as free samples**: deduct from purchases; debit advertisement in P&L.

steps.title: Solved example 1: Manager’s commission
steps.body:
NP before commission ₹2,20,000; commission 10% on NP after charging it.

- Commission = 2,20,000 × 10/110 = **₹20,000**.
- Check: 2,20,000 − 20,000 = 2,00,000; 10% of 2,00,000 = 20,000 ✔. (If “before charging”: ₹22,000.)

steps.title: Solved example 2: Fire loss
steps.body:
Goods costing ₹20,000 destroyed; insurer admitted ₹15,000.

- Trading A/c Cr: By Loss by fire 20,000.
- P&L Dr: Loss by fire 5,000.
- Balance Sheet assets: Insurance claim receivable 15,000.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using r/100 when the question says “after charging”.
- Showing only the uninsured part in the Trading Account.
- Treating goods given as samples as drawings.

activity.prompt: Net profit before manager’s commission ₹3,15,000. Commission 5% of net profit AFTER charging it. Commission?

quiz.q: Commission 10% on NP before charging, NP ₹1,50,000:
quiz.why: Commission of 10% on net profit before charging it is 10% × 1,50,000 = ₹15,000.

quiz.q: Goods ₹5,000 taken by owner: Trading treatment?
quiz.why: Goods taken by the owner reduce purchases in the Trading A/c, and are shown as drawings.
Loss of goods by fire that the insurer does not cover is an abnormal loss. It is not part of the normal cost of goods, so it is debited to the Profit & Loss A/c, not shown in the Trading A/c.

quiz.q: Insurance claim admitted is shown as…
quiz.why: Once the insurer admits the claim, the firm has a right to receive that money. A sum to be received is a receivable, so it appears as a current asset in the Balance Sheet.
Free samples are given to attract customers, so the cost is promotion. It is debited to Advertisement, and the same amount is deducted from Purchases because those goods were not sold.

scenes.text: Exam question: prepare Trading and P&L Account and Balance Sheet from a trial balance with six adjustments.
A clear order of work saves time.
Let us solve one completely.

steps.title: The data
steps.body:
TB of Meera Traders on 31 March 2026 — Debits: Opening stock 40,000; Purchases 2,60,000; Wages 30,000; Salaries 48,000; Rent 22,000; Insurance 6,000; Debtors 80,000; Machinery 1,50,000; Cash 22,000; Drawings 24,000; Bad debts 2,000. Credits: Capital 2,50,000; Sales 4,00,000; Creditors 30,000; PDD 4,000. Total each side **₹6,84,000**.

Adjustments: (1) Closing stock 60,000. (2) Outstanding salaries 4,000. (3) Prepaid insurance 1,500. (4) Depreciation on machinery 10%. (5) Further bad debts 2,000; PDD 5%. (6) Interest on capital 6%.

steps.title: Trading Account
steps.body: Dr: Opening stock 40,000; Purchases 2,60,000; Wages 30,000 = 3,30,000. Cr: Sales 4,00,000; Closing stock 60,000 = 4,60,000. **Gross profit = ₹1,30,000**.

steps.title: Profit and Loss Account
steps.body:
Dr: Salaries 52,000; Rent 22,000; Insurance 4,500; Depreciation 15,000; Bad debts & PDD (2,000 + 2,000 + 3,900 − 4,000) 3,900; Interest on capital 15,000 → total 1,12,400.
Cr: Gross profit 1,30,000.
**Net profit = ₹17,600**.

steps.title: Balance Sheet as at 31 March 2026
steps.body:
Liabilities: Capital 2,50,000 + IOC 15,000 + NP 17,600 − Drawings 24,000 = 2,58,600; Creditors 30,000; Outstanding salaries 4,000 → **₹2,92,600**.
Assets: Machinery 1,50,000 − 15,000 = 1,35,000; Closing stock 60,000; Debtors 80,000 − 2,000 − 3,900 = 74,100; Prepaid insurance 1,500; Cash 22,000 → **₹2,92,600** ✔

steps.title: Order of work in exams
steps.body: 1. Tick TB items as you use them. 2. Write each adjustment’s two effects beside it. 3. Trading → P&L → Balance Sheet. 4. Check totals. 5. If they differ, recheck items used twice or not at all.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting interest on capital in the Balance Sheet (added to capital).
- Using old PDD in the Balance Sheet.
- Missing one leg of an adjustment so the Balance Sheet does not tally.

activity.prompt: Final accounts checklist
items: Every TB item used exactly once
Closing stock in Trading and Balance Sheet
Bad debts and new PDD worked out
Capital updated with NP, IOC and drawings

quiz.q: In the problem, salaries debited to P&L are…
quiz.why: Salaries charged to P&L include the amount paid plus the amount still unpaid. Here ₹48,000 paid + ₹4,000 outstanding = ₹52,000. Adding only one of them would understate the expense.
Net debtors = debtors less further bad debts less the new provision. So ₹80,000 − ₹2,000 − ₹3,900 = ₹74,100. Each deduction brings debtors down to the amount expected to be collected.

quiz.q: Interest on capital at 6% on ₹2,50,000 is…
quiz.why: Interest on capital = capital × rate = ₹2,50,000 × 6/100 = ₹15,000. It is a charge against profit, so it is debited to P&L (Appropriation).
Only the part of insurance that belongs to this year is charged to P&L. The prepaid ₹1,500 belongs to next year, so ₹6,000 − ₹1,500 = ₹4,500.

quiz.q: If the Balance Sheet does not tally, first check…
quiz.why: When the Balance Sheet does not tally, the usual cause is an item counted twice or left out. The title, font or date do not affect the totals, so check the items first.

questions.q: Outstanding rent is shown as…
questions.why: Outstanding rent is rent that has been used but not yet paid. The firm owes it, so it is a payable and is shown as a current liability. It is not an asset or income.

questions.q: Prepaid insurance is…
questions.why: Prepaid insurance is paid this year but covers next year. So it is deducted from this year's insurance expense and shown as a current asset. It is not added, because that would overstate the expense.

questions.q: Accrued commission is…
questions.why: Accrued commission is commission earned but not yet received. The firm will receive it, so it is a receivable and an asset. It is added to commission income.

questions.q: Interest on drawings is…
questions.why: Interest the proprietor pays on drawings is income for the business. So it is credited to P&L (and deducted from capital). It is not an expense of the firm.

questions.q: Debtors ₹70,000; further bad debts ₹2,000; PDD 5%. New PDD?
questions.why: Debtors after further bad debts = ₹70,000 − ₹2,000 = ₹68,000. New PDD = 5% of ₹68,000 = ₹3,400. Provision is made only on debtors that remain.

questions.q: NP before commission ₹1,32,000; manager 10% of NP after charging. Commission?
questions.why: The commission is 10% of profit after charging it, so it is 10/110 of profit before commission. ₹1,32,000 × 10/110 = ₹12,000. Taking 10% of ₹1,32,000 gives ₹13,200, which is the common trap.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Adjustments given outside the TB are recorded twice. Reason (R): Every adjustment has a dual effect.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Both statements are true. An adjustment outside the trial balance has not been recorded yet, so it is recorded in two places (for example, expense in P&L and liability in the Balance Sheet). The dual effect explains why.

questions.q: Wages ₹45,000 in TB; outstanding wages ₹5,000. Wages in Trading A/c?
questions.why: Wages for the year include those paid and those still due. ₹45,000 + ₹5,000 outstanding = ₹50,000 in the Trading A/c. Outstanding expenses are always added to the expense.

questions.q: Goods ₹30,000 lost by fire; insurer admits ₹22,000. Amount debited to P&L?
questions.why: The loss is the part the insurer does not pay. ₹30,000 − ₹22,000 = ₹8,000 is debited to P&L. The ₹22,000 is a claim receivable, so it goes to the Balance Sheet.

questions.q: TB: Debtors ₹1,02,000; bad debts ₹2,500; old PDD ₹6,000. Further bad debts ₹2,000; PDD 5%. Net P&L charge?
Case: Rent received ₹26,000 in TB for 13 months (₹2,000 per month). Credited to P&L?
questions.why: ₹26,000 covers 13 months, but only 12 months belong to this year. One month (₹2,000) is received in advance, so income = ₹26,000 − ₹2,000 = ₹24,000.

questions.q: Insurance ₹18,000 paid on 1 Oct 2025 for one year; year ends 31 March 2026. Prepaid?
questions.why: The policy runs 1 Oct 2025 to 30 Sep 2026. By 31 March 2026, 6 months are used and 6 months are left. Prepaid = ₹18,000 × 6/12 = ₹9,000.

questions.q: Goods ₹4,000 given as free samples. Treatment?
questions.why: Goods given as free samples are advertising, not sales. So their cost is deducted from Purchases and debited to Advertisement. Ignoring them would overstate gross profit.

questions.q: Case: Loan ₹2,00,000 @ 12% taken on 1 Oct 2025; no interest paid. Interest charged to P&L for 2025-26?
questions.why: Interest is charged for the time the loan was used. From 1 Oct 2025 to 31 March 2026 is 6 months. ₹2,00,000 × 12% × 6/12 = ₹12,000, shown as outstanding interest.

questions.q: Debtors ₹1,00,000; new PDD ₹5,000; provision for discount 2%. Net debtors in BS?
questions.why: Provision for discount is made on debtors after bad debts and PDD. ₹1,00,000 − ₹5,000 = ₹95,000. 2% of ₹95,000 = ₹1,900. Net debtors = ₹95,000 − ₹1,900 = ₹93,100.

questions.q: Capital ₹3,00,000; IOC ₹18,000; drawings ₹36,000; IOD ₹1,800; NP ₹50,000. Closing capital?
questions.why: Closing capital = opening capital + interest on capital + net profit − drawings − interest on drawings. 3,00,000 + 18,000 + 50,000 − 36,000 − 1,800 = ₹3,30,200.

questions.q: Which is NOT an adjustment item?
questions.why: Adjustments are items given outside the trial balance, like outstanding wages or closing stock. Purchases is already in the trial balance, so it is not an adjustment.

courses.title: Revision & Practice · Class 11 Accountancy
courses.summary: Two-page formula and rules sheet for the whole year, exam traps, and two mixed mock papers covering every chapter.
outcomes: Learners can recall every key rule and formula
Learners can apply them under time pressure
Learners can diagnose weak chapters from mock results

lessons.title: Formula sheet I: concepts, recording and BRS

scenes.text: It is the night before Nikhil’s final exam.
He wants everything on two pages.
Here is that sheet.

steps.title: Concepts in one line each
steps.body: Entity · Money measurement · Going concern · Accounting period · Cost · Dual aspect · Revenue recognition · Matching · Full disclosure · Consistency · Conservatism · Materiality · Objectivity. Bases: cash vs accrual. Systems: double vs single entry.

steps.title: Equation and rules
steps.body:
- A = L + C; Capital = A − L.
- Closing capital = Opening + Additional capital + Profit − Drawings.
- Profit = Closing capital − Opening capital + Drawings − Additional capital.
- Debit: increase in assets, expenses, losses, drawings. Credit: increase in liabilities, capital, revenues, gains.
- Golden rules: Personal — receiver/giver; Real — comes in/goes out; Nominal — expenses & losses/incomes & gains.

steps.title: Books and GST
steps.body:
- Purchases/Sales books: credit **goods** only, net of trade discount.
- Contra entry: cash ↔ bank, marked C, not posted.
- Petty cash (imprest): reimburse amount spent.
- GST: intra-state CGST + SGST; inter-state IGST. IGST credit order: IGST → CGST → SGST.

steps.title: BRS signs (starting from cash book Dr balance)
steps.body:
**Add**: cheques issued not presented; credits by bank only (interest, direct deposits); cash book undercasting of receipts.
**Less**: cheques deposited not collected; bank charges, direct payments, dishonoured cheques.
Starting from passbook: reverse every sign. Overdraft: treat as negative.

steps.title: Errors
steps.body: One-sided (affect TB): casting, wrong amount posting, wrong side (2×), partial omission. Two-sided (do not affect TB): complete omission, principle, compensating, wrong account correct side. Suspense only for one-sided.

steps.title: Top exam traps
steps.body:
- Goods withdrawn → credit Purchases, not Sales/Stock.
- Cash discount on invoice price, not list price.
- Wrong-side posting difference = double.
- Installation wages → asset.

cards.back: Closing capital − Opening capital + Drawings − Additional capital
Sent by buyer when returning goods

quiz.q: Capital at end ₹3,40,000; start ₹3,00,000; drawings ₹25,000; additional capital ₹20,000. Profit?
