quiz.why: Closing capital = opening + additional capital + profit − drawings. So profit = 3,40,000 − 3,00,000 − 20,000 + 25,000 = ₹45,000. Work backwards from the closing figure.

quiz.q: Starting from passbook, bank charges are…
quiz.why: A bank reconciliation starting from the passbook works the opposite way to starting from the cash book. Bank charges are not yet in the passbook balance of the cash book, so they are added back in the reverse rule.

quiz.q: Machinery debited to Purchases A/c is…
quiz.why: Machinery is an asset, so it should be debited to Machinery A/c. Debiting Purchases is an error of principle. The debit is still a debit, so the trial balance still agrees.
Trade discount is only a reduction in list price at the time of sale. Only the net price is entered, so the discount appears in no book of account.
A contra entry has both debit and credit in the cash book (for example cash deposited into bank). It is complete within the cash book, so it is not posted to the ledger.

lessons.title: Formula sheet II: depreciation and final accounts

scenes.text: Page two: numbers that carry the most marks.
Depreciation, provisions, adjustments.
Learn the formula, then practise.

steps.title: Depreciation
steps.body:
- SLM = (Cost − Scrap) ÷ Life; Rate = Dep ÷ Cost × 100.
- WDV: Dep = Rate × Opening BV.
- Part year: × months/12.
- Profit/loss on sale = Sale price − BV on date of sale (after part-year depreciation).
- Provision method: asset at cost; accumulated depreciation separately.

steps.title: Provisions and reserves
steps.body: Provision = charge against profit (doubtful debts, tax, depreciation). Reserve = appropriation of profit (general, specific; capital reserve from capital profits).

steps.title: Trading and P&L
steps.body:
- COGS = Opening stock + Net purchases + Direct expenses − Closing stock.
- GP = Net sales − COGS. GP on cost r% → GP on sales = r/(100 + r).
- Operating profit = NP + non-operating expenses − non-operating incomes.

steps.title: Adjustments
steps.body:
- Outstanding exp: + expense; liability. Prepaid: − expense; asset.
- Accrued income: + income; asset. Advance income: − income; liability.
- Net bad-debt charge = BD (TB) + further BD + new PDD − old PDD.
- Provision for discount = % × (Debtors − further BD − new PDD).
- Manager’s commission after charging = NP × r/(100 + r).
- IOC: P&L Dr, + capital. IOD: P&L Cr, − capital.
- Fire loss: Trading Cr (full cost); P&L Dr (uninsured); claim = asset.

steps.title: Top exam traps
steps.body:
- WDV rate on cost every year.
- PDD on debtors before deducting further bad debts.
- Old PDD shown in Balance Sheet.
- Carriage outwards in Trading.

activity.prompt: Sales ₹4,80,000; GP is 20% on cost. What is the gross profit?

quiz.why: On WDV each year's depreciation is taken on the reduced value. After year 1: ₹50,000 × 0.8 = ₹40,000; after year 2: ₹40,000 × 0.8 = ₹32,000.

quiz.q: Debtors ₹40,000; PDD 5%; discount 2%. Provision for discount?
quiz.why: PDD is made first, then the discount provision on the remaining debtors. ₹40,000 − 5% (₹2,000) = ₹38,000. 2% of ₹38,000 = ₹760.
Income received in advance is money taken for a service not yet given. The firm owes that service, so it is a liability, not income of this year.

quiz.q: Manager 10% after charging; NP before ₹77,000. Commission?
quiz.why: Commission of 10% on profit after charging it is 10/110 of the profit before commission. ₹77,000 × 10/110 = ₹7,000. Using 10% of ₹77,000 (₹7,700) is the trap.
A reserve is a part of profit set aside for future use. It is an appropriation of profit, not a charge against it and not a liability to outsiders.

scenes.text: Set a 30-minute timer.
Attempt each question before opening the explanation.
Note the chapters where you lose marks.

steps.title: How to use the mocks
steps.body: The course test below contains **Mock A (Q1–12)** and **Mock B (Q13–24)**, mixing MCQ, assertion–reason, case-based and numerical items across all chapters. Aim for 80%+. For each wrong answer, revisit that chapter’s lesson.

steps.title: Worked item 1: Journal + ledger
steps.body:
Q: Sold goods list price ₹30,000 to Kavya at 10% trade discount, 5% cash discount, she paid half immediately. Entry?

- Net = 27,000; half = 13,500; cash discount 5% on 13,500 = 675; cash = 12,825.
- Cash A/c Dr 12,825; Discount Allowed Dr 675; Kavya Dr 13,500; To Sales 27,000.

steps.title: Worked item 2: BRS
steps.body:
Q: Passbook overdraft ₹15,000; cheques deposited not collected ₹4,000; cheques issued not presented ₹6,000; interest on OD ₹500 not in cash book. Overdraft per cash book?

- Start −15,000. Deposits not collected: cash book already recorded them → cash book OD smaller → +4,000 → −11,000.
- Cheques not presented: cash book OD larger → −6,000 → −17,000.
- Interest not in cash book: cash book OD smaller → +500 → **−16,500** (OD ₹16,500).

steps.title: Exam technique
steps.body: Read “before/after charging”, “on cost/on sales”, “from cash book/passbook” twice. Show working notes — partial marks need them.

activity.prompt: Goods list price ₹40,000, trade discount 10%, cash discount 2% (paid fully at once). Discount allowed amount?

quiz.q: Which is recorded: trade or cash discount?
quiz.why: Cash discount is allowed for prompt payment, so it is a real gain or loss and is recorded in the books. Trade discount is deducted from the price on the invoice and is not recorded.

quiz.q: Passbook OD ₹10,000; cheques issued not presented ₹3,000. OD per cash book?
quiz.why: Cheques issued but not yet presented are already in the cash book but not in the passbook. So the cash book overdraft is bigger: ₹10,000 + ₹3,000 = ₹13,000.

quiz.q: Machinery ₹80,000 (1 Jan 2026), 10% SLM, year ends 31 March. Dep?
quiz.why: Depreciation is only for the time the machine was used. From 1 Jan to 31 March is 3 months. ₹80,000 × 10% × 3/12 = ₹2,000.
At the start of the year, assets are debited and liabilities and capital are credited. So the opening entry credits liabilities and capital, so that the debit and credit totals match.

quiz.q: Assertion: TB agreement proves accuracy. Correct?
quiz.why: The statement is false. A trial balance that agrees can still hide errors, such as omission of an entry, compensating errors and errors of principle, which affect both sides equally.

questions.q: [Mock A] The concept that records assets at purchase price is…
questions.why: The cost concept says assets are recorded at their purchase price (historical cost). This keeps records objective. Going concern and conservatism are about other things.

questions.q: [Mock A] Goods withdrawn by owner are credited to…
questions.why: Goods taken by the owner for personal use reduce the stock available for sale. The entry is Drawings Dr and Purchases Cr, so purchases are reduced.

questions.q: [Mock A] Credit purchase of a computer by a shoe shop is recorded in…
questions.why: The purchases book is only for credit purchases of goods that the firm deals in. A computer is an asset for a shoe shop, so it is recorded in the journal proper.

questions.q: [Mock A] Assets ₹9,00,000; capital ₹6,20,000. Liabilities?
questions.why: Assets = liabilities + capital, so liabilities = assets − capital. ₹9,00,000 − ₹6,20,000 = ₹2,80,000.

questions.q: [Mock A] Cash book Dr ₹18,000; cheques deposited not collected ₹5,000; interest credited ₹200. Passbook?
questions.why: Cheques deposited but not yet collected are still in the cash book only, so they are deducted. Interest credited by the bank is only in the passbook, so it is added. 18,000 − 5,000 + 200 = ₹13,200.

questions.q: [Mock A] Intra-state sale ₹60,000 at 12% GST. CGST?
questions.why: At 12% GST, an intra-state sale is split equally into CGST and SGST of 6% each. 6% of ₹60,000 = ₹3,600.

questions.q: [Mock A] Assertion (A): Wrong-side posting of ₹500 causes a TB difference of ₹1,000. Reason (R): One side is understated and the other overstated.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true. Posting ₹500 on the wrong side makes one side ₹500 too high and the other ₹500 too low, so the totals differ by ₹1,000. R explains A.

questions.q: [Mock A] Machine ₹1,00,000 at 15% WDV. Depreciation in year 2?
questions.why: WDV depreciation in year 2 is charged on the reduced balance. Year 1: 15% of ₹1,00,000 = ₹15,000, leaving ₹85,000. Year 2: 15% of ₹85,000 = ₹12,750.

questions.q: [Mock A] Profit ₹50,000; furniture ₹8,000 debited to Purchases. Correct profit?
questions.why: Furniture is a capital item, but it was charged to Purchases as an expense. This made profit too low by ₹8,000. Correct profit = ₹50,000 + ₹8,000 = ₹58,000.

questions.q: [Mock A] Case: Debtors ₹2,10,000; further bad debts ₹10,000; PDD 5%; old PDD ₹8,000; TB bad debts ₹3,000. P&L charge?
[Mock A] Petty cash imprest ₹2,500; closing balance ₹420. Reimbursement?
questions.why: With the imprest system, the amount reimbursed equals what was spent. ₹2,500 − ₹420 left = ₹2,080, which restores the fund to ₹2,500.

questions.q: [Mock A] An advance received from a customer is…
questions.why: An advance from a customer is money received before the goods or service are given. The firm owes goods or a refund, so it is a current liability, not revenue yet.

questions.q: [Mock B] Which is an external user?
questions.why: External users are outside the business, like creditors, banks and tax authorities. Managers, employees and the owner work in or own the firm, so they are internal users.

questions.q: [Mock B] Provision for tax is a…
questions.why: Provision for tax is money set aside for a known liability whose exact amount is not certain. Reserves are made out of profit; a provision is a charge against profit.

questions.q: [Mock B] Overdraft per cash book ₹12,000; cheques issued not presented ₹4,500. OD per passbook?
questions.why: Cheques issued but not presented are in the cash book but not in the passbook. So the passbook overdraft is smaller: ₹12,000 − ₹4,500 = ₹7,500.

questions.q: [Mock B] Net sales ₹7,50,000; GP 25% on cost. GP?
questions.why: GP is 25% on cost, so it is 25/125 of sales. ₹7,50,000 × 25/125 = ₹1,50,000. Taking 25% of sales (₹1,87,500) is wrong because the base is cost.

questions.q: [Mock B] NP before commission ₹2,64,000; manager 10% after charging. Commission?
questions.why: Commission is 10% of profit after charging it, so it is 10/110 of profit before commission. ₹2,64,000 × 10/110 = ₹24,000.

questions.q: [Mock B] Asset cost ₹2,00,000; accumulated dep ₹85,000; sold ₹1,25,000. Result?
questions.why: Book value = cost − accumulated depreciation = ₹2,00,000 − ₹85,000 = ₹1,15,000. Sale price ₹1,25,000 is higher, so profit = ₹10,000.

questions.q: [Mock B] Rent ₹30,000 paid for 15 months up to 30 June 2026; year ends 31 March 2026. Prepaid rent?
questions.why: The rent covers 15 months up to 30 June 2026. The months after 31 March (April, May, June) are 3 months. ₹30,000 ÷ 15 = ₹2,000 a month, so prepaid = 3 × ₹2,000 = ₹6,000.

questions.q: [Mock B] Case: Opening stock 60,000; purchases 5,00,000; returns 20,000; wages 40,000; closing stock 80,000; sales 7,00,000. GP?
[Mock B] Assertion (A): Capital reserves are generally not distributed as dividend. Reason (R): They arise from capital profits.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true and R explains A. Capital reserves come from capital profits (such as profit on sale of fixed assets), which are not earned from normal trading, so they are not paid out as dividend.

questions.q: [Mock B] Which error does NOT affect the trial balance?
questions.why: A compensating error is where one error is cancelled by another, so debit and credit totals stay equal. The other errors listed change one side only, so they upset the trial balance.

questions.q: [Mock B] Insurance ₹24,000 paid 1 Aug 2025 for a year; prepaid on 31 March 2026?
questions.why: The policy runs from 1 Aug 2025 to 31 July 2026. On 31 March 2026, 8 months are used and 4 months remain. Prepaid = ₹24,000 × 4/12 = ₹8,000.

questions.q: [Mock B] Interest on drawings is shown in P&L on the…
questions.why: Interest on drawings is charged to the owner, so it is income for the firm. It is shown on the credit side of P&L and added to the loss of drawings in capital.

school-c11-biology-a.title: Class 11 Biology — Part A (Ch 1 to Ch 10)
school-c11-biology-a.description: All 19 chapters of Class 11 Biology, chapter by chapter: diversity, structure, cell biology, plant physiology and human physiology, with solved questions, quizzes, chapter tests and a revision course.

courses.title: Ch 1 · The Living World
courses.summary: What makes something living, the vast diversity of organisms, scientific naming (binomial nomenclature), classification and the taxonomic hierarchy from species to kingdom.
outcomes: Learners can distinguish defining from non-defining features of life
Learners can write scientific names correctly using binomial nomenclature
Learners can explain identification, nomenclature, classification and taxonomy
Learners can arrange taxonomic categories and place common organisms in them

lessons.title: What is 'living'?

scenes.text: In a lab, a salt crystal 'grows' in a solution. Rohan asks: is it alive?
Growth alone cannot decide. Biologists look for features that only living things show.

steps.title: Features of living organisms
steps.body:
- **Growth:** increase in mass and number of cells. In living things growth is from *inside*; non-living crystals and mountains grow by accumulation on the surface — so growth is **not a defining** feature.
- **Reproduction:** producing offspring. Not defining either — mules, worker bees and infertile couples do not reproduce but are alive.
- **Metabolism:** the sum of all chemical reactions in the body. **Defining** — no non-living object shows it (though isolated reactions can be run in a test tube).
- **Cellular organisation:** all living bodies are made of cells. **Defining**.
- **Consciousness:** sensing and responding to the environment (light, water, temperature, other organisms). **Defining**; humans alone also have *self-consciousness*.

steps.title: Solved question 1
steps.body:
Why is reproduction not a defining property of life?

- Step 1: a defining property must be present in *all* living organisms and absent in non-living things.
- Step 2: many living organisms (mules, sterile worker bees) do not reproduce.
- Answer: since some living beings lack it, reproduction cannot define life.

steps.title: Solved question 2
steps.body:
A virus is inert outside a host but multiplies inside one. Is growth a defining feature?

- Growth occurs in non-living crystals too (by surface accumulation).
- Hence growth cannot separate living from non-living; viruses remain a borderline case discussed in Chapter 2.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling growth or reproduction a 'defining' characteristic.
- Forgetting that unicellular organisms show growth by cell division and that growth and reproduction are synonymous in them.
- Thinking only animals respond to stimuli — plants respond to light, water, touch.

activity.prompt: Is it a defining feature of life?

quiz.q: Which is a defining property of living organisms?
quiz.why: Metabolism, the sum of all chemical reactions in the body, is found in every living thing and in no non-living thing. Growth and movement also occur in non-living things like crystals and clouds, and some living things cannot reproduce.
Living things grow from inside, by cell division and increase in cell number. Non-living things such as crystals grow only by adding material on the surface.

quiz.q: In unicellular organisms, growth and reproduction are
quiz.why: In single-celled organisms, cell division makes the organism grow and also makes new individuals. So growth and reproduction are the same event, which makes them synonymous.
A mule is a living organism but it is sterile and cannot reproduce. So reproduction cannot be called a defining property of life, since not every living thing shows it.
Self-consciousness is awareness of oneself and the surroundings. Humans show this, while crystals, bacteria and plants do not in this sense.

sources: NCERT Class 11 Biology (The Living World)

lessons.title: Diversity and naming of organisms

scenes.text: The mango is 'aam' in Hindi, 'mamidi' in Telugu and 'mango' in English. A scientist in Brazil needs one name everyone understands.
That name is Mangifera indica — given by a worldwide system of rules.

steps.title: Biodiversity and nomenclature
steps.body:
About 1.7–1.8 million species have been described, and many more await discovery. To study them we need **identification** (correct description), **nomenclature** (naming) and **classification** (grouping).

Rules: plants follow the **ICBN** (International Code of Botanical Nomenclature, now the International Code of Nomenclature for algae, fungi and plants); animals follow the **ICZN** (International Code of Zoological Nomenclature).

steps.title: Binomial nomenclature
steps.body:
Given by **Carolus Linnaeus**. Each name has two parts: **genus** (generic name) + **specific epithet**.
- Names are in Latin or Latinised and written in *italics* (or underlined separately when handwritten).
- Genus starts with a capital letter; epithet with a small letter: *Mangifera indica*.
- The author's name may follow in abbreviated form: *Mangifera indica* Linn.

steps.title: Solved question 1: spot the error
steps.body:
Correct the name 'homo Sapiens'.

- Genus capital, epithet small: **Homo sapiens** (italics in print, each word underlined separately in handwriting).

steps.title: Solved question 2
steps.body:
Why are scientific names Latinised?

- Latin is a 'dead' language whose meanings do not drift, so names stay stable worldwide and avoid confusion between local names.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Capitalising the species epithet (*Panthera Leo* ✗).
- Writing both words with one continuous underline in handwriting.
- Thinking the common name is the scientific name.

activity.prompt: Complete the rules.
activity.text: The first word of a scientific name is the ___ and the second is the specific ___.

quiz.why: Carolus Linnaeus popularised binomial nomenclature, giving each organism a two-part Latin name of genus and species. Darwin, Mendel and Whittaker are known for other work.
In a scientific name the genus starts with a capital letter and the species epithet with a small letter, so it is Mangifera indica. Both parts are italicised.
Animal names follow the International Code of Zoological Nomenclature (ICZN). ICBN is for plants, and IUCN and WHO are not naming codes.
Scientific names are written in Latin and are printed in italics, or underlined when handwritten. This marks them out from the rest of the text.

quiz.q: Approximately how many species have been described?
quiz.why: About 1.7 to 1.8 million species have been described so far. The other numbers are far too small or too large for the described species.

sources: NCERT Class 11 Biology (The Living World)

lessons.title: Classification and taxonomy

scenes.text: A library with a million books is useless unless books are grouped by subject, shelf and section.
Classification does the same for living things — it groups them so we can study them.

steps.title: Key terms
steps.body:
- **Classification:** grouping organisms into convenient categories based on easily observable characters.
- **Taxon (pl. taxa):** a group at any level, e.g. 'mammals', 'dogs', 'plants'.
- **Taxonomy:** characterisation, identification, nomenclature and classification. Based on external and internal structure, cell structure, development and ecology.
- **Systematics:** taxonomy plus evolutionary relationships (Latin *systema*, systematic arrangement); Linnaeus wrote *Systema Naturae*.

steps.title: Solved question 1
steps.body:
Distinguish taxonomy and systematics.

- Taxonomy: identifies, names and classifies.
- Systematics: does the same **and** considers evolutionary relationships between organisms.

steps.title: Solved question 2
steps.body: Is 'wheat' a taxon? Yes — any named group at any rank (here a species) is a taxon; so are 'cereals' (informal) and 'Poaceae' (family).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using taxonomy and systematics as exact synonyms.
- Thinking a taxon must be a species — taxa exist at every level.
- Believing classification is only about appearance; modern taxonomy also uses cell structure, development and molecular data.

activity.prompt: Match the term to its meaning.

quiz.why: Systema Naturae was written by Carolus Linnaeus, the father of modern taxonomy. Aristotle, Darwin and Whittaker are known for other works.

options: a group at any taxonomic level
quiz.why: A taxon is a group of organisms at any level of classification, such as a species, genus or order. It is not just one rank, and it is not a name.
Systematics covers naming and identifying organisms, and also the evolutionary relationships between them. That extra part is what separates it from simple taxonomy.
Taxonomy uses many lines of evidence, such as external and internal structure, development and ecology. One feature like colour or size alone is not enough.

options: makes the study of diverse organisms manageable
quiz.why: There are millions of species, so grouping them by similarities makes studying them manageable. Classification does not remove variation or create species.

sources: NCERT Class 11 Biology (The Living World)

lessons.title: Taxonomic categories and hierarchy

scenes.text: Your postal address goes from house to city to state to country. A lion's 'address' goes from species up to kingdom.
Panthera leo → Panthera → Felidae → Carnivora → Mammalia → Chordata → Animalia.

steps.title: The hierarchy
steps.body:
From lowest to highest: **Species → Genus → Family → Order → Class → Phylum (animals) / Division (plants) → Kingdom**.

- **Species:** organisms with fundamental similarities (interbreeding natural populations), e.g. *leo*, *tigris*, *pardus* of genus *Panthera*.
- **Genus:** related species, e.g. *Panthera* (lion, tiger, leopard); *Felis* (cat) is a different genus.
- **Family:** related genera, e.g. Felidae (cats) vs Canidae (dogs); Solanaceae includes *Solanum*, *Petunia*, *Datura*.
- **Order:** related families: Carnivora includes Felidae and Canidae.
- **Class:** related orders: Mammalia includes Primata and Carnivora.
- **Phylum:** Chordata includes fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds, mammals.
Common characters **decrease** as we go up the hierarchy.

steps.title: Solved question 1: place the organisms
steps.body:
- **Human:** *Homo sapiens*, Hominidae, Primata, Mammalia, Chordata.
- **Housefly:** *Musca domestica*, Muscidae, Diptera, Insecta, Arthropoda.
- **Mango:** *Mangifera indica*, Anacardiaceae, Sapindales, Dicotyledonae, Angiospermae (division).
- **Wheat:** *Triticum aestivum*, Poaceae, Poales, Monocotyledonae, Angiospermae.

steps.title: Solved question 2
steps.body:
Which have more characters in common: members of the same genus or of the same class?

- Lower categories share more characters, so members of the **same genus**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Getting the order wrong (Order comes above Family).
- Using 'phylum' for plants (use 'division').
- Thinking higher categories have more common features — it is the opposite.

steps.title: Taxonomic aids
steps.body: Herbaria (pressed, labelled plant specimens), botanical gardens, museums, zoological parks and identification **keys** (paired contrasting statements called couplets) help taxonomists identify organisms.

activity.prompt: Arrange from lowest to highest category.

quiz.q: The family of the housefly is
quiz.why: The housefly belongs to family Muscidae. Diptera is its order and Insecta is its class, and Hominidae is the human family.

quiz.q: Which category has the most common characters among its members?
quiz.why: Species is the lowest category, so its members share the most characters. Higher ranks like genus, order and kingdom group more varied organisms, so they have fewer common characters.

quiz.q: Lion, tiger and leopard share the genus
quiz.why: Lion, tiger and leopard are closely related, so they share the genus Panthera (P. leo, P. tigris, P. pardus). Homo is for humans, Canis for dogs and Felis for domestic cats.
Wheat belongs to family Poaceae, which is placed in the order Poales. Primata is for humans and monkeys, and Diptera is for flies.

quiz.q: In plants, the category above class is
quiz.why: Botanists use division for the rank above class in plants. Zoologists call the same rank phylum.

sources: NCERT Class 11 Biology (The Living World)

questions.q: Which is a defining property of life?
questions.why: Cellular organisation is present in all living organisms and in no non-living object. Growth, reproduction and increase in mass can be shown by some non-living things or are absent in some living things.

questions.q: The correct way to write the scientific name of the tiger is
questions.why: The tiger's name is Panthera tigris: genus with a capital, species epithet with a small letter, both in italics. The other forms break this rule.

questions.q: Basic unit of classification is
questions.why: Species is the basic unit of classification and the lowest category. All the higher ranks are made by grouping species.

questions.q: Family of mango is
questions.why: Mango (Mangifera indica) is placed in family Anacardiaceae. Poaceae is for grasses, Felidae for cats and Solanaceae for potato and tomato.

questions.q: Carnivora includes
questions.why: Order Carnivora includes families such as Felidae (cats) and Canidae (dogs). Hominidae is not in this order, and Poaceae and Muscidae are not animals of that order.

questions.q: The number of described species is about
questions.why: About 1.7 to 1.8 million species have been described. The numbers 17,000 and 170,000 are too small, and 17 million is not the described count.

questions.q: Assertion: Growth cannot be taken as a defining property of life. Reason: non-living objects like crystals also grow.
options: Both true and R explains A
Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Both statements are true and R explains A. Crystals also grow, by adding material on the outside, so growth alone cannot tell living from non-living.

questions.q: Which statement is wrong?
options: Genus has one or more species
Higher categories have more common characters
questions.why: The wrong statement is that higher categories have more common characters. Going up the ranks, groups get larger and members share fewer characters; species share the most.

questions.q: Housefly belongs to class
questions.why: The housefly belongs to class Insecta. Diptera is its order, Muscidae its family, and Arthropoda its phylum.

questions.q: Which pair of plants belong to the same family?
questions.why: Solanum and Datura are both in family Solanaceae. Mango belongs to Anacardiaceae and wheat to Poaceae, so the other pairs differ.

questions.q: The term 'systematics' differs from taxonomy because it includes
questions.why: Systematics includes taxonomy but also studies evolutionary relationships (phylogeny). Naming, identification and classification are already part of taxonomy.

questions.q: Case: A student writes 'Musca Domestica' in an answer. The mistake is
questions.why: In a scientific name only the genus begins with a capital letter. So Musca domestica is correct, and capitalising the specific epithet (Domestica) is the mistake.

questions.q: Case: A botanist collects, presses and labels plant specimens for reference. She is building a
questions.why: A herbarium is a store of dried, pressed and labelled plant specimens used for reference and study. A zoo and an animal museum deal with animals, and a key is for identification.

questions.q: Which shows correct ascending order?
questions.why: Going up in rank, the order is species, genus, family, order, class. Each higher rank groups together several members of the rank below.

questions.q: Which is common to all living organisms but cannot be shown by any non-living object?
questions.why: Metabolism is the chemical reactions in a living cell, and it occurs in every living organism and in no non-living object. Growth, movement and size increase can be seen in non-living things.

questions.q: Human and housefly share which category?
questions.why: Humans and houseflies are both animals, so they share kingdom Animalia. Their phyla differ (Chordata and Arthropoda), so they share no lower rank.

questions.q: Wheat and mango share which categories?
questions.why: Wheat and mango are both flowering plants, so they share the kingdom and the division Angiospermae. Wheat is a monocot and mango a dicot, so class, order and family differ.

questions.q: An identification key uses
questions.why: An identification key is made of couplets, which are pairs of contrasting characters. Each choice leads to the next step until the organism is identified.

courses.title: Ch 2 · Biological Classification
courses.summary: From two kingdoms to Whittaker's five-kingdom system; Monera, Protista and Fungi in detail; Plantae and Animalia in outline; and the acellular world of viruses, viroids, plus lichens.
outcomes: Learners can explain the criteria behind the five-kingdom classification
Learners can describe the main groups of bacteria and their importance
Learners can identify the major protist groups with examples
Learners can classify fungi into their classes with examples
Learners can describe viruses, viroids and lichens

lessons.title: From two kingdoms to five

scenes.text: Euglena makes food by photosynthesis in light but eats like an animal in the dark.
In a plant-vs-animal system it does not fit. Whittaker's five kingdoms solved such puzzles.

steps.title: History
steps.body:
- **Aristotle:** plants (trees, shrubs, herbs) and animals (with or without red blood).
- **Linnaeus:** two kingdoms — Plantae and Animalia. Problems: prokaryotes and eukaryotes, unicellular and multicellular, photosynthetic and non-photosynthetic organisms were mixed together.
- **R.H. Whittaker (1969):** five kingdoms — **Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae, Animalia**.

steps.title: Whittaker's criteria
steps.body:
- Cell structure (prokaryotic / eukaryotic)
- Body organisation (unicellular / multicellular)
- Mode of nutrition (autotrophic / heterotrophic)
- Reproduction
- Phylogenetic relationships

Cell wall: absent in animals, cellulose in plants, chitin in fungi, non-cellulosic (peptidoglycan) in bacteria.

steps.title: Solved question 1
steps.body:
Why were fungi separated from plants?

- Fungi are heterotrophic (no chlorophyll), have chitin cell walls, and store glycogen — unlike plants.

steps.title: Solved question 2
steps.body: Which kingdom has prokaryotes? **Monera** — the only prokaryotic kingdom; all others are eukaryotic.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying Whittaker proposed three kingdoms — he proposed five (1969).
- Placing unicellular eukaryotes in Monera (they go in Protista).
- Thinking all bacteria are harmful.

activity.prompt: Match the kingdom to its key feature.

quiz.why: R.H. Whittaker proposed the five-kingdom classification in 1969. Linnaeus gave the two-kingdom system and binomial names, and Aristotle and Darwin are not linked to it.

quiz.q: Which is not a Whittaker criterion?
quiz.why: Whittaker used cell structure, body organisation, mode of nutrition, reproduction and phylogenetic relationship. Colour of the organism was not a criterion.
The cell wall of fungi is made of chitin, a polysaccharide. Plants have cellulose and bacteria have peptidoglycan.
Monera includes all bacteria, which are prokaryotes. Protista, Fungi, Plantae and Animalia are made of eukaryotic cells.
The two-kingdom system put everything in plants or animals. It could not separate prokaryotes (like bacteria) from eukaryotes, nor unicellular from multicellular organisms.

sources: NCERT Class 11 Biology (Biological Classification)

lessons.title: Kingdom Monera: bacteria

scenes.text: Grandma adds a spoon of curd to warm milk; by morning it has set.
Bacteria (Lactobacillus) did it. Monera are tiny but run much of the living world.

steps.title: Bacteria
steps.body:
Most abundant micro-organisms; found everywhere, even hot springs and deep oceans. Shapes: **coccus** (spherical), **bacillus** (rod), **vibrium** (comma), **spirillum** (spiral).

Nutrition: mostly heterotrophic (decomposers), some autotrophic — **photosynthetic** or **chemosynthetic** (oxidise nitrates, nitrites, ammonia; help recycle N, P, Fe, S).

steps.title: Groups
steps.body:
- **Archaebacteria:** extreme habitats — **halophiles** (salty), **thermoacidophiles** (hot springs), **methanogens** (marshy areas, gut of cattle; produce methane/biogas). Different cell wall structure.
- **Eubacteria ('true bacteria'):** rigid cell wall, flagellum if motile. **Cyanobacteria** (blue-green algae) have chlorophyll a; some (*Nostoc*, *Anabaena*) fix nitrogen in **heterocysts**; may form blooms.
- **Mycoplasma:** no cell wall, smallest living cells, can survive without oxygen; many are pathogenic.
- Reproduction mainly by **fission**; spores in bad conditions; DNA transfer as a primitive sexual process.

steps.title: Solved question 1
steps.body: Why are methanogens useful? They live in the rumen of cattle and produce methane from dung — the basis of **biogas** plants.

steps.title: Solved question 2
steps.body: Which structure in Anabaena fixes nitrogen? The specialised cells called **heterocysts**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling cyanobacteria true algae (they are prokaryotes).
- Saying all bacteria are pathogens — many are essential (curd, nitrogen fixation, antibiotics).
- Confusing Mycoplasma (no wall) with archaebacteria.

activity.prompt: Sort the organism.

quiz.why: Rod-shaped bacteria are bacilli. Cocci are spherical, vibrio is comma-shaped and spirilla are spiral.
Methanogens are archaebacteria that live in harsh places such as marshes and the guts of ruminants, and make methane. Mycoplasma and cyanobacteria are different groups.
Nostoc is a cyanobacterium that forms heterocysts, thick-walled cells where nitrogen is fixed. Amoeba, yeast and Mycoplasma lack them.

quiz.q: Smallest living cells lacking cell walls are
quiz.why: Mycoplasma are the smallest living cells and have no cell wall. Viruses are smaller, but they are not cells.
Bacteria mainly reproduce by binary fission, where one cell divides into two. Spores, seeds and hyphal budding are not their main method.

sources: NCERT Class 11 Biology (Biological Classification)

lessons.title: Kingdom Protista

scenes.text: Fishermen see the sea turn red and fish die in large numbers.
A bloom of dinoflagellates like Gonyaulax releases toxins — protists at work.

steps.title: Protista
steps.body: All **single-celled eukaryotes**; mostly aquatic; nucleus and membrane-bound organelles; some have flagella or cilia. Link with plants, animals and fungi.

steps.title: Groups
steps.body:
- **Chrysophytes:** diatoms and desmids (golden algae). Diatoms have silica walls in two thin overlapping shells; their deposits form **diatomaceous earth** (used in polishing, filtering oils). Chief producers in oceans.
- **Dinoflagellates:** marine, photosynthetic, stiff cellulose plates; two flagella; red dinoflagellates (*Gonyaulax*) cause **red tides**.
- **Euglenoids:** freshwater, **pellicle** (protein-rich, flexible) instead of a wall, two flagella; photosynthetic in light, heterotrophic in dark (*Euglena*).
- **Slime moulds:** saprophytic; form a **plasmodium** in favourable conditions; spores with true walls, extremely resistant.
- **Protozoans:** heterotrophs — **amoeboid** (*Amoeba*, *Entamoeba*), **flagellated** (*Trypanosoma* — sleeping sickness), **ciliated** (*Paramoecium*, with a gullet), **sporozoans** (*Plasmodium* — malaria).

steps.title: Solved question 1
steps.body: What is diatomaceous earth? Silica-walled diatom shells that accumulated over billions of years; used in polishing and filtration because silica does not decay.

steps.title: Solved question 2
steps.body: Why is Euglena called a connecting link? It has chlorophyll (plant-like) but no cell wall and can feed heterotrophically (animal-like).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying dinoflagellates have silica walls (it is diatoms).
- Placing Plasmodium (malaria) among bacteria — it is a sporozoan protist.
- Confusing pellicle (euglenoids) with a cell wall.

activity.prompt: Match the protist to its feature.

quiz.why: Red tides are caused by rapid growth of dinoflagellates such as Gonyaulax, which colour the sea red. Their toxins can kill fish.

quiz.q: Euglenoids lack a cell wall but have a
quiz.why: Euglenoids have no cell wall. Instead they have a protein-rich, flexible layer called the pellicle, which lets the body change shape.
Malaria is caused by Plasmodium, a sporozoan protozoan. Trypanosoma causes sleeping sickness and Entamoeba causes amoebic dysentery.

quiz.q: Slime moulds form an aggregation called
quiz.why: Under suitable conditions slime moulds form a mass called a plasmodium, which can grow several feet long. Mycelium belongs to fungi.

quiz.q: Chief producers in the oceans are
quiz.why: Diatoms are the chief producers in the oceans, because they photosynthesise in vast numbers. Slime moulds and protozoans are not major producers there.

sources: NCERT Class 11 Biology (Biological Classification)

lessons.title: Kingdom Fungi

scenes.text: Bread left for a week grows white-and-black fuzz.
That fuzz is Rhizopus, a fungus — a cousin of the mushrooms we eat and the yeast that makes bread rise.

steps.title: General features
steps.body:
- Heterotrophic: **saprophytes** (dead matter), **parasites**, or **symbionts** (lichens with algae, **mycorrhiza** with plant roots).
- Body of thread-like **hyphae** forming a **mycelium**; **coenocytic** hyphae are continuous with many nuclei; others have septae. Yeasts are unicellular.
- Cell wall of **chitin** and polysaccharides.
- Reproduction: vegetative (fragmentation, fission, budding); asexual spores (conidia, sporangiospores, zoospores); sexual spores (oospores, ascospores, basidiospores). Sexual cycle: **plasmogamy → karyogamy → meiosis**; in ascomycetes and basidiomycetes a **dikaryon** (n + n) stage occurs.

steps.title: Classes
steps.body:
- **Phycomycetes:** aseptate coenocytic mycelium; zoospores or aplanospores; *Mucor*, *Rhizopus* (bread mould), *Albugo* (parasite on mustard).
- **Ascomycetes (sac fungi):** septate; conidia; ascospores in asci inside **ascocarps**; *Aspergillus*, *Claviceps*, *Neurospora* (genetics), yeast (*Saccharomyces*), *Penicillium*; morels and truffles are edible.
- **Basidiomycetes:** mushrooms, bracket fungi, puffballs; basidiospores on **basidia** in basidiocarps; no asexual spores usually; *Agaricus* (mushroom), *Ustilago* (smut), *Puccinia* (rust).
- **Deuteromycetes (imperfect fungi):** sexual stage unknown; reproduce by conidia; *Alternaria*, *Colletotrichum*, *Trichoderma*.

steps.title: Solved question 1
steps.body: Why are Deuteromycetes called 'imperfect fungi'? Only their asexual (imperfect) stage is known; when the sexual stage is found, they are moved to Ascomycetes or Basidiomycetes.

steps.title: Solved question 2
steps.body: Identify the class: a septate fungus producing basidiospores on club-shaped basidia → **Basidiomycetes** (e.g. *Agaricus*).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Putting *Penicillium* in Phycomycetes (it is an ascomycete).
- Calling mushrooms plants.
- Mixing the sequence: plasmogamy (cytoplasm fusion) comes before karyogamy (nuclear fusion).

activity.prompt: Place the fungus in its class.

quiz.why: Coenocytic hyphae have no cross walls (aseptate) and many nuclei in one continuous cytoplasm. Septate hyphae have cross walls.
Ascospores are formed inside sac-like asci, the spore bags of Ascomycetes. Basidiospores are made on basidia and conidia on conidiophores.

quiz.q: Smut and rust are caused by
quiz.why: Smut is caused by Ustilago and rust by Puccinia, both Basidiomycetes. Mucor and Rhizopus are moulds, and Albugo causes white rust.

quiz.q: The correct order in fungal sexual reproduction is
quiz.why: In fungi the cytoplasm of two cells fuses first (plasmogamy), then the nuclei fuse (karyogamy), and meiosis follows to give haploid spores. A dikaryotic stage comes between the first two.
Neurospora is an ascomycete used as a model organism in biochemical and genetic work. It is not used for baking, cheese or nitrogen fixation.

sources: NCERT Class 11 Biology (Biological Classification)

lessons.title: Plantae, Animalia, viruses, viroids and lichens

scenes.text: Tobacco plants in a field show patchy mosaic leaves. Filtering the juice does not remove the infectious agent.
Ivanowsky and Beijerinck had found viruses — too small for bacterial filters, alive only inside cells.

steps.title: Plantae and Animalia (outline)
steps.body:
- **Plantae:** eukaryotic, chlorophyll-containing, cellulose walls; a few are partly heterotrophic (insectivorous *Bladderwort*, *Venus fly trap*; parasitic *Cuscuta*). Life cycle shows **alternation of generations** (haploid gametophyte, diploid sporophyte).
- **Animalia:** heterotrophic multicellular eukaryotes without cell walls; holozoic nutrition; store food as glycogen or fat; definite growth pattern; sexual reproduction by copulation.

steps.title: Viruses, viroids, lichens
steps.body:
- **Viruses:** not cells; inert outside a host, multiply inside — obligate parasites. Nucleoprotein: genetic material **RNA or DNA** (never both) in a protein coat (**capsid** of capsomeres). Plant viruses usually single-stranded RNA; animal viruses ss/ds RNA or ds DNA; bacteriophages usually ds DNA. Diseases: mumps, smallpox, herpes, influenza, AIDS; mosaic in plants.
- History: **D.J. Ivanowsky (1892)** — agents of tobacco mosaic disease smaller than bacteria; **M.W. Beijerinck (1898)** — 'contagium vivum fluidum'; **W.M. Stanley (1935)** — viruses can be crystallised.
- **Viroids:** discovered by **T.O. Diener (1971)**; free low-molecular-weight RNA without protein coat; cause potato spindle tuber disease.
- **Lichens:** symbiotic association of an **alga (phycobiont)** and a **fungus (mycobiont)**; good **pollution indicators** — they do not grow in polluted areas.

steps.title: Solved question 1
steps.body: Why are viruses called obligate parasites? They have no metabolic machinery of their own and can multiply only inside a living host cell.

steps.title: Solved question 2
steps.body: Viroid vs virus: a viroid is just free RNA (no protein coat) and much smaller; a virus has a protein capsid around its RNA or DNA.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying viruses contain both DNA and RNA.
- Placing viruses in Monera — they are not included in the five kingdoms.
- Mixing up phycobiont (alga) and mycobiont (fungus).

statements.s: Viruses can be crystallised.
Viroids have a protein coat.
Lichens grow abundantly in polluted cities.
statements.why: They are pollution indicators and are absent there.

statements.s: Cuscuta is a parasitic plant.
statements.why: It lacks chlorophyll and draws food from host plants.

statements.s: Bacteriophages usually contain double-stranded DNA.

quiz.why: M.W. Beijerinck described the infectious sap of tobacco mosaic disease as contagium vivum fluidum (living infectious fluid) in 1898. Ivanowsky had earlier shown the agent passed through filters.
T.O. Diener discovered viroids in 1971. They are smaller than viruses and are free RNA without a protein coat.

quiz.q: In lichens, the algal partner is called the
quiz.why: In lichens, the alga is the phycobiont (phyco means alga) and the fungus is the mycobiont. They live together to the benefit of both.

quiz.q: The protein coat of a virus is the
quiz.why: The protein coat of a virus is the capsid, built from units called capsomeres. It protects the nucleic acid inside.
The Venus fly trap is an insectivorous plant that catches insects. Albugo and Rhizopus are fungi, and Cuscuta is a parasitic plant.

sources: NCERT Class 11 Biology (Biological Classification)

questions.q: Whittaker proposed five-kingdom classification in
questions.why: Whittaker proposed the five-kingdom classification in 1969. Linnaeus's work is from 1753 and Darwin's from 1859.

questions.q: Cyanobacteria are also called
questions.why: Cyanobacteria are photosynthetic bacteria, also called blue-green algae. They are not red algae, sac fungi or slime moulds.

questions.q: Bread mould is
questions.why: Bread mould is Rhizopus, a phycomycete. Agaricus is a mushroom, and Puccinia and Ustilago are plant pathogens.

questions.q: Diatomaceous earth is made of
questions.why: Diatom cell walls are made of silica, which does not decay. Their deposits form diatomaceous earth, which is used for polishing and filtering.

questions.q: Sleeping sickness is caused by
questions.why: Sleeping sickness is caused by Trypanosoma, a flagellated protozoan. Plasmodium causes malaria and Entamoeba causes amoebic dysentery.

questions.q: Which is an imperfect fungus?
questions.why: Alternaria is a deuteromycete, called an imperfect fungus because its sexual stage is not known. Agaricus, Mucor and Neurospora have known sexual stages.

questions.q: Assertion: Mycoplasma are not affected by penicillin. Reason: they lack a cell wall.
options: Both true and R explains A
Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Both statements are true and R explains A. Penicillin blocks cell wall synthesis, and Mycoplasma has no cell wall, so it has no target and is not affected.

questions.q: Methanogens are found in
options: the rumen of cattle and marshes
questions.why: Methanogens live in oxygen-poor places such as marshes and the rumen of cattle, where they make methane. They are not found only in hot springs or salt pans.

questions.q: Viruses that infect bacteria are
questions.why: Viruses that infect bacteria are called bacteriophages, meaning bacteria eaters. Viroids and prions are not viruses, and lichens are fungus-alga partnerships.

questions.q: Dikaryotic stage is characteristic of
questions.why: The dikaryotic (n + n) stage, where two nuclei live in one cell, is typical of Ascomycetes and Basidiomycetes. Phycomycetes, bacteria and protozoa lack it.

questions.q: Which pair is mismatched?
questions.why: Albugo is a phycomycete, not an ascomycete, so that pair is mismatched. Penicillium is an ascomycete, Trichoderma is a deuteromycete and Puccinia is a basidiomycete.

questions.q: Case: Villagers feed cattle dung into a closed tank and cook with the gas formed. The microbes doing this are
questions.why: Cattle dung in a closed tank is broken down without oxygen by methanogens, which produce methane (biogas). Cyanobacteria and diatoms do not do this.

questions.q: Case: A city's old trees once covered with lichens now show none after heavy traffic increased. This suggests
questions.why: Lichens are very sensitive to sulphur dioxide, so they disappear where air is polluted. Heavy traffic raises SO₂, which explains the loss.

questions.q: Which feature is shared by euglenoids and dinoflagellates?
questions.why: Euglenoids and dinoflagellates both have two flagella. Silica walls belong to diatoms, and cellulose plates only to dinoflagellates.

questions.q: The infectious agent of potato spindle tuber disease is
questions.why: Potato spindle tuber disease is caused by a viroid. A viroid is free RNA of low molecular weight, with no protein coat.

questions.q: Chemosynthetic autotrophic bacteria obtain energy by
options: oxidising inorganic substances like nitrates and ammonia
questions.why: Chemosynthetic autotrophic bacteria get energy by oxidising inorganic substances such as nitrates, nitrites and ammonia. They use that energy to make their own food, instead of using light.

questions.q: Which statement about fungi is correct?
options: Yeast is unicellular and Neurospora is an ascomycete
questions.why: Yeast is unicellular and Neurospora is an ascomycete, so this is correct. Fungi can be multicellular; fungal walls are chitin; and Basidiomycetes do not usually form conidia.

questions.q: Which is the correct match of scientist and discovery?
questions.why: W.M. Stanley showed in 1935 that viruses can be crystallised. Diener found viroids, Beijerinck gave the contagium vivum fluidum idea and Whittaker proposed five kingdoms.

courses.title: Ch 3 · Plant Kingdom
courses.summary: Algae (green, brown, red), bryophytes, pteridophytes, gymnosperms and angiosperms with key features, examples and economic importance, plus plant life-cycle patterns.
outcomes: Learners can classify algae by pigments, stored food and examples
Learners can describe the gametophyte-dominant life of bryophytes
Learners can explain why pteridophytes are the first vascular plants and what heterospory means
Learners can compare gymnosperms and angiosperms including double fertilisation

lessons.title: Algae

scenes.text: Some ice creams and jellies use agar or carrageen as thickeners.
These come from red algae; algin comes from brown algae. Algae feed oceans and industries alike.

steps.title: General features
steps.body:
Simple, chlorophyll-bearing, thalloid, autotrophic, mostly aquatic. Forms range from colonial (*Volvox*) and filamentous (*Ulothrix*, *Spirogyra*) to giant kelps.

Reproduction: vegetative (fragmentation), asexual (zoospores), sexual — **isogamous** (similar gametes, e.g. *Spirogyra* — non-flagellated, *Ulothrix* flagellated), **anisogamous** (dissimilar size, *Eudorina*), **oogamous** (large non-motile egg + small motile sperm, *Volvox*, *Fucus*).

Uses: about half of total CO₂ fixation on Earth; food (*Porphyra*, *Laminaria*, *Sargassum*); *Chlorella* is protein-rich, used as food supplement even by space travellers.

steps.title: Three classes
steps.body:
- **Chlorophyceae (green):** chlorophyll a, b; stored food **starch** (in pyrenoids); cellulose wall; 2–8 equal apical flagella; *Chlamydomonas*, *Volvox*, *Ulothrix*, *Spirogyra*, *Chara*.
- **Phaeophyceae (brown):** chlorophyll a, c, carotenoids and **fucoxanthin**; stored food **laminarin** and **mannitol**; wall with **algin**; body with holdfast, stipe and frond; 2 unequal lateral flagella; *Ectocarpus*, *Dictyota*, *Laminaria*, *Sargassum*, *Fucus*.
- **Rhodophyceae (red):** chlorophyll a, d and **r-phycoerythrin**; stored food **floridean starch**; no flagella; *Polysiphonia*, *Porphyra*, *Gracilaria*, *Gelidium*. **Agar** from *Gelidium* and *Gracilaria*; carrageen from red algae.

steps.title: Solved question 1
steps.body: A marine alga has fucoxanthin and stores mannitol. Name the class. → **Phaeophyceae** (brown algae).

steps.title: Solved question 2
steps.body: Why can red algae live in deep water? Their **r-phycoerythrin** absorbs the blue-green light that penetrates deepest.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying red algae have flagella (they have none).
- Mixing stored foods: starch (green), laminarin/mannitol (brown), floridean starch (red).
- Thinking agar comes from brown algae.

activity.prompt: Sort into the correct algal class.

quiz.why: Agar comes from the red algae Gelidium and Gracilaria. Spirogyra and Chlamydomonas are green algae, and Laminaria and Fucus are brown algae.

quiz.q: Stored food of brown algae is
quiz.why: Brown algae store food as laminarin and mannitol. Red algae store floridean starch and green algae store starch.
Oogamy means a large non-motile egg fuses with a small motile male gamete. It is seen in Volvox and Fucus. Spirogyra shows conjugation and Ulothrix shows isogamy.
Chlorella is a unicellular green alga rich in protein. It is used as a food supplement, for example by space travellers.
Red algae (Rhodophyceae) contain chlorophyll a and d, along with phycoerythrin. Green algae have a and b, and brown algae have a and c.

sources: NCERT Class 11 Biology (Plant Kingdom)

lessons.title: Bryophytes

scenes.text: After monsoon, old walls and rocks turn green and velvety.
Those are mosses and liverworts — the 'amphibians of the plant kingdom'.

steps.title: Features
steps.body:
- Live on land but need water for sexual reproduction → **amphibians of the plant kingdom**; common in damp, shady places.
- Plant body is the haploid **gametophyte** (dominant); attached by **rhizoids**; no true roots, stems or leaves.
- Sex organs multicellular: **antheridium** (male) with biflagellate **antherozoids**; flask-shaped **archegonium** (female) with one egg.
- Zygote → **sporophyte** (foot, seta, capsule), dependent on the gametophyte; meiosis in the capsule → spores.
- Importance: early colonisers of rocks (with lichens), prevent soil erosion; **Sphagnum** gives **peat** (fuel, packing material that holds water).

steps.title: Liverworts and mosses
steps.body:
- **Liverworts** (*Marchantia*): thalloid, dorsiventral; asexual by fragmentation and **gemmae** (green buds in gemma cups).
- **Mosses** (*Funaria*, *Polytrichum*, *Sphagnum*): gametophyte has two stages — creeping green **protonema** (from spore) and leafy stage; elaborate spore dispersal.

steps.title: Solved question 1
steps.body: Why are bryophytes called amphibians of the plant kingdom? They live on land but need water for the antherozoids to swim to the egg.

steps.title: Solved question 2
steps.body: Which generation is dominant in a moss? The haploid **gametophyte**; the sporophyte depends on it for nutrition.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling rhizoids true roots.
- Saying the sporophyte is independent in bryophytes.
- Confusing gemmae (liverworts) with protonema (mosses).

activity.prompt: Match the bryophyte term.

quiz.q: The dominant phase of bryophytes is
quiz.why: In bryophytes the main plant body is the haploid gametophyte. The sporophyte is smaller and depends on it for food.
Peat, used as fuel and as packing material, is formed from Sphagnum, a moss. Funaria is also a moss but is not a peat source.

quiz.q: Water is needed in bryophytes for
quiz.why: In bryophytes the male gametes (antherozoids) are flagellated and must swim through water to the egg. So water is needed for fertilisation.

quiz.q: The sporophyte of a moss consists of
quiz.why: The moss sporophyte has a foot, a seta (stalk) and a capsule that holds the spores. It has no true roots, stem or leaves.
Gemmae are small green buds in gemma cups, used for vegetative reproduction in liverworts such as Marchantia. Mosses reproduce vegetatively in different ways.

sources: NCERT Class 11 Biology (Plant Kingdom)

lessons.title: Pteridophytes

scenes.text: On a trip to Darjeeling, Aditi notices ferns with brown dots under their leaves.
The dots are sori — clusters of sporangia. Ferns were the first land plants with true conducting tissue.

steps.title: Features
steps.body:
- First terrestrial plants with **vascular tissues** — xylem and phloem.
- Main plant body is the diploid **sporophyte** with true root, stem and leaves (small **microphylls** in *Selaginella*; large **macrophylls** in ferns).
- Sporangia on leaf-like **sporophylls**; may form compact **strobili/cones** (*Selaginella*, *Equisetum*).
- Spores germinate into small, free-living, mostly photosynthetic **prothallus** (gametophyte) needing cool, damp places; water needed for fertilisation.
- **Homosporous** (one kind of spore) in most; **heterosporous** (megaspores and microspores) in *Selaginella* and *Salvinia* — a precursor to the **seed habit**.
- Classes: Psilopsida (*Psilotum*), Lycopsida (*Selaginella*, *Lycopodium*), Sphenopsida (*Equisetum*), Pteropsida (*Dryopteris*, *Pteris*, *Adiantum*).
- Uses: medicinal, soil binders, ornamental.

steps.title: Solved question 1
steps.body: Why is heterospory important? Megaspores retained on the parent develop into female gametophytes, and the zygote develops into an embryo there — an evolutionary step towards seeds.

steps.title: Solved question 2
steps.body: What is a prothallus? The small, free-living haploid gametophyte of a pteridophyte that bears antheridia and archegonia.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying pteridophytes produce seeds.
- Calling the prothallus the main plant body.
- Writing that all pteridophytes are heterosporous.

statements.s: Pteridophytes are the first plants with xylem and phloem.
The main plant body of a fern is haploid.
Selaginella is heterosporous.
Equisetum belongs to Sphenopsida.
Pteridophytes do not need water for fertilisation.

quiz.why: Heterospory means two kinds of spores, small microspores and large megaspores. It is seen in Selaginella and Salvinia, while Dryopteris and Pteris are homosporous.

quiz.q: The gametophyte of pteridophytes is called
quiz.why: In pteridophytes the gametophyte is a small, free-living, thalloid structure called a prothallus. Protonema belongs to mosses, and capsule and gemma are other structures.
Leaves that bear sporangia are called sporophylls. In some plants they form compact cones (strobili).
Adiantum, the maidenhair fern, is a fern of the class Pteropsida, so it is a pteridophyte. It is not a moss, liverwort or gymnosperm.

quiz.q: Small leaves as in Selaginella are called
quiz.why: Small leaves, as in Selaginella, are microphylls. Large leaves, as in ferns, are macrophylls.

sources: NCERT Class 11 Biology (Plant Kingdom)

lessons.title: Gymnosperms, angiosperms and life cycles

scenes.text: Giant redwoods (Sequoia) are among the tallest trees; the smallest flowering plant, Wolffia, floats on ponds.
Both make seeds — but only Wolffia's seeds are enclosed in a fruit.

steps.title: Gymnosperms
steps.body:
- **Naked seeds** — ovules not enclosed in an ovary.
- Medium to tall trees and shrubs; *Sequoia* is one of the tallest trees.
- Roots generally tap roots; in *Pinus* roots have fungal association (**mycorrhiza**); *Cycas* has **coralloid roots** with N₂-fixing cyanobacteria.
- Leaves needle-like in conifers (reduce water loss, thick cuticle, sunken stomata).
- Heterosporous: microsporangia in **male cones** (pollen grains), megasporangia (ovules) in **female cones**; pollination by wind; gametophytes not free-living.

steps.title: Angiosperms and life cycles
steps.body:
- **Flowering plants**; seeds enclosed in **fruits**; from *Wolffia* to tall *Eucalyptus*; divided into **dicots** and **monocots**.
- Stamen (anther + filament), pistil (stigma, style, ovary); embryo sac has 7 cells: egg apparatus (egg + 2 synergids), 3 antipodals, 2 polar nuclei forming the secondary nucleus.
- **Double fertilisation:** one male gamete + egg → zygote (2n); the other + secondary nucleus → **primary endosperm nucleus (3n)** (**triple fusion**).

**Life-cycle patterns:** **haplontic** (sporophyte is only the zygote; *Volvox*, *Spirogyra*, some *Chlamydomonas*), **diplontic** (dominant sporophyte; seed plants, *Fucus*), **haplo-diplontic** (both multicellular phases; bryophytes, pteridophytes, *Ectocarpus*, *Polysiphonia*, kelps).

steps.title: Solved question 1
steps.body: What is the ploidy of endosperm in angiosperms? Triploid (3n) — formed by fusion of a male gamete (n) with two polar nuclei (n + n).

steps.title: Solved question 2
steps.body: Name a gymnosperm with coralloid roots and say why they are special. *Cycas* — they house nitrogen-fixing cyanobacteria.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying gymnosperms bear fruits.
- Forgetting that triple fusion involves two polar nuclei (one secondary nucleus) + a male gamete.
- Calling *Fucus* haplontic — it is diplontic.

activity.prompt: Match the life cycle pattern.

quiz.why: In gymnosperms the ovules are not enclosed in an ovary, so the seeds are naked. In angiosperms the ovary becomes a fruit that covers the seeds.
Cycas has coralloid roots, which grow upward and house nitrogen-fixing cyanobacteria. Pinus has mycorrhizal roots, and the others are different.
Angiosperm endosperm forms by triple fusion of one male gamete (n) with two polar nuclei (n + n), giving 3n. So it is triploid.

quiz.q: Number of cells in a typical angiosperm embryo sac is
quiz.why: A typical embryo sac has 7 cells (egg apparatus 3, antipodals 3, central cell 1) but 8 nuclei, since the central cell has two polar nuclei.

quiz.q: Mycorrhiza is seen in roots of
quiz.why: Pinus roots have a mycorrhizal association with fungi, which helps absorb water and minerals. Cycas roots instead have cyanobacteria in coralloid roots.

sources: NCERT Class 11 Biology (Plant Kingdom)

questions.q: Chlorophyll a and b are present in
questions.why: Green algae (Chlorophyceae) contain chlorophyll a and b. Red algae have a and d, and brown algae have a and c.

questions.q: Amphibians of the plant kingdom are
questions.why: Bryophytes are called the amphibians of the plant kingdom because they live on land but need water for fertilisation. Pteridophytes and gymnosperms do not need it in the same way.

questions.q: First vascular plants are
questions.why: Pteridophytes are the first plants with vascular tissue (xylem and phloem). Algae and bryophytes lack it.

questions.q: Algin is obtained from
questions.why: Algin is obtained from the cell walls of brown algae. Agar comes from red algae and peat from mosses.

questions.q: The smallest flowering plant is
questions.why: Wolffia is the smallest flowering plant, a tiny floating aquatic plant. Eucalyptus and Sequoia are among the tallest trees.

questions.q: In mosses, the stage developing directly from a spore is
questions.why: In mosses a spore grows into a creeping, green, branched filament called the protonema. The leafy gametophyte develops later from it.

questions.q: Assertion: Red algae can grow at great depths. Reason: r-phycoerythrin absorbs blue-green light that penetrates deep water.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
Both true and R explains A
questions.why: Both statements are true and R explains A. The red pigment r-phycoerythrin absorbs blue-green light, which is the light that reaches deep water, so red algae can photosynthesise at depth.

questions.q: Which pair has equal and apical flagella?
questions.why: Green algae (Chlorophyceae) have 2 to 8 equal flagella at the apex. Brown algae have two unequal lateral flagella, and red algae have none.

questions.q: Heterospory foreshadows
questions.why: In heterospory the megaspore is kept inside the parent sporangium and the embryo develops there. This is the first step towards the seed habit.

questions.q: Triple fusion results in
questions.why: Triple fusion is the fusion of one male gamete with the two polar nuclei (secondary nucleus). It forms the primary endosperm nucleus, while the other male gamete fuses with the egg to form the zygote.

questions.q: Case: A student finds a plant with roots, stem and leaves, no seeds, and brown sori under its leaves. It belongs to
questions.why: A plant with roots, stem and leaves, no seeds and sori on its leaves is a fern. Ferns are pteridophytes, since they have vascular tissue and reproduce by spores.

questions.q: Case: A food scientist needs a gelling agent for microbial culture plates. She will choose
questions.why: Agar from red algae is a jelly-forming substance used to make solid culture media for microbes. Algin is a thickener and peat is fuel.

questions.q: Which alga is mismatched with its class?
questions.why: Fucus is a brown alga (Phaeophyceae), not a red alga. The other pairs are correct.

questions.q: In gymnosperms, the male and female gametophytes
options: do not have an independent free-living existence
questions.why: In gymnosperms the male and female gametophytes are very reduced and stay inside the sporangia, so they are not free-living. In bryophytes and pteridophytes they are free-living.

questions.q: Ectocarpus shows which life cycle?
questions.why: Ectocarpus, a brown alga, has a haplo-diplontic life cycle, with both a haploid and a diploid phase that are multicellular. In a haplontic cycle only the haploid stage is multicellular.

questions.q: An embryo sac has 8 nuclei but how many cells?
questions.why: The embryo sac has 7 cells and 8 nuclei. The central cell has two polar nuclei in a single cell, so the cell count is one less than the nuclei count.

questions.q: Which statement is correct?
options: Bryophyte sporophytes depend on the gametophyte, while pteridophyte sporophytes are independent
Both have independent gametophytes and dependent sporophytes
questions.why: In bryophytes the gametophyte is dominant and the sporophyte depends on it. In pteridophytes the sporophyte is independent and dominant. Bryophytes lack xylem.

questions.q: Number of chromosomes in a Cycas leaf cell is 2n = 22 (example). The endosperm of gymnosperms (female gametophyte tissue) would have
questions.why: In gymnosperms the endosperm is the female gametophyte tissue, which is haploid (n). If 2n = 22, then n = 11. Angiosperm endosperm is different, as it is triploid.

courses.title: Ch 4 · Animal Kingdom
courses.summary: The basis of animal classification and a phylum-by-phylum tour from Porifera to Chordata, with the vertebrate classes, distinctive features and standard examples.
outcomes: Learners can use levels of organisation, symmetry, germ layers, coelom, segmentation and notochord to classify animals
Learners can describe non-chordate phyla with examples
Learners can list the fundamental chordate characters and subphyla
Learners can distinguish the vertebrate classes from Cyclostomata to Mammalia

lessons.title: Basis of classification

scenes.text: A new zookeeper must group animals scientifically, not by size or colour.
She asks six questions: organisation, symmetry, germ layers, body cavity, segmentation, notochord.

steps.title: Criteria
steps.body:
- **Levels of organisation:** cellular (sponges), tissue (coelenterates), organ (platyhelminthes), organ system (annelids to chordates).
- **Digestive system:** incomplete (one opening, e.g. platyhelminthes) vs complete (mouth + anus).
- **Circulatory system:** open (blood in open spaces) vs closed (blood in vessels).
- **Symmetry:** asymmetrical (most sponges), **radial** (coelenterates, ctenophores, adult echinoderms), **bilateral** (annelids, arthropods, etc.).
- **Germ layers:** **diploblastic** (ectoderm, endoderm with mesoglea between: coelenterates) vs **triploblastic** (with mesoderm: platyhelminthes to chordates).
- **Coelom:** **acoelomate** (platyhelminthes), **pseudocoelomate** (aschelminthes; mesoderm scattered), **coelomate** (annelids to chordates).
- **Segmentation (metamerism):** serial repetition, e.g. earthworm.
- **Notochord:** rod-like mesodermal structure on the dorsal side in chordates.

steps.title: Solved question 1
steps.body: Classify a flatworm by these criteria: organ level, bilateral, triploblastic, **acoelomate**, incomplete gut, no segmentation, no notochord.

steps.title: Solved question 2
steps.body: Why are roundworms called pseudocoelomates? Their body cavity is not fully lined by mesoderm; mesoderm is present as scattered pouches between ectoderm and endoderm.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling coelenterates triploblastic (they are diploblastic).
- Assuming adult echinoderms are bilateral (larvae are bilateral, adults radial).
- Forgetting that sponges are at the cellular level.

activity.prompt: Pick the body-cavity type.

quiz.why: Coelenterates have two germ layers (ectoderm and endoderm), so they are diploblastic. Annelids, arthropods and chordates have three layers.
Radial symmetry means any plane through the central axis gives equal halves. It is seen in coelenterates and adult echinoderms.
A pseudocoelom is a body cavity not fully lined by mesoderm. It is found in Aschelminthes (roundworms). Annelids have a true coelom and flatworms have none.
Metamerism means the body is divided into repeated segments. It is clearly seen in the earthworm, an annelid. Sponge, Hydra and Ascaris are not segmented.

quiz.q: Sponges show which level of organisation?
quiz.why: Sponges are at the cellular level of organisation, since their cells are loosely arranged and do not form true tissues. Tissue and organ levels appear in higher groups.

sources: NCERT Class 11 Biology (Animal Kingdom)

lessons.title: Porifera to Aschelminthes

scenes.text: A swimmer at a beach feels a sharp sting from a jellyfish.
Cnidoblasts on its tentacles fire tiny threads — the signature of phylum Coelenterata.

steps.title: Porifera and Coelenterata
steps.body:
- **Porifera (sponges):** mostly marine, asymmetrical, cellular level; **water canal system** — water enters by **ostia**, passes the **spongocoel**, exits by the **osculum**; **choanocytes** (collar cells) line the canals; skeleton of **spicules** or spongin; hermaphrodite; internal fertilisation; *Sycon*, *Spongilla* (freshwater), *Euspongia* (bath sponge).
- **Coelenterata (Cnidaria):** aquatic, radial, tissue level, diploblastic; **cnidoblasts** (with nematocysts) for anchorage, defence, prey capture; gastro-vascular cavity with a single opening (hypostome); two forms — **polyp** (sessile, *Hydra*, *Adamsia*) and **medusa** (free-swimming, *Aurelia*); **metagenesis** (alternation of polyp and medusa) in *Obelia*; corals with CaCO₃ skeleton; *Physalia* (Portuguese man-of-war), *Pennatula*, *Gorgonia*, *Meandrina*.

steps.title: Ctenophora, Platyhelminthes, Aschelminthes
steps.body:
- **Ctenophora (comb jellies, sea walnuts):** marine, radial, diploblastic; eight external rows of ciliated **comb plates** for locomotion; **bioluminescence**; *Pleurobrachia*, *Ctenoplana*.
- **Platyhelminthes (flatworms):** dorso-ventrally flattened, bilateral, triploblastic, acoelomate, organ level; mostly endoparasites with hooks and suckers; **flame cells** for osmoregulation and excretion; hermaphrodite; *Taenia* (tapeworm), *Fasciola* (liver fluke); *Planaria* shows high **regeneration**.
- **Aschelminthes (roundworms):** circular in cross-section; pseudocoelomate; complete alimentary canal with muscular pharynx; sexes separate (dioecious) with **sexual dimorphism** (females longer); *Ascaris* (roundworm), *Wuchereria* (filarial worm), *Ancylostoma* (hookworm).

steps.title: Solved question 1
steps.body: What is metagenesis? Alternation between the asexual polyp and sexual medusa forms in some cnidarians, e.g. *Obelia*: polyps bud medusae; medusae form gametes; the zygote grows into a polyp.

steps.title: Solved question 2
steps.body: Which cells help sponges in feeding and water flow? **Choanocytes** — their flagella drive water through the canal system and trap food.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying water enters a sponge through the osculum (it exits there).
- Putting comb jellies in Coelenterata.
- Thinking roundworms are hermaphrodites — sexes are separate.

activity.prompt: Match the animal to its phylum.

quiz.why: Choanocytes, or collar cells, line the spongocoel and canals of sponges. Their flagella drive the water current. Flame cells belong to flatworms and cnidoblasts to coelenterates.
Ctenophores have eight rows of ciliated comb plates, which beat to move the animal. So comb plates help in locomotion.
Flame cells (protonephridia) are excretory and osmoregulatory structures in flatworms such as Planaria. Annelids have nephridia and sponges have none.
Obelia shows metagenesis, where the sessile polyp and free-swimming medusa alternate. Ascaris, Taenia and Hydra do not show this.
Wuchereria bancrofti, the filarial worm, causes filariasis (elephantiasis). Ancylostoma is the hookworm and Taenia is the tapeworm.

sources: NCERT Class 11 Biology (Animal Kingdom)

lessons.title: Annelida to Hemichordata

scenes.text: A silk saree, honey in the kitchen and lac on old furniture — all come from arthropods.
Bombyx (silkworm), Apis (honey bee) and Laccifer (lac insect) belong to the largest animal phylum.

steps.title: Annelida and Arthropoda
steps.body:
- **Annelida:** bilateral, triploblastic, metamerically segmented, coelomate; longitudinal and circular muscles; closed circulatory system; **nephridia** for excretion; *Nereis* (aquatic, dioecious, with parapodia), *Pheretima* (earthworm) and *Hirudinaria* (blood-sucking leech) are monoecious.
- **Arthropoda:** the **largest phylum** (over two-thirds of named species); chitinous **exoskeleton**; **jointed appendages**; body of head, thorax, abdomen; open circulation; respiration by gills, book gills, book lungs or tracheae; excretion by **Malpighian tubules**; compound eyes, statocysts; mostly dioecious. Economic: *Apis* (honey), *Bombyx* (silk), *Laccifer* (lac); vectors *Anopheles*, *Culex*, *Aedes*; gregarious pest *Locusta*; living fossil *Limulus* (king crab).

steps.title: Mollusca, Echinodermata, Hemichordata
steps.body:
- **Mollusca:** second largest phylum; soft body with calcareous **shell**; head, muscular foot, visceral hump; **mantle** and mantle cavity with feather-like gills; rasping tongue **radula**; *Pila* (apple snail), *Pinctada* (pearl oyster), *Sepia* (cuttlefish), *Loligo* (squid), *Octopus* (devil fish), *Aplysia* (sea hare), *Dentalium* (tusk shell), *Chaetopleura* (chiton).
- **Echinodermata:** spiny skin with calcareous ossicles; exclusively marine; adults radial, larvae bilateral; **water vascular system** for locomotion, feeding and respiration (tube feet); no excretory system; *Asterias* (star fish), *Echinus* (sea urchin), *Antedon* (sea lily), *Cucumaria* (sea cucumber), *Ophiura* (brittle star).
- **Hemichordata:** worm-like marine animals with **proboscis, collar and trunk**; stomochord (once thought to be a notochord); **proboscis gland** for excretion; *Balanoglossus*, *Saccoglossus*. Now treated as a separate phylum under non-chordates.

steps.title: Solved question 1
steps.body: Name the excretory organs of earthworm and cockroach. Earthworm — **nephridia**; cockroach — **Malpighian tubules**.

steps.title: Solved question 2
steps.body: Why is *Limulus* called a living fossil? It has survived with little change for hundreds of millions of years.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling a starfish a fish or a sea horse a mollusc.
- Saying echinoderms have an excretory system (they lack one).
- Placing Balanoglossus in Chordata.

activity.prompt: Place each animal in its phylum.

quiz.q: The largest phylum of animals is
quiz.why: Arthropoda is the largest phylum, with more than two-thirds of all named animal species. Mollusca is second.
The radula is a rasping, file-like feeding organ found in molluscs. Annelids, echinoderms and arthropods do not have it.

quiz.q: Water vascular system is found in
quiz.why: The water vascular system, with tube feet for movement, is a feature of echinoderms such as starfish. Sponges, molluscs and annelids lack it.

quiz.q: Malpighian tubules are excretory organs of
quiz.why: Malpighian tubules are the excretory organs of insects and other arthropods. Earthworms use nephridia and flatworms use flame cells.
Balanoglossus is a hemichordate, with a body in three parts: proboscis, collar and trunk. It is not a mollusc or an echinoderm.

sources: NCERT Class 11 Biology (Animal Kingdom)

lessons.title: Phylum Chordata: features and lower classes

scenes.text: In muddy ponds, Clarias (magur) gulps air at the surface.
From lancelets to fish, chordates share a notochord, a dorsal nerve cord and gill slits at some stage.

steps.title: Fundamental chordate features
steps.body:
- **Notochord** (at least in the embryo)
- **Dorsal, hollow, single nerve cord**
- **Pharyngeal gill slits**
- **Post-anal tail**
- Ventral heart; closed circulation; triploblastic, coelomate, bilateral.

Subphyla: **Urochordata** (notochord only in larval tail: *Ascidia*, *Salpa*, *Doliolum*), **Cephalochordata** (notochord head to tail throughout life: *Branchiostoma*/amphioxus) — together called protochordates; **Vertebrata** (notochord replaced by a vertebral column in adults). *All vertebrates are chordates, but not all chordates are vertebrates.*

steps.title: Cyclostomata and fishes
steps.body:
- **Cyclostomata:** jawless; sucking circular mouth; 6–15 pairs of gill slits; cartilaginous cranium; ectoparasites on fish; migrate to fresh water to spawn and die; *Petromyzon* (lamprey), *Myxine* (hagfish).
- **Chondrichthyes:** cartilaginous endoskeleton; **placoid scales**; gill slits separate, no operculum; **no air bladder** → must swim constantly to avoid sinking; powerful jaws; some have electric organs (*Torpedo*) or poison sting (*Trygon*); internal fertilisation, many viviparous; *Scoliodon* (dog fish), *Pristis* (saw fish), *Carcharodon* (great white shark).
- **Osteichthyes:** bony endoskeleton; **operculum** covers gills; **air bladder** regulates buoyancy; cycloid/ctenoid scales; mostly oviparous; marine (*Exocoetus* flying fish, *Hippocampus* sea horse), freshwater (*Labeo*, *Catla*, *Clarias*), aquarium (*Betta*, *Pterophyllum*).

steps.title: Solved question 1
steps.body: Why do sharks keep swimming? Cartilaginous fishes lack an air bladder, so they sink if they stop.

steps.title: Solved question 2
steps.body: Is *Hippocampus* a horse? No — it is a bony fish (Osteichthyes), the sea horse.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling Branchiostoma a vertebrate.
- Placing dog fish (*Scoliodon*) in Osteichthyes.
- Thinking urochordates keep the notochord in adults.

activity.prompt: Match the animal to its group.

quiz.q: Which is not a fundamental chordate character?
quiz.why: Chordates have a dorsal, hollow nerve cord. A ventral solid nerve cord is typical of non-chordates, so it is not a chordate character. Notochord, gill slits and post-anal tail are chordate features.
Cartilaginous fishes (Chondrichthyes) have no air bladder, so they must keep swimming to avoid sinking. Bony fishes like Catla and Labeo have one.

quiz.q: Notochord extends from head to tail throughout life in
quiz.why: In Cephalochordata, such as Amphioxus, the notochord runs from head to tail and stays throughout life. In urochordates it is only in the larval tail.
Torpedo, the electric ray, has electric organs that can give a shock. Labeo, Trygon and Pristis do not have electric organs of this kind.

quiz.q: Operculum covering gills is found in
quiz.why: Bony fishes (Osteichthyes) have an operculum covering the gills. Cartilaginous fishes have separate gill slits with no cover.

sources: NCERT Class 11 Biology (Animal Kingdom)

lessons.title: Amphibia, Reptilia, Aves and Mammalia

story.title: Who lays eggs, who gives milk?

scenes.text: The platypus lays eggs — yet feeds its young with milk.
Milk-producing mammary glands, not live birth, are the true badge of mammals.

steps.title: Amphibia and Reptilia
steps.body:
- **Amphibia:** live in water and on land; most have two pairs of limbs; moist skin without scales; tympanum; **cloaca**; respiration by gills, lungs and skin; **3-chambered heart** (2 auricles, 1 ventricle); cold-blooded; external fertilisation, oviparous, indirect development; *Bufo* (toad), *Rana* (frog), *Hyla* (tree frog), *Salamandra*, *Ichthyophis* (limbless).
- **Reptilia:** creep or crawl; dry cornified skin with epidermal **scales or scutes**; no external ear opening; heart usually 3-chambered but **4-chambered in crocodiles**; cold-blooded; internal fertilisation, oviparous, direct development; snakes and lizards shed skin; *Chelone* (turtle), *Testudo* (tortoise), *Chameleon*, *Calotes* (garden lizard), *Crocodilus*, *Alligator*, *Hemidactylus* (wall lizard); poisonous snakes *Naja* (cobra), *Bungarus* (krait), *Vipera* (viper).

steps.title: Aves and Mammalia
steps.body:
