- **Aves:** feathers; forelimbs modified into **wings**; beak; hind limbs with scales; dry skin with only the oil gland at tail base; **pneumatic** (hollow, air-filled) long bones; crop and gizzard; air sacs supplement lungs; **4-chambered heart**; warm-blooded; oviparous, direct development; *Corvus* (crow), *Columba* (pigeon), *Psittacula* (parrot), *Struthio* (ostrich), *Pavo* (peacock), *Aptenodytes* (penguin), *Neophron* (vulture).
- **Mammalia:** **mammary glands**; hair on skin; external ears (**pinnae**); different types of teeth; 4-chambered heart; warm-blooded; lungs; mostly viviparous. Oviparous *Ornithorhynchus* (platypus); viviparous *Macropus* (kangaroo), *Pteropus* (flying fox), *Camelus*, *Macaca* (monkey), *Rattus*, *Canis* (dog), *Felis* (cat), *Elephas*, *Equus* (horse), *Delphinus* (dolphin), *Balaenoptera* (blue whale), *Panthera tigris*, *Panthera leo*.

steps.title: Solved question 1
steps.body: Which reptile has a four-chambered heart? The **crocodile**.

steps.title: Solved question 2
steps.body: Is a bat a bird? No. *Pteropus* has hair, external ears and mammary glands — a flying **mammal**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying all mammals give birth (platypus lays eggs).
- Saying amphibians have scales.
- Calling whales and dolphins fish — they are mammals.

activity.prompt: Sort into the correct class.

quiz.why: A cloaca is a common chamber into which the gut, urinary and genital ducts open. It is present in amphibians (and reptiles and birds). Placental mammals do not have one.
Birds have pneumatic bones with air cavities, which make the skeleton light for flight. Fishes, amphibians and reptiles have solid bones.
Ornithorhynchus, the platypus, is a mammal that lays eggs. Macropus (kangaroo), Delphinus (dolphin) and Pteropus (flying fox) give birth to young.
Naja, the cobra, is a poisonous reptile. Hemidactylus (wall lizard), Testudo (tortoise) and Calotes (garden lizard) are not poisonous.
Birds (Aves) and mammals (Mammalia) are warm-blooded, keeping a constant body temperature (homoiothermous). Fishes, amphibians and reptiles are cold-blooded.

sources: NCERT Class 11 Biology (Animal Kingdom)

questions.q: Sponges belong to phylum
questions.why: Sponges have many pores on the body and belong to Porifera, meaning pore-bearers. Coelenterata, Annelida and Ctenophora are different phyla.

questions.q: Cnidoblasts are found in
questions.why: Cnidoblasts are stinging cells found in coelenterates (cnidarians) like Hydra, used for defence and catching prey. Ctenophores have colloblasts instead.

questions.q: The second largest animal phylum is
questions.why: Mollusca is the second largest animal phylum after Arthropoda.

questions.q: Hookworm is
questions.why: The hookworm is Ancylostoma, a roundworm parasite of the intestine. Wuchereria causes filariasis and Taenia is a tapeworm.

questions.q: Bioluminescence is well marked in
questions.why: Ctenophores (comb jellies) show bioluminescence, which means they can produce light. Sponges, flatworms and earthworms are not noted for it.

questions.q: The sea hare is
questions.why: The sea hare is Aplysia, a mollusc. Pinctada is the pearl oyster, Antedon is a sea lily and Hippocampus is the sea horse.

questions.q: Assertion: Crocodiles are reptiles with a four-chambered heart. Reason: All reptiles have four-chambered hearts.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
Both true and R explains A
questions.why: The assertion is true: crocodiles have a four-chambered heart. The reason is false, because most reptiles have a three-chambered heart. So A is true and R is false.

questions.q: Which group has an open circulatory system?
questions.why: Arthropods have an open circulatory system, in which blood flows into body spaces (haemocoel). Annelids and chordates mostly have a closed system.

questions.q: Which pair is correctly matched?
questions.why: Pheretima, the earthworm, excretes by nephridia. Planaria has flame cells, the cockroach has Malpighian tubules and sponges have no nephridia.

questions.q: Animals with a notochord only in the larval tail are
questions.why: In urochordates (such as Ascidia) the notochord is present only in the larval tail. In cephalochordates it stays through life, and hemichordates have none.

questions.q: Case: A marine animal has spiny skin, tube feet, radial adults and bilateral larvae, and no excretory system. It is in
questions.why: Spiny skin, tube feet, radial adults and bilateral larvae are echinoderm features, and these animals have a water vascular system. Ctenophores and coelenterates do not have tube feet.

questions.q: Case: A parasite in human intestine is long, round in section, with females longer than males. It is
questions.why: A long, round-sectioned intestinal parasite with sexes separate and females longer than males is Ascaris, a roundworm. Taenia and Fasciola are flat worms.

questions.q: Which feature is common to Chondrichthyes and Osteichthyes?
questions.why: Both Chondrichthyes and Osteichthyes have paired fins and gills. Placoid scales belong only to cartilaginous fishes, and the operculum and air bladder belong only to bony fishes.

questions.q: Metamerism and a closed circulatory system together indicate
questions.why: A body divided into repeated segments (metamerism) together with a closed circulatory system is typical of annelids such as the earthworm. Arthropods have open circulation.

questions.q: Which statement is incorrect?
questions.why: The incorrect statement is that all chordates are vertebrates. Protochordates (urochordates and cephalochordates) are chordates without a backbone. All vertebrates are chordates.

questions.q: Which group shows triploblastic, acoelomate, bilaterally symmetrical, organ-level organisation?
questions.why: Flatworms (Platyhelminthes) are triploblastic, acoelomate, bilaterally symmetrical, with organ-level organisation. Sponges and coelenterates are not triploblastic, and roundworms have a pseudocoelom.

questions.q: A living fossil among arthropods is
questions.why: Limulus, the king crab, is called a living fossil because it has changed little over a very long time. Locusta, Apis and Bombyx are ordinary insects.

questions.q: Arrange in order of increasing complexity of body cavity: earthworm, Ascaris, liver fluke
questions.why: A liver fluke has no body cavity (acoelomate), Ascaris has a pseudocoelom, and the earthworm has a true coelom. So the order of complexity is liver fluke, Ascaris, earthworm.

courses.title: Ch 5 · Morphology of Flowering Plants
courses.summary: External structure of roots, stems, leaves, inflorescences, flowers, fruits and seeds, their modifications, and semi-technical description of common families.
outcomes: Learners can identify root, stem and leaf types and their modifications
Learners can describe phyllotaxy, venation and leaf types
Learners can describe flower symmetry, ovary position, aestivation and placentation
Learners can describe dicot and monocot seeds and read floral formulae

lessons.title: The root and its modifications

scenes.text: An old banyan tree in the village square has dozens of pillar-like roots coming down from its branches.
These prop roots support the huge canopy — a root doing an unusual job.

steps.title: Root systems and regions
steps.body:
- **Tap root system:** primary root from the radicle with lateral roots (dicots, e.g. mustard).
- **Fibrous root system:** primary root short-lived, replaced by many roots from the stem base (monocots, e.g. wheat).
- **Adventitious roots:** arise from parts other than the radicle (grass, *Monstera*, banyan).
- Regions from tip: **root cap** (protects tip) → **meristematic region** → **region of elongation** → **region of maturation** (root hairs absorb water and minerals).

steps.title: Modifications
steps.body:
- **Storage:** tap roots of carrot, turnip; adventitious roots of sweet potato.
- **Support:** **prop roots** (banyan), **stilt roots** from lower nodes (maize, sugarcane).
- **Respiration:** **pneumatophores** grow upward in swampy mangroves like *Rhizophora* to get oxygen.

steps.title: Solved question 1
steps.body: Sweet potato vs potato: sweet potato is a swollen **adventitious root**; potato is an underground **stem** (tuber) with eyes (nodes with buds).

steps.title: Solved question 2
steps.body: Why do mangrove roots grow upward? Waterlogged mud has little oxygen; pneumatophores carry air to the roots.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling potato a root.
- Mixing prop roots (from branches) with stilt roots (from lower stem nodes).
- Thinking root hairs are in the elongation region (they are in the maturation region).

activity.prompt: Match the plant with its root modification.

quiz.why: Monocots such as wheat have fibrous roots, a cluster of thin roots from the base. Dicots like mustard have a tap root system.
Root hairs arise from the region of maturation, where cells have differentiated. They absorb water and minerals. The root cap only protects the tip.
Pneumatophores are roots that grow upward out of the soil in swampy plants (mangroves) and take in air for respiration. They are not for climbing or storage.
Turnip is a modified tap root, swollen to store food. Roots that grow from parts other than the radicle are adventitious.

quiz.q: Roots arising from parts other than the radicle are
quiz.why: Roots that come from parts of the plant other than the radicle are called adventitious roots. The primary root from the radicle is the tap root.

sources: NCERT Class 11 Biology (Morphology of Flowering Plants)

lessons.title: The stem and its modifications

scenes.text: Rina cuts ginger and notices rings and tiny buds on it.
Nodes and buds mean ginger is a stem — a rhizome — even though it grows underground.

steps.title: The stem
steps.body: Develops from the **plumule**; bears **nodes** (where leaves arise) and **internodes**; has buds (terminal or axillary). Functions: spreading branches, conducting water, minerals and food; some stems store food, support, protect or perform vegetative propagation.

steps.title: Modifications
steps.body:
- **Underground storage:** potato (tuber), ginger, turmeric (rhizome), zaminkand, *Colocasia* (corm), onion (bulb — stem is the disc).
- **Stem tendrils** from axillary buds for climbing: cucumber, pumpkins, watermelon, grapevine.
- **Thorns** from axillary buds: *Citrus*, *Bougainvillea*.
- **Flattened (phylloclade) or fleshy cylindrical** green stems in arid plants: *Opuntia* (flattened), *Euphorbia* (fleshy cylindrical).
- **Sub-aerial** for spreading: **runners** (grass, strawberry), **stolons** (mint, jasmine), **offsets** (*Pistia*, *Eichhornia*), **suckers** (banana, pineapple, *Chrysanthemum*).

steps.title: Solved question 1
steps.body: How do you prove a thorn of *Bougainvillea* is a stem? It arises from an **axillary bud** (in the axil of a leaf), the position of a branch.

steps.title: Solved question 2
steps.body: Which modification helps *Eichhornia* spread on water? **Offsets** — one internode long, with a rosette of leaves and a tuft of roots at each node.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking all tendrils are stems — pea tendrils are leaves.
- Calling ginger a root.
- Confusing thorns (stem) and spines (leaf).

activity.prompt: What type of stem modification?

quiz.why: Potato is a stem tuber. The eyes are nodes with buds, which shows it is a stem, not a root.
Stem tendrils develop from axillary buds, which is where branches arise. They help climbing plants such as grapevine and cucumber.

Suckers are lateral branches that grow from the base of the main stem, as in banana and pineapple. Pistia has stolons, grass has runners and mint has suckers too, but banana and pineapple are the standard examples.

quiz.q: Opuntia's green flattened stem is a
quiz.why: In Opuntia the leaves are reduced to spines and the stem is flat, green and does the photosynthesis. Such a stem is called a phylloclade.
Colocasia stores food in a corm, a short, thick, vertical underground stem. It is not a tuber, rhizome or bulb.

sources: NCERT Class 11 Biology (Morphology of Flowering Plants)

lessons.title: The leaf

scenes.text: Sanjay compares neem and mango leaves. Neem has many leaflets on one axis; mango has a single blade.
Where do you find the bud? Only at the base of the whole leaf — that is how you tell simple from compound.

steps.title: Parts and venation
steps.body:
A leaf develops at a node, with a bud in its axil. Parts: **leaf base** (may have **stipules**; swollen **pulvinus** in legumes), **petiole**, **lamina** with midrib and veins.
- **Reticulate venation** (network) — dicots.
- **Parallel venation** — monocots.

steps.title: Types, phyllotaxy, modifications
steps.body:
- **Simple:** lamina entire or incised without reaching the midrib. **Compound:** incisions reach the midrib → leaflets. **Pinnately compound** (leaflets on a common rachis, neem); **palmately compound** (leaflets at one point, silk cotton).
- **Phyllotaxy:** **alternate** (china rose, mustard, sunflower), **opposite** (*Calotropis*, guava), **whorled** (*Alstonia*).
- **Modifications:** tendrils (pea), spines (cacti), fleshy storage leaves (onion, garlic), **phyllode** (flattened petiole in Australian *Acacia*), insectivorous pitcher plant and Venus fly trap.

steps.title: Solved question 1
steps.body: How to tell a compound leaf from a branch with leaves? A bud is present in the axil of the **petiole** of a compound leaf but **not** in the axils of its leaflets.

steps.title: Solved question 2
steps.body: Phyllotaxy of guava? **Opposite** — a pair of leaves at each node, opposite each other.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling leaflets separate leaves.
- Mixing alternate (one leaf per node) with opposite (two per node).
- Assuming all monocots lack reticulate venation without checking (rule of thumb only).

activity.prompt: Match.

quiz.why: The pulvinus is a swollen leaf base found in leguminous plants. It helps leaf movements. Ferns, grasses and pines do not have it.
Parallel venation, with veins running side by side, is typical of monocots such as grasses. Dicots have reticulate venation.
The spines of cacti are modified leaves. Reducing the leaf area lowers water loss in dry places, while the stem does photosynthesis.
In alternate phyllotaxy one leaf grows at each node, as in china rose and mustard. Alstonia has whorled and Calotropis and guava have opposite arrangement.
The fleshy scale leaves of an onion bulb store food. They do not store seeds or air.

sources: NCERT Class 11 Biology (Morphology of Flowering Plants)

lessons.title: Inflorescence and the flower

scenes.text: Under a hand lens, a pea flower has one big petal, two side petals and two fused at the bottom.
Its shape, symmetry and arrangement can be written in a short code — a floral formula.

steps.title: Inflorescence and flower parts
steps.body:
- **Racemose:** main axis keeps growing, flowers borne laterally in acropetal order.
- **Cymose:** main axis ends in a flower; limited growth; basipetal order.

A flower has four whorls on the **thalamus**: **calyx** (sepals), **corolla** (petals), **androecium** (stamens), **gynoecium** (carpels). If calyx and corolla are not distinct → **perianth** (lily).
- **Symmetry:** actinomorphic (radial: mustard, datura, chilli), zygomorphic (bilateral: pea, gulmohur, bean, *Cassia*), asymmetric (canna).
- **Ovary position:** **hypogynous** (superior ovary: mustard, china rose, brinjal), **perigynous** (half-inferior: plum, rose, peach), **epigynous** (inferior: guava, cucumber, ray florets of sunflower).

steps.title: Aestivation and placentation
steps.body:
- **Aestivation:** **valvate** (margins touch, *Calotropis*), **twisted** (one margin overlaps the next, china rose, lady's finger, cotton), **imbricate** (irregular overlap, *Cassia*, gulmohur), **vexillary/papilionaceous** (standard, wings, keel — pea, bean).
- Stamens: **epipetalous** (attached to petals, brinjal), **epiphyllous** (to perianth, lily); **monoadelphous** (china rose), **diadelphous** (pea), **polyadelphous** (citrus).
- **Placentation:** **marginal** (pea), **axile** (china rose, tomato, lemon), **parietal** (mustard, *Argemone*), **free central** (*Dianthus*, *Primrose*), **basal** (sunflower, marigold).

steps.title: Solved question 1
steps.body: Describe the pea flower: zygomorphic, vexillary aestivation, diadelphous stamens (9) + 1, monocarpellary superior ovary with marginal placentation.

steps.title: Solved question 2
steps.body: Why is the ovary of guava called inferior? The thalamus grows around and fuses with the ovary; other floral parts arise above it (epigynous).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing twisted (regular overlap in one direction) with imbricate (irregular).
- Calling a rose flower hypogynous (it is perigynous).
- Forgetting that in the vexillary arrangement the large standard petal overlaps the wings, which overlap the keel.

activity.prompt: Ovary position.

quiz.why: In twisted aestivation each petal overlaps the next one in a regular way, as in china rose. Pea has vexillary and Cassia has imbricate aestivation.
In axile placentation the placenta is on the central axis of a many-chambered ovary, as in tomato and lemon. Pea has marginal and mustard has parietal placentation.
Diadelphous means stamens joined in two bundles. In pea, nine filaments are joined and one is free (9 + 1). China rose has one bundle (monadelphous).
A zygomorphic flower can be divided into equal halves in only one plane (bilateral symmetry). Pea is zygomorphic, while mustard, datura and chilli are actinomorphic.
In basal placentation the placenta is at the base of the ovary and carries a single ovule, as in sunflower and marigold. Pea, Dianthus and Argemone differ.

sources: NCERT Class 11 Biology (Morphology of Flowering Plants)

lessons.title: Fruits, seeds and families

scenes.text: Both mango and coconut have a hard stony layer inside — they are drupes.
The edible part differs: fleshy mesocarp in mango, endosperm in coconut.

steps.title: Fruit and seed
steps.body:
- **Fruit:** mature ovary after fertilisation; **parthenocarpic** if formed without fertilisation. Wall = **pericarp** (epicarp, mesocarp, endocarp). Mango and coconut are **drupes** (one-seeded, from monocarpellary superior ovary); mango has fleshy edible mesocarp; coconut has fibrous mesocarp.
- **Dicot seed (gram, bean):** seed coat (**testa**, **tegmen**), **hilum** (scar of attachment), **micropyle**; embryo with embryonal axis and two cotyledons; endosperm absent in most (castor has endosperm).
- **Monocot seed (maize):** usually endospermic; endosperm separated from embryo by the protein-rich **aleurone layer**; one shield-shaped cotyledon (**scutellum**); plumule and radicle enclosed by **coleoptile** and **coleorhiza**.

steps.title: Families (floral formula)
steps.body:
Symbols: ⊕ actinomorphic, % zygomorphic, ⚥ bisexual, K calyx, C corolla, P perianth, A androecium, G gynoecium (G with line above number = superior), ( ) fused.
- **Fabaceae** (pea family): % ⚥ K(5) C1+2+(2) A(9)+1 G1; e.g. gram, soybean, groundnut; pulses, oils, fodder.
- **Solanaceae** (potato family): ⊕ ⚥ K(5) C(5) A5 G(2); e.g. potato, brinjal, tomato, chilli; tobacco, *Petunia*.
- **Liliaceae** (lily family): ⊕ ⚥ P(3+3) A3+3 G(3); e.g. *Asparagus*, aloe, tulip, *Gloriosa*; colchicine source.

steps.title: Solved question 1
steps.body: Which layer in maize seed stores protein? The **aleurone layer** around the endosperm.

steps.title: Solved question 2
steps.body: Read K(5) C(5) A5 G(2): five fused sepals, five fused petals, five free stamens, bicarpellary syncarpous gynoecium — Solanaceae.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling coconut 'water' the mesocarp — it is liquid endosperm.
- Mixing hilum (scar) and micropyle (pore).
- Writing Fabaceae stamens as monoadelphous (they are diadelphous).

steps.title: Note
steps.body: Some rationalised editions treat the semi-technical description of families in brief; floral formulae remain useful for practicals and NEET.

activity.prompt: Match the seed part.

quiz.why: Mango is a drupe, a one-seeded fleshy fruit with a hard, stony endocarp. A berry has no stony layer around the seed.

quiz.q: A fruit formed without fertilisation is
quiz.why: A fruit that forms without fertilisation is parthenocarpic, as in banana. A drupe is a fruit type and polyembryony means several embryos.

quiz.q: Floral formula K(5) C(5) A5 G(2) belongs to
quiz.why: The floral formula K(5) C(5) A5 G(2) means joined sepals and petals, five stamens and a two-fused-carpel ovary. This matches Solanaceae, the potato family.
Liliaceae flowers have a perianth, in which sepals and petals look alike (tepals). Brassicaceae, Solanaceae and Fabaceae have separate calyx and corolla.

quiz.q: Endosperm is present in mature seeds of
quiz.why: Castor and maize have endospermic seeds, where the endosperm stays in the mature seed as food store. Gram, pea and bean have non-endospermic seeds, where the endosperm is used up and food is stored in the cotyledons.

sources: NCERT Class 11 Biology (Morphology of Flowering Plants)

questions.q: Prop roots are found in
questions.why: Banyan tree has prop roots, which grow down from the branches as hanging roots and then act as pillars for support. Maize has stilt roots, and Rhizophora has pneumatophores.

questions.q: Ginger is a
questions.why: Ginger is a rhizome, a thick underground stem with nodes and buds. It is a stem, not a root, because it has nodes and scale leaves.

questions.q: A leaf with leaflets on a common axis (rachis) is
questions.why: In a pinnately compound leaf, leaflets are attached along a common axis called the rachis, as in neem. In a palmately compound leaf, the leaflets arise from one point at the petiole tip.

questions.q: Pea tendrils are modified
questions.why: In pea the leaflets are modified into tendrils, which are thin coiling structures that help the plant climb. They are leaf parts, not stems or roots.

questions.q: Stilt roots are found in
questions.why: Stilt roots grow from the lower nodes of the stem and support the plant, as in maize and sugarcane. Banyan has prop roots, and sweet potato and carrot are storage roots.

questions.q: Free central placentation is seen in
questions.why: In free central placentation the ovules sit on a central axis, and the ovary has no partitions (septa). It is seen in Dianthus. Tomato has axile and pea has marginal placentation.

questions.q: Assertion: Potato is a stem. Reason: It has nodes (eyes) bearing buds.
options: Both true and R explains A
Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Both statements are true, and R explains A. Eyes of the potato are nodes that carry buds, which shows that the potato is a modified stem, not a root.

questions.q: Which flower is perigynous?
questions.why: In perigynous flowers the ovary is at the centre and the other parts are on the rim of the thalamus, as in plum. Mustard is hypogynous, and guava and cucumber are epigynous.

questions.q: Vexillary aestivation is characteristic of
questions.why: Vexillary aestivation, with a large standard petal covering the two wing petals, which cover the keel, is typical of Fabaceae (the pea family).

questions.q: Epipetalous stamens are found in
questions.why: Epipetalous stamens are attached to the petals, as in brinjal (Solanaceae). In pea the stamens are diadelphous, and in china rose they are monadelphous.

questions.q: Case: A student finds a seed with a single shield-shaped cotyledon and an aleurone layer. The seed is most likely
questions.why: A seed with a single shield-shaped cotyledon (scutellum) and an aleurone layer is a monocot seed, so it is maize. Gram, pea and bean are dicot seeds with two cotyledons.

questions.q: Case: Floating plants in a pond spread quickly by short horizontal branches each with a rosette of leaves. This is
questions.why: Eichhornia and Pistia spread by offsets, short horizontal branches with a rosette of leaves above and roots below. Runners and stolons are longer, and suckers grow from underground stems.

questions.q: Which is correctly matched?
questions.why: Twisted aestivation is seen in cotton, lady's finger and china rose, where each petal overlaps the next in a regular way. Vexillary is in pea, valvate in Calotropis and imbricate in Cassia.

questions.q: In Fabaceae the gynoecium is
questions.why: In Fabaceae the gynoecium has a single carpel (monocarpellary, G1) with marginal placentation, and it forms a legume. Axile placentation is seen in other families.

questions.q: Which stem modification is mismatched?
questions.why: Bougainvillea has thorns, which are modified axillary branches, not tendrils. Citrus has thorns, Opuntia has a phylloclade and strawberry has runners.

questions.q: Phyllode is a modified
questions.why: A phyllode is a flattened, leaf-like petiole that does the photosynthesis. It is seen in Australian Acacia, where the true leaf is small or missing.

questions.q: In P(3+3) A3+3 G(3) the ovary is tricarpellary and syncarpous; the family is
questions.why: P(3+3) A3+3 G(3) means a perianth of two whorls of three tepals, six stamens and a fused tricarpellary ovary. This is the floral formula of Liliaceae, the lily family.

questions.q: In a racemose inflorescence the main axis keeps growing and the flowers are borne
options: all at the same level at once
only at the tip of the axis
questions.why: In racemose inflorescence the main axis keeps growing and the flowers arise from the sides in acropetal order. The oldest flowers are at the base and the youngest are near the tip.

courses.title: Ch 6 · Anatomy of Flowering Plants
courses.summary: Meristems and plant tissues, the three tissue systems, and the internal structure of dicot and monocot roots, stems and leaves.
outcomes: Learners can name meristems and simple and complex permanent tissues
Learners can describe epidermal, ground and vascular tissue systems
Learners can distinguish dicot and monocot roots and stems from transverse sections
Learners can compare dorsiventral and isobilateral leaves

lessons.title: Meristems and plant tissues

scenes.text: A lawn mower cuts grass every week, but the grass keeps growing back from below.
Intercalary meristems at the base of grass leaves keep dividing — plant growth is tissue-driven.

steps.title: Meristems
steps.body:
- **Apical meristem:** at tips of root and shoot; primary growth in length.
- **Intercalary meristem:** between mature tissues (grasses); regrowth after grazing.
- **Lateral meristem:** cylindrical, in mature regions; e.g. fascicular vascular cambium, interfascicular cambium, cork cambium → secondary growth (increase in girth).

Primary meristems (apical, intercalary) appear early; lateral meristems are secondary.

steps.title: Permanent tissues
steps.body:
**Simple:**
- **Parenchyma:** thin cellulose walls, isodiametric; photosynthesis, storage, secretion.
- **Collenchyma:** thickened corners (cellulose, hemicellulose, pectin); mechanical support to young stems and petioles; below epidermis in dicots.
- **Sclerenchyma:** lignified, dead; **fibres** (long, pointed) and **sclereids** (in nut shells, guava pulp, pear, tea leaves).

**Complex:**
- **Xylem:** tracheids, **vessels** (characteristic of angiosperms), xylem fibres, xylem parenchyma (only living part). Conducts water and minerals. **Protoxylem** (first-formed) and **metaxylem**; **endarch** (protoxylem towards centre, stems) and **exarch** (towards periphery, roots).
- **Phloem:** sieve tube elements (with sieve plates; no nucleus at maturity), companion cells, phloem parenchyma (absent in most monocots), phloem fibres (bast). Gymnosperms have albuminous cells and sieve cells instead.

steps.title: Solved question 1
steps.body: Which xylem element is living? **Xylem parenchyma** — the others (tracheids, vessels, fibres) are dead at maturity.

steps.title: Solved question 2
steps.body: Root xylem arrangement? **Exarch** — protoxylem lies towards the periphery, metaxylem towards the centre.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying gymnosperms have vessels (they generally lack them).
- Calling sieve tube elements nucleated at maturity.
- Mixing collenchyma (living, corner thickenings) with sclerenchyma (dead, lignified).

activity.prompt: Match the tissue to its feature.
pairs: Gritty cells of pear and guava

quiz.why: Lateral meristem (cambium) divides sideways and adds to the girth of stems and roots. This is secondary growth. Apical meristem increases length.

quiz.q: The only living xylem element is
quiz.why: Vessels, tracheids and fibres are dead at maturity. Xylem parenchyma is the only living xylem element, and it stores food and helps in sideways conduction of water.
Phloem fibres are called bast fibres. They are sclerenchyma and are used to make jute and hemp, and they are the only dead element of phloem.
In roots the protoxylem lies towards the outside and the metaxylem towards the centre. This is called exarch xylem. In stems the arrangement is endarch.
Gymnosperm phloem has no companion cells and no sieve tubes. It has sieve cells and albuminous cells instead, while angiosperms have sieve tubes with companion cells.

sources: NCERT Class 11 Biology (Anatomy of Flowering Plants)

lessons.title: Tissue systems

scenes.text: Under a microscope, a leaf peel shows tiny mouths opening and closing.
Stomata, formed by guard cells, let gases in and water vapour out — part of the epidermal tissue system.

steps.title: Three systems
steps.body:
- **Epidermal tissue system:** epidermis (single layer, cuticle on the outside of shoots), **stomata**, and appendages (trichomes, root hairs).
  - Guard cells are **bean-shaped** in dicots, **dumb-bell-shaped** in grasses; they have chloroplasts; surrounding subsidiary cells form the stomatal apparatus.
  - **Root hairs** are unicellular extensions of root epidermal cells; **trichomes** on stems are usually multicellular.
- **Ground tissue system:** all tissues except epidermis and vascular bundles — cortex, pericycle, pith, medullary rays; in leaves it is the **mesophyll**.
- **Vascular tissue system:** xylem and phloem in vascular bundles.
  - **Radial:** xylem and phloem on different radii (roots).
  - **Conjoint:** on the same radius (stems, leaves); phloem usually outside.
  - **Open:** cambium between xylem and phloem (dicot stems); **closed:** no cambium (monocots).

steps.title: Solved question 1
steps.body: Why can dicot stems grow in girth but monocot stems usually cannot? Dicot bundles are **open** (have cambium); monocot bundles are **closed**.

steps.title: Solved question 2
steps.body: Which plants have dumb-bell shaped guard cells? **Grasses** (monocots).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling root hairs multicellular.
- Saying roots have conjoint bundles (they are radial).
- Thinking the cuticle covers roots (it is absent on roots).

activity.prompt: Type of vascular bundle.

quiz.why: Grasses (monocots) have dumb-bell-shaped guard cells, whereas dicots have bean-shaped guard cells. The shape tells the stomata of the two groups apart.
Root hairs are long, thin extensions of single epidermal cells, so they are unicellular. They increase the surface area for absorption of water and minerals.
Roots have radial vascular bundles, where xylem and phloem lie on different radii and alternate with each other. In stems and leaves they are conjoint, on the same radius.
Open vascular bundles have cambium between the xylem and phloem, so they can make secondary tissue. Closed bundles lack it.

quiz.q: Ground tissue in leaves is called
quiz.why: The ground tissue of a leaf is the mesophyll, which has many chloroplasts and does photosynthesis. Cortex and pith are the ground tissues of stems and roots.

sources: NCERT Class 11 Biology (Anatomy of Flowering Plants)

lessons.title: Anatomy of roots and stems

scenes.text: In the practical exam, Aman gets a thin stained slice and must say: root or stem? dicot or monocot?
A short checklist of features gives the answer every time.

steps.title: Roots
steps.body:
**Dicot root (sunflower):** epiblema with root hairs → cortex (parenchyma) → **endodermis** with **Casparian strips** (suberin) → **pericycle** (origin of lateral roots and cambium) → **2–4 xylem and phloem patches** (radial, exarch) → small or no pith.

**Monocot root (maize):** similar layers but **more than six (polyarch)** xylem bundles; **large, well-developed pith**; no secondary growth.

steps.title: Stems
steps.body:
**Dicot stem (sunflower):** epidermis with cuticle and trichomes → **hypodermis of collenchyma** → cortical parenchyma → **endodermis (starch sheath)** → pericycle (semilunar sclerenchyma patches) → **vascular bundles in a ring**, conjoint, **open**, endarch → medullary rays → large pith.

**Monocot stem (maize):** sclerenchymatous hypodermis; **numerous scattered** vascular bundles each with a **sclerenchymatous bundle sheath**; conjoint, **closed**; peripheral bundles smaller; **water-containing cavities**; no distinct pith; phloem parenchyma absent.

steps.title: Solved question 1
steps.body: Section shows scattered bundles with bundle sheaths and water cavities → **monocot stem**.

steps.title: Solved question 2
steps.body: Section shows radial bundles, 4 xylem patches, small pith, Casparian strips → **dicot root**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling the starch sheath of stems the 'Casparian strip' (Casparian strips are in root endodermis).
- Saying monocot roots have small pith.
- Missing that dicot stem bundles form a ring.

activity.prompt: Identify the section.

items.text: Ring of open conjoint bundles, collenchymatous hypodermis
Scattered closed bundles with bundle sheaths
Starch sheath and semilunar sclerenchyma patches

quiz.why: Casparian strips on the endodermal cell walls are made of suberin, a waxy material that water cannot pass through. This forces water to enter the cells.
Lateral roots arise from the pericycle, a layer inside the endodermis, so they have an internal (endogenous) origin. They then break through the cortex and epidermis.
The hypodermis in a dicot stem is made of collenchyma, which has thickened corners and gives mechanical support to the young stem. In monocot stems it is sclerenchymatous.

quiz.q: Scattered vascular bundles are a feature of
quiz.why: Vascular bundles scattered through the ground tissue are typical of monocot stems, such as maize. A dicot stem has them in a ring.

quiz.q: Endodermis of the dicot stem is also called
quiz.why: The endodermis of a dicot stem has many starch grains, so it is also called the starch sheath. A bundle sheath is a different layer found around bundles in leaves.

sources: NCERT Class 11 Biology (Anatomy of Flowering Plants)

lessons.title: Anatomy of leaves

story.title: Grass leaves on a hot day

scenes.text: On a hot afternoon, a lawn's grass leaves roll inwards.
Bulliform cells lose water and the leaf curls — reducing water loss. Leaf anatomy explains it.

steps.title: Dorsiventral (dicot) leaf
steps.body:
- Upper (adaxial) and lower (abaxial) epidermis with cuticle; **more stomata on the lower surface** (upper may have none).
- **Mesophyll:** **palisade parenchyma** (elongated, vertical, below the upper epidermis) and **spongy parenchyma** (oval/round, loosely arranged, with large air spaces) below.
- Vascular bundles in veins and midrib, surrounded by thick-walled **bundle sheath** cells; reticulate venation → bundles of varying size.

steps.title: Isobilateral (monocot) leaf
steps.body:
- Stomata on **both** surfaces.
- Mesophyll **not** differentiated into palisade and spongy.
- In grasses, some adaxial epidermal cells along veins form large, empty, colourless **bulliform cells**; when turgid they open the leaf, when flaccid the leaf curls inward to reduce water loss.
- Parallel venation → bundles of nearly similar size (except main veins).

steps.title: Solved question 1
steps.body: Why is the palisade on the upper side? It receives more sunlight; its closely packed chloroplast-rich cells maximise photosynthesis.

steps.title: Solved question 2
steps.body: A leaf section with stomata on both sides and uniform mesophyll → **isobilateral (monocot)** leaf.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying bulliform cells are present in dicot leaves.
- Mixing up adaxial (upper) and abaxial (lower).
- Claiming monocot leaves have palisade tissue.

statements.s: Dicot leaves usually have more stomata on the lower surface.
statements.why: Reduces water loss from the sunlit upper surface.

statements.s: Isobilateral leaves have distinct palisade and spongy layers.
Bulliform cells help grass leaves curl.
statements.why: They lose turgor in water stress.

statements.s: Bundle sheath cells surround vascular bundles in leaves.
The adaxial surface is the lower surface.

quiz.why: In a dorsiventral leaf the palisade parenchyma is made of long cells arranged vertically just below the upper (adaxial) epidermis. The spongy cells lie below it.
Spongy parenchyma cells are loosely arranged with large air spaces between them. These spaces help in gas exchange. The cells still contain chloroplasts.
Bulliform cells are large, empty, colourless cells on the upper epidermis of grass (monocot) leaves. When they lose water the leaf curls, which reduces water loss.

quiz.q: Stomata on both surfaces is typical of
quiz.why: Isobilateral leaves, typical of monocots, have stomata on both surfaces equally. Dorsiventral leaves have more stomata on the lower side.

quiz.q: Vascular bundles of a dicot leaf vary in size because of
quiz.why: A dicot leaf has reticulate venation, a network of veins of different sizes. So the vascular bundles vary in size. Parallel venation gives bundles of similar size.

sources: NCERT Class 11 Biology (Anatomy of Flowering Plants)

questions.q: Apical meristem causes
questions.why: Apical meristem is at the tips of roots and shoots. It makes cells that add to the length of the plant, which is primary growth. Girth is increased by lateral meristem.

questions.q: Vessels are characteristic of
questions.why: Vessels are characteristic of angiosperms, though a few angiosperms lack them. Gymnosperms and pteridophytes mostly have only tracheids, and bryophytes have no xylem.

questions.q: Bean-shaped guard cells occur in
questions.why: Bean-shaped guard cells are found in dicot stomata. Grasses (monocots) have dumb-bell-shaped guard cells. Algae have no stomata.

questions.q: Sclereids are common in
questions.why: Sclereids are short, hard cells with thick walls. They give a gritty texture in the pulp of fruits like pear and guava, and they are also in seed coats.

questions.q: Polyarch condition is seen in
questions.why: Polyarch means more than six xylem bundles. Monocot roots are polyarch, while dicot roots have two to four (diarch to tetrarch).

questions.q: Collenchyma provides
questions.why: Collenchyma has living cells with thickened corners. It gives mechanical support to young stems and leaf stalks, and it lets them bend without breaking.

questions.q: Assertion: Monocot stems usually show no secondary growth. Reason: their vascular bundles are closed.
options: Both true and R explains A
Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true and R explains A. Monocot bundles are closed (no cambium), so they cannot add secondary tissue, and monocot stems do not show secondary growth.

questions.q: Endarch protoxylem is found in
questions.why: In stems the protoxylem is towards the centre (pith) and the metaxylem is outside. This is endarch. In roots the protoxylem is outside (exarch).

questions.q: Which is absent in most monocots?
questions.why: Most monocots lack phloem parenchyma, so that is the answer. Sieve tubes and companion cells are present, and vessels are found in xylem.

questions.q: Water-containing cavities in vascular bundles are a feature of
questions.why: In the monocot stem (such as maize) each vascular bundle has a water-containing cavity formed by the breakdown of the protoxylem. Dicot stems and roots lack this.

questions.q: Case: A transverse section shows a ring of 8 conjoint open bundles, hypodermis of collenchyma and a large pith. It is
questions.why: A ring of conjoint, open bundles, with a collenchymatous hypodermis and a large pith, is a dicot stem such as sunflower. Monocot stems have scattered bundles.

questions.q: Case: A student notices that maize leaves curl during midday heat. The cells responsible are
questions.why: Bulliform cells in grass leaves lose turgor in the midday heat and the leaf curls inward, which reduces water loss. Guard cells open and close stomata, not curl the leaf.

questions.q: Casparian strips are located in the
questions.why: Casparian strips are suberised bands on the radial and transverse walls of the endodermal cells of roots. They are not found in the pith, epidermis or pericycle.

questions.q: Which statement about phloem is incorrect?
options: Sieve tube elements have a large nucleus at maturity
questions.why: The incorrect statement is that mature sieve tube elements have a large nucleus. They lose their nucleus at maturity, and the companion cell helps them. The other statements are correct.

questions.q: Interfascicular cambium arises from
questions.why: Interfascicular cambium forms from cells of the medullary rays between the vascular bundles. It joins the fascicular cambium to make a complete cambial ring.

questions.q: In a dorsiventral leaf, the abaxial epidermis generally has
questions.why: In a dorsiventral leaf the lower (abaxial) epidermis has more stomata than the upper epidermis. Palisade cells are in the mesophyll, and bulliform cells are in grasses.

questions.q: Which combination identifies a monocot root?
options: Radial bundles with 2–4 xylem, no pith
Radial bundles, polyarch xylem, large pith
questions.why: A monocot root has radial bundles, polyarch xylem (more than six) and a large pith. Dicot roots have two to four xylem bundles and little or no pith.

questions.q: The only living element among xylem components, and the tissue that forms lateral roots, are respectively
questions.why: Xylem parenchyma is the only living xylem cell type, and lateral roots arise from the pericycle. Vessels, tracheids and fibres are dead, and the endodermis and cortex do not form lateral roots.

courses.title: Ch 7 · Structural Organisation in Animals
courses.summary: Animal tissues — epithelial, connective, muscular and neural — then organ and organ-system organisation studied through the cockroach and the frog.
outcomes: Learners can classify epithelia and state where each is found
Learners can distinguish loose, dense and specialised connective tissues
Learners can compare the three muscle types and describe neural tissue
Learners can describe the morphology and organ systems of cockroach and frog

lessons.title: Epithelial tissue

scenes.text: Scrape the inside of your cheek gently with a clean toothpick and view under a microscope: flat cells like paving stones.
Epithelia cover and line every surface of the body.

steps.title: Simple epithelium (single layer)
steps.body:
- **Squamous:** flat cells; walls of blood vessels, air sacs (alveoli) of lungs; diffusion boundary.
- **Cuboidal:** cube-like; ducts of glands, tubular parts of nephrons; **microvilli** in the proximal convoluted tubule; secretion and absorption.
- **Columnar:** tall cells, nuclei at base; lining of stomach and intestine (microvilli for absorption).
- **Ciliated** (cuboidal or columnar with cilia): move particles or mucus — bronchioles, fallopian tubes.
- **Glandular:** unicellular (goblet cells of alimentary canal) or multicellular (salivary gland). **Exocrine** glands secrete via ducts (mucus, saliva, earwax, oil, milk, digestive enzymes); **endocrine** glands are ductless and release hormones into the blood.

steps.title: Compound epithelium and junctions
steps.body:
- **Compound epithelium:** two or more layers; mainly **protection** against chemical and mechanical stress; dry skin surface, moist buccal cavity, pharynx, inner lining of ducts of salivary glands and pancreatic ducts.
- **Cell junctions:** **tight junctions** stop substances leaking; **adhering junctions** cement cells together; **gap junctions** connect cytoplasm for rapid passage of ions, small molecules and sometimes big molecules.

steps.title: Solved question 1
steps.body: Why do air sacs have squamous epithelium? Thin flat cells make a very short diffusion path for O₂ and CO₂.

steps.title: Solved question 2
steps.body: Which epithelium lines the PCT and why? **Cuboidal with microvilli (brush border)** — increases surface area for reabsorption.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying the stomach is lined by squamous epithelium (it is columnar).
- Calling the skin surface simple epithelium (it is compound).
- Mixing exocrine (with ducts) and endocrine (ductless).

activity.prompt: Match the epithelium to its location.

quiz.why: Goblet cells are single mucus-secreting cells in the lining of the gut and airways, so they are unicellular glands. Salivary glands are multicellular glands.

options: rapid transfer between cytoplasm of adjoining cells
quiz.why: Gap junctions connect the cytoplasm of neighbouring cells with small channels. This allows rapid transfer of ions and small molecules between cells, so cells can communicate.
Compound epithelium has several layers of cells, so it is mainly protective. Its function is protection against wear and tear, as in skin. It is not for diffusion or absorption.
Hormones are made by endocrine glands, which have no ducts and release hormones into the blood. Exocrine glands, such as sweat glands, release secretions through ducts.
Blood vessels are lined by a thin layer of flat cells, the endothelium, which is simple squamous epithelium. This allows easy diffusion across the wall.

sources: NCERT Class 11 Biology (Structural Organisation in Animals)

lessons.title: Connective tissue

scenes.text: Rahul twists his ankle playing football; the doctor says a ligament is stretched.
Ligaments join bone to bone; tendons join muscle to bone — both are dense connective tissue.

steps.title: General
steps.body: Most abundant and widely distributed tissue; links and supports other tissues. Except blood, cells secrete **collagen** or **elastin** fibres and a **ground substance** (matrix of modified polysaccharides).

steps.title: Types
steps.body:
- **Loose connective tissue:** cells and fibres loosely arranged in semi-fluid ground substance. **Areolar** (beneath skin; fibroblasts, macrophages, mast cells) and **adipose** (fat storage below skin).
- **Dense connective tissue:** fibres and fibroblasts compactly packed. **Dense regular** — collagen fibres in parallel rows: **tendons** (muscle to bone), **ligaments** (bone to bone). **Dense irregular** — fibres in varied directions: skin.
- **Specialised:** **cartilage** (chondrocytes in cavities of a pliable matrix; tip of nose, outer ear, between adjacent vertebrae, limbs and hands in adults); **bone** (hard matrix of calcium salts and collagen; **osteocytes** in lacunae; bone marrow produces blood cells); **blood** (fluid connective tissue: plasma, RBCs, WBCs, platelets).

steps.title: Solved question 1
steps.body: Which connective tissue stores fat? **Adipose tissue**, located mainly beneath the skin.

steps.title: Solved question 2
steps.body: Why is blood called a connective tissue? It originates from mesoderm and has cells in a fluid matrix (plasma); it connects body parts by transport.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Swapping tendon (muscle–bone) and ligament (bone–bone).
- Saying cartilage has calcium salts like bone — cartilage matrix is solid but pliable.
- Forgetting that blood cells do not secrete fibres.

activity.prompt: Which connective tissue?

quiz.why: Tendons connect muscle to bone. Ligaments connect bone to bone. Both are dense regular connective tissue.
Bone cells are osteocytes, which lie in small spaces called lacunae in the hard matrix. Chondrocytes are cartilage cells, and fibroblasts and adipocytes belong to other connective tissues.
Mast cells are found in areolar tissue, which is a loose connective tissue. This tissue also has fibroblasts and macrophages. Bone, cartilage and neurons do not have mast cells.

quiz.q: Dense irregular connective tissue is present in the
quiz.why: Skin has dense irregular connective tissue, where fibres run in many directions. Tendons and ligaments have dense regular tissue with fibres in rows.

options: tip of the nose and outer ear
quiz.why: Cartilage is a flexible, firm tissue found at the tip of the nose, the outer ear and in joints. The heart wall, intestine and liver do not contain it.

sources: NCERT Class 11 Biology (Structural Organisation in Animals)

lessons.title: Muscle and neural tissue

scenes.text: Your heart has beaten more than 100,000 times today without your asking.
Cardiac muscle and the neural signals that coordinate it are specialised tissues.

steps.title: Muscle tissue
steps.body:
Long cylindrical fibres with **myofibrils**; contract in response to stimulation.
- **Skeletal:** attached to bones; **striated**, voluntary, multinucleate fibres bundled in parallel (e.g. biceps).
- **Smooth:** fusiform, tapering ends, no striations, involuntary; walls of blood vessels, stomach, intestine.
- **Cardiac:** only in the heart; striated, branched, involuntary; **intercalated discs** (cell junctions) let cells contract as a unit.

steps.title: Neural tissue
steps.body:
Exerts the greatest control over responsiveness.
- **Neurons** are excitable; when stimulated, an electrical disturbance travels along the membrane and passes to neighbouring neurons, muscles or glands.
- **Neuroglia** protect and support neurons and make up **more than half** the volume of neural tissue.

steps.title: Solved question 1
steps.body: Why does the heart contract as one unit? **Intercalated discs** with fusion points let the contraction spread rapidly through all cardiac cells.

steps.title: Solved question 2
steps.body: Muscle type in the wall of the intestine? **Smooth muscle** — involuntary, non-striated, fusiform.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling cardiac muscle voluntary.
- Saying smooth muscle is striated.
- Thinking neurons make up most of the volume of neural tissue (neuroglia do).

activity.prompt: Match.
pairs: Support neurons, >50% of neural tissue volume

quiz.why: Cardiac muscle fibres are joined end to end by intercalated discs, which let the heart cells contract in a coordinated way. Skeletal and smooth muscle do not have them.
Smooth muscle fibres are fusiform, meaning they are spindle-shaped and taper at both ends. Skeletal fibres are long cylinders and cardiac fibres are branched.
The biceps is a muscle attached to bone and under voluntary control, so it is made of skeletal muscle. Cartilage is not muscle.

quiz.q: Most of the volume of neural tissue is made of
quiz.why: Neuroglia are supporting cells of the nervous system and make up more than half the volume of neural tissue. Neurons are fewer in volume.

quiz.q: Which muscle is involuntary and striated?
quiz.why: Cardiac muscle is striated like skeletal muscle but involuntary like smooth muscle. Skeletal muscle is striated and voluntary, and smooth is non-striated and involuntary.

sources: NCERT Class 11 Biology (Structural Organisation in Animals)

lessons.title: Cockroach: morphology and organ systems

scenes.text: At night, a cockroach scuttles across the kitchen and freezes when the light is switched on.
It is Periplaneta americana — a perfect model of an insect body plan.

steps.title: Morphology
steps.body:
*Periplaneta americana* is brown, 34–53 mm long, nocturnal, omnivorous. Body: **head, thorax, abdomen**, covered by a chitinous exoskeleton of **sclerites** (tergites dorsally, sternites ventrally) joined by arthrodial membranes.
- **Head:** triangular, highly mobile; pair of **compound eyes**; thread-like **antennae**; **mouth parts** — labrum (upper lip), a pair of mandibles, a pair of maxillae, labium (lower lip); **hypopharynx** acts as tongue.
- **Thorax:** prothorax, mesothorax, metathorax, each with a pair of walking legs. Forewings (**tegmina**) arise from the mesothorax (opaque, leathery); hind wings from the metathorax (transparent, used in flight).
- **Abdomen:** 10 segments. Both sexes have **anal cerci** on the 10th segment; males also have **anal styles**. In females the 7th sternum forms a genital pouch.

steps.title: Organ systems
steps.body:
- **Digestion:** mouth → pharynx → oesophagus → **crop** (storage) → **gizzard/proventriculus** (with chitinous teeth for grinding) → midgut with **6–8 hepatic caeca** at its start → hindgut (ileum, colon, rectum) → anus.
- **Excretion:** **Malpighian tubules** at the junction of midgut and hindgut; also fat body, nephrocytes, uricose glands; **uricotelic**.
- **Circulation:** **open** system; colourless blood (haemolymph) in haemocoel; heart is an elongated tube with **13 chambers**.
- **Respiration:** network of **tracheae** opening by **10 pairs of spiracles**.
- **Nervous system:** segmentally arranged ganglia on a ventral nerve cord; three ganglia in thorax, six in abdomen; brain represented by the **supra-oesophageal ganglion**. Each compound eye has about 2000 **ommatidia** → **mosaic vision** (more sensitive, less resolution).
- **Reproduction:** sexes separate. Male: a pair of testes (4th–6th abdominal segments), **mushroom-shaped gland**, sperm stored as **spermatophores**. Female: two ovaries, each of **eight ovarioles**; fertilised eggs are packed in **oothecae** (about 9–10 oothecae, each with 14–16 eggs). Development is **paurometabolous** — nymphs moult about 13 times to become adults.

steps.title: Solved question 1
steps.body: Where are hepatic caeca located and what do they do? At the junction of foregut and midgut; they secrete digestive juice.

steps.title: Solved question 2
steps.body: Why does a cockroach live for a week without its head? The head has only part of the nervous system; most control is by ganglia along the ventral nerve cord.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying the cockroach heart has 3 chambers (it has 13).
- Mixing anal cerci (both sexes) and anal styles (only males).
- Writing 'closed circulation' for insects.

activity.prompt: Match the cockroach structure to its role.

quiz.why: The forewings of a cockroach are tough, opaque coverings called tegmina, attached to the mesothorax. The hind wings are thin and used for flying. Elytra are the hard forewings of beetles.
Male cockroaches have a pair of anal styles on the ninth segment. Females lack them. Both sexes have anal cerci.

quiz.q: Number of chambers in the cockroach heart is
quiz.why: The cockroach heart is a long tube with 13 chambers, one in each segment, from the thorax to the abdomen. This is not the same as the four-chambered heart of mammals.
Cockroach shows paurometabolous development, with gradual change. The young are nymphs that look like small adults and grow by moulting. Holometabolous insects have a pupa.

quiz.q: The mushroom-shaped gland is part of the
quiz.why: The mushroom-shaped gland is an accessory gland of the male reproductive system of the cockroach. It is on the sixth to seventh abdominal segments.

sources: NCERT Class 11 Biology (Structural Organisation in Animals)

lessons.title: Frog: morphology and organ systems

scenes.text: Every monsoon night, the fields fill with croaking frogs.
Only males croak — their vocal sacs amplify the call. The frog shows a vertebrate body plan in a simple form.

steps.title: Morphology
steps.body:
The common Indian frog (*Rana tigrina*, now often named *Hoplobatrachus tigerinus*) is **cold-blooded** (poikilothermous); shows **camouflage** (colour change); escapes extreme heat and cold by **aestivation** (summer sleep) and **hibernation** (winter sleep).
- Smooth, slippery, moist skin (mucus); absorbs water through skin — does not drink.
- Body: head and trunk; **no neck, no tail**; eyes bulged, covered by **nictitating membrane**; **tympanum** receives sound.
- Forelimbs with **4 digits**, hind limbs with **5 digits** (webbed, for swimming).
- **Sexual dimorphism:** males have **vocal sacs** and a **copulatory pad** on the first digit of the forelimb.

steps.title: Organ systems
steps.body:
- **Digestion:** short alimentary canal (carnivore); **bilobed** tongue; food captured by the tongue; stomach → intestine → rectum → **cloaca**; liver secretes bile stored in gall bladder; pancreas secretes pancreatic juice.
- **Respiration:** **cutaneous** (through skin) in water and on land; **pulmonary** (lungs) on land; buccal cavity also helps. During aestivation and hibernation, gas exchange is through the skin.
- **Circulation:** closed; **3-chambered heart** (two atria, one ventricle) with **sinus venosus** (opens into right atrium) and **conus arteriosus**; **hepatic portal** and **renal portal** systems; RBCs are **nucleated**; lymph system too.
- **Excretion:** pair of kidneys; **ureotelic**; urinogenital duct in males; ureters open into the cloaca.
- **Nervous system:** brain enclosed in a cranium; **10 pairs of cranial nerves**.
- **Reproduction:** separate sexes; external fertilisation in water; eggs develop into **tadpoles** which undergo **metamorphosis** to adults.

steps.title: Solved question 1
steps.body: How can you tell a male frog from a female? Males have vocal sacs and a copulatory pad on the first finger of the forelimb.

steps.title: Solved question 2
steps.body: How does a frog breathe during hibernation? Only through its moist skin (**cutaneous respiration**).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying frogs drink water through the mouth (they absorb through skin).
- Calling the frog heart four-chambered.
- Saying frogs are ammonotelic as adults (adults are ureotelic).

statements.s: Frogs have a neck and a tail.
The frog heart has three chambers.
Frog RBCs are nucleated.
Frogs have 12 pairs of cranial nerves.
Fertilisation in frogs is internal.

quiz.q: Summer sleep of frogs is called
quiz.why: Aestivation is the summer sleep (inactive period in hot, dry weather) of frogs. Hibernation is the winter sleep. Camouflage and metamorphosis are different things.

quiz.q: Number of digits in the frog forelimb is
quiz.why: The frog forelimb has four digits and the hind limb has five. The hind limb digits are webbed for swimming.
Frogs are ureotelic. They excrete mainly urea, which is made in the liver and removed by the kidneys. Uric acid is for birds and reptiles.
The nictitating membrane is a transparent third eyelid of the frog. It protects the eye when the frog is in water.

quiz.q: The larval stage of a frog is the
quiz.why: The larva of a frog is the tadpole. It lives in water, breathes with gills and changes into the adult frog by metamorphosis. A caterpillar is an insect larva.

sources: NCERT Class 11 Biology (Structural Organisation in Animals)

questions.q: Simple squamous epithelium lines the
options: walls of blood vessels and air sacs
questions.why: Simple squamous epithelium is made of thin, flat cells, which suits places where substances diffuse. It lines the walls of blood vessels and air sacs (alveoli).

questions.q: Ligaments connect
questions.why: Ligaments connect bone to bone and are made of dense regular connective tissue. Tendons connect muscle to bone.

questions.q: Cardiac muscle is
questions.why: Cardiac muscle shows cross-striations like skeletal muscle, but it works without our control, so it is involuntary. It is found only in the heart.

questions.q: The cockroach respires through
questions.why: The cockroach breathes through a system of air tubes called tracheae, which open at the surface through spiracles. It has no lungs or gills.

questions.q: Frogs show sexual dimorphism through
options: vocal sacs and copulatory pads in males
questions.why: In male frogs there are vocal sacs and copulatory pads on the first digit of the forelimbs. Females lack them. This difference is sexual dimorphism.

questions.q: Microvilli are found in the epithelium of
questions.why: Microvilli are tiny brush-border projections that increase surface area for absorption. They are found in the epithelium of the proximal convoluted tubule and the intestine.

questions.q: Assertion: Insects have an open circulatory system. Reason: Blood in a cockroach flows through a haemocoel.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
Both true and R explains A
questions.why: Both are true and R explains A. Insects have an open circulatory system, where blood (haemolymph) flows in open body spaces called haemocoel instead of closed vessels.

questions.q: In cockroach, Malpighian tubules are present at the junction of
questions.why: Malpighian tubules open at the junction of the midgut and hindgut of the cockroach and remove waste. Hepatic caeca are at the junction of foregut and midgut.

questions.q: Which junction prevents substances from leaking across a tissue?
questions.why: Tight junctions seal neighbouring cells together and stop substances leaking across the tissue. Gap junctions allow communication, and adhering junctions hold cells together.

questions.q: The brain of a cockroach is represented by the
questions.why: The brain of the cockroach is the supra-oesophageal ganglion, which lies in the head above the oesophagus. The nerve cord and other ganglia run behind it.

questions.q: Case: A tissue in a biopsy shows chondrocytes in small cavities within a pliable solid matrix. It is
questions.why: Chondrocytes lying in small cavities within a firm but flexible matrix are cartilage cells. Bone cells are osteocytes in a hard matrix, and areolar tissue is loose.

questions.q: Case: A frog buried in mud during summer survives for weeks. It is undergoing ___ and respires by ___
questions.why: A frog buried in mud in the summer is aestivating, which is summer inactivity. It breathes through the skin (cutaneous respiration), since its body activity is very low.

questions.q: Number of ovarioles in each ovary of a female cockroach is
questions.why: Each ovary of a female cockroach has 8 ovarioles, which make the eggs. So the cockroach has 16 ovarioles in all.

questions.q: Mosaic vision in cockroach gives
questions.why: Mosaic vision uses many ommatidia, each forming part of the image. It gives more sensitivity (works in dim light) but less resolution (a coarser image).

questions.q: Which is not found in the frog?
questions.why: The frog heart has three chambers (two atria and one ventricle), so the four-chambered heart is not found in the frog. Nucleated RBCs, renal portal system and sinus venosus are present.

questions.q: Neuroglia make up
options: more than half the volume of neural tissue
questions.why: Neuroglia are the supporting cells of neural tissue and make up more than half of its volume. Neurons, which carry impulses, make up less.

questions.q: The mouth parts of cockroach in order from front: labrum, mandibles, maxillae, labium. The tongue-like structure among them is the
questions.why: The hypopharynx is the tongue-like structure of the cockroach, lying in the cavity enclosed by the mouth parts. The labrum is the upper lip, and the labium is the lower lip.

questions.q: Which correctly pairs tissue and location?
options: Dense irregular — skin; adipose — below skin; ciliated — fallopian tube
questions.why: Dense irregular tissue is in skin, adipose tissue lies below the skin, and ciliated epithelium lines the fallopian tube. These are all correct. In the other options the tissues and places are mixed up.

courses.title: Ch 8 · Cell: The Unit of Life
courses.summary: Cell theory, prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells, the plasma membrane and cell wall, the endomembrane system, energy organelles, ribosomes, cytoskeleton, cilia, centrioles and the nucleus.
outcomes: Learners can state the cell theory and its history
Learners can describe the parts of a prokaryotic cell including the cell envelope
Learners can explain the fluid mosaic model and the endomembrane system
Learners can describe mitochondria, plastids, ribosomes, cilia, centrioles and the nucleus

lessons.title: Cell theory and an overview of cells

scenes.text: In 1665, Robert Hooke looked at a thin slice of cork and saw tiny boxes.
He called them 'cells'. Two centuries later, scientists realised every living thing is built from them.

steps.title: Cell theory
steps.body:
- **Matthias Schleiden (1838)**, a botanist: plants are composed of different kinds of cells.
- **Theodore Schwann (1839)**, a zoologist: animal cells have a thin outer layer (plasma membrane); plant cells also have a cell wall; bodies of animals and plants are composed of cells and their products.
- **Rudolf Virchow (1855):** *Omnis cellula-e cellula* — new cells arise from pre-existing cells.

Modern cell theory: (i) all living organisms are composed of cells and their products; (ii) all cells arise from pre-existing cells.

steps.title: Cell sizes and shapes
steps.body:
- **Mycoplasma** — smallest cells, about 0.3 µm; bacteria 3–5 µm.
- **Largest isolated single cell:** the egg of an ostrich.
- Human RBC about 7.0 µm in diameter; nerve cells are among the longest.
- Shapes vary with function: disc-like (RBC), amoeboid (WBC), branched (neuron), columnar, elongated, polygonal.
- **Prokaryotic** cells lack a membrane-bound nucleus and organelles; **eukaryotic** cells have them.

steps.title: Solved question 1
steps.body: Who first explained that new cells come from pre-existing cells? **Rudolf Virchow (1855)**, which completed the cell theory.

steps.title: Solved question 2
steps.body: Why was Schleiden and Schwann's theory incomplete? It did not explain how new cells form.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying Robert Hooke proposed the cell theory (he only named cells).
- Calling viruses cells.
- Saying the human egg is the largest cell (the ostrich egg is the largest isolated single cell).

activity.prompt: Put the discoveries in order.

events.text: Schleiden: plants are made of cells
Schwann: animals and plants are made of cells
Singer and Nicolson: fluid mosaic model

quiz.why: Rudolf Virchow stated in 1855 that new cells arise from pre-existing cells (omnis cellula-e cellula). Schleiden and Schwann gave the cell theory, and Hooke first saw cells.
Mycoplasma are the smallest known cells, about 0.3 µm. Bacteria are larger, and red blood cells are about 7 µm across.

quiz.q: The largest isolated single cell is the
quiz.why: The ostrich egg is the largest isolated single cell. A nerve cell is long but thin, and the human egg is much smaller.
Theodor Schwann was a zoologist who studied animal cells. Schleiden was the botanist who studied plants, and together they formed the cell theory.
Prokaryotic cells have no membrane-bound nucleus. Their DNA lies in a region called the nucleoid. They still have ribosomes, DNA and a cell membrane.

sources: NCERT Class 11 Biology (Cell: The Unit of Life)

lessons.title: Prokaryotic cells

story.title: The antibiotic that kills some bacteria

scenes.text: A doctor tells Meera her infection is Gram-positive and prescribes a specific antibiotic.
Gram staining sorts bacteria by their cell envelope — the key feature of prokaryotic cells.

steps.title: Cell envelope and structure
steps.body:
Bacteria (cocci, bacilli, vibrio, spirillum), blue-green algae, mycoplasma and PPLO are prokaryotes.
- **Cell envelope** = outer **glycocalyx** (loose **slime layer** or tough **capsule**) + **cell wall** + **plasma membrane**; together a protective unit.
- **Gram-positive** bacteria take up Gram stain; **Gram-negative** do not.
- **Mesosomes:** infoldings of the plasma membrane (vesicles, tubules, lamellae) — help wall formation, DNA replication and distribution, respiration, secretion, increase surface area.
- Genetic material is a naked circular **genomic DNA** (nucleoid) plus small circular **plasmids** (e.g. antibiotic resistance; used in genetic engineering).
- **Ribosomes 70S** (50S + 30S subunits) — protein synthesis; a chain of ribosomes on one mRNA = **polysome**.
- **Inclusion bodies** (not membrane-bound) store reserves: phosphate granules, cyanophycean granules, glycogen granules; **gas vacuoles** in blue-green, purple and green photosynthetic bacteria.
- **Flagella** (filament, hook, basal body) for motility; **pili** (tubular protein) and **fimbriae** (small bristles) for attachment.
- **Chromatophores:** membranous extensions with pigments in cyanobacteria.

steps.title: Solved question 1
steps.body: What is a polysome and what does it do? Several ribosomes attached to one mRNA, translating it into many copies of a protein at once.

steps.title: Solved question 2
steps.body: Give two functions of mesosomes. Help in cell wall formation and in DNA replication and its distribution to daughter cells (also respiration, secretion).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing prokaryotic ribosomes as 80S (they are 70S).
- Saying plasmids are essential for survival — they give extra traits.
- Calling mesosomes true organelles like mitochondria.

activity.prompt: Match the prokaryotic structure to its role.

quiz.why: Bacterial ribosomes are 70S, made of a 50S and a 30S subunit. The 80S ribosomes are in eukaryotic cytoplasm. The values do not add arithmetically because S is a sedimentation unit.

options: do not retain the Gram stain
quiz.why: Gram-negative bacteria lose the crystal violet stain when washed and take up the counterstain, so they do not retain the Gram stain. Gram-positive bacteria retain it. Both types have cell walls.

quiz.q: A chain of ribosomes on one mRNA is a
quiz.why: Several ribosomes attached to a single mRNA and translating it form a chain called a polysome (polyribosome). A nucleoid is the DNA region and a plasmid is a small DNA ring.
Glycogen granules in bacteria are inclusion bodies, which store reserve food. They are not enclosed by a membrane, unlike organelles.

quiz.q: Structures used for motility in bacteria are
quiz.why: Bacteria move with flagella, which have a filament, hook and basal body. Pili and fimbriae are for attachment or transfer of DNA, and capsules protect the cell.

sources: NCERT Class 11 Biology (Cell: The Unit of Life)

lessons.title: Cell membrane, cell wall and the endomembrane system

scenes.text: Proteins made in one part of a cell must reach others — or leave the cell entirely.
The ER makes, the Golgi packs and labels, vesicles deliver — a cellular postal system.

steps.title: Plasma membrane and cell wall
steps.body:
- Membrane mainly lipids (phospholipids in a **bilayer**, polar heads outward, hydrophobic tails inward), proteins and carbohydrates; cholesterol too. In human RBC membrane ~52% protein and ~40% lipids.
- **Fluid mosaic model (Singer and Nicolson, 1972):** quasi-fluid lipid layer lets proteins move laterally; integral and peripheral proteins.
- Functions: transport — **passive** (diffusion, osmosis — water moves) and **active** (uses ATP, e.g. Na⁺/K⁺ pump); cell growth, junctions, secretion, endocytosis, cell division.
- **Cell wall** (plants and fungi): algae — cellulose, galactans, mannans, CaCO₃; plants — cellulose, hemicellulose, pectins, proteins. Primary wall grows; secondary wall forms inside. **Middle lamella** (mainly **calcium pectate**) glues cells; **plasmodesmata** connect cytoplasm of neighbouring cells.

steps.title: Endomembrane system
steps.body:
ER, Golgi, lysosomes and vacuoles function in coordination (mitochondria, chloroplasts and peroxisomes are NOT part of it).
- **ER:** **RER** (with ribosomes) — protein synthesis and secretion; **SER** — lipid synthesis, steroid hormones in animal cells.
- **Golgi apparatus** (Camillo Golgi, 1898): flat cisternae with a convex **cis (forming) face** and concave **trans (maturing) face**; packages materials; site of formation of **glycoproteins and glycolipids**.
- **Lysosomes:** membrane vesicles from Golgi, rich in hydrolytic enzymes (lipases, proteases, carbohydrases) active at **acidic pH**.
- **Vacuoles:** bound by **tonoplast**; up to 90% of a plant cell's volume; contractile vacuole for excretion and osmoregulation in *Amoeba*; food vacuoles in protists.

steps.title: Solved question 1
steps.body: Why do lysosomes not digest the cell normally? Their enzymes are enclosed by a membrane and work best at acidic pH inside the lysosome.

steps.title: Solved question 2
steps.body: Which cells have abundant SER? Cells making steroid hormones (e.g. adrenal cortex, gonads) and lipids.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Including mitochondria in the endomembrane system.
- Saying water moves by active transport during osmosis (it is passive).
- Swapping cis (forming) and trans (maturing) faces.

activity.prompt: Is it part of the endomembrane system?

quiz.q: Fluid mosaic model was proposed by
quiz.why: Singer and Nicolson proposed the fluid mosaic model of the cell membrane in 1972. Watson and Crick worked on the structure of DNA.
The middle lamella is the layer that cements neighbouring plant cells together. It is mainly calcium pectate. Cellulose is the main part of the primary wall.

quiz.q: Glycoproteins and glycolipids are formed in the
quiz.why: The Golgi apparatus is the packaging and modifying centre, where proteins and lipids get sugar groups to form glycoproteins and glycolipids. The nucleus and lysosomes do not do this.
Lysosomal enzymes are hydrolytic and work best at acidic pH, which is maintained inside lysosomes. At neutral or alkaline pH they work poorly.

quiz.q: The membrane around a plant vacuole is the
quiz.why: The membrane around a plant vacuole is the tonoplast. Plasmalemma is the cell membrane, and thylakoid and cisterna belong to other structures.

sources: NCERT Class 11 Biology (Cell: The Unit of Life)

lessons.title: Energy organelles, ribosomes, cytoskeleton and cilia

scenes.text: A marathon runner's leg muscles need huge amounts of ATP.
Muscle cells are packed with mitochondria — the sites of aerobic respiration.

steps.title: Mitochondria and plastids
steps.body:
- **Mitochondria:** double membrane; inner membrane folds into **cristae** (increase surface area); matrix has a single circular DNA, a few RNA, **70S ribosomes**; sites of aerobic respiration (ATP) — 'power houses'; divide by fission.
- **Plastids** (plants, euglenoids): **chloroplasts** (chlorophyll + carotenoids; photosynthesis), **chromoplasts** (fat-soluble carotenoids — yellow, orange, red), **leucoplasts** (colourless storage: **amyloplasts** starch, **elaioplasts** oils/fats, **aleuroplasts** proteins).
- Chloroplast: double membrane; **stroma** with **thylakoids** stacked as **grana**, linked by stroma lamellae; stroma contains enzymes for carbohydrate and protein synthesis, circular DNA and 70S ribosomes.

steps.title: Ribosomes, cytoskeleton, cilia, centrosome, microbodies
steps.body:
- **Ribosomes** (George Palade, 1953): no membrane; ribonucleoprotein; eukaryotic **80S** (60S + 40S); 'S' = sedimentation coefficient (Svedberg unit).
- **Cytoskeleton:** microtubules, microfilaments, intermediate filaments — support, motility, shape.
- **Cilia and flagella:** covered by plasma membrane; core **axoneme** with **9 + 2** arrangement (nine doublets of peripheral microtubules + two central singlets) joined by radial spokes; arise from the **basal body** (centriole-like).
- **Centrosome:** two **centrioles**, perpendicular, each a cartwheel of **nine peripheral triplets** of tubulin; form basal bodies and **spindle fibres** in animal cells.
- **Microbodies:** small membrane-bound vesicles with enzymes, in plant and animal cells.

steps.title: Solved question 1
steps.body: Why are mitochondria and chloroplasts called semi-autonomous? They have their own DNA and 70S ribosomes and can make some of their own proteins.

steps.title: Solved question 2
steps.body: Microtubule arrangement in a centriole vs a cilium axoneme? Centriole: 9 triplets (no central tubules). Axoneme: 9 doublets + 2 central singlets (9 + 2).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying ribosomes have a membrane.
- Mixing chromoplasts (coloured) with leucoplasts (colourless).
- Writing the cilium pattern as 9 + 0.

activity.prompt: Match the leucoplast to its stored product.

quiz.q: Infoldings of the inner mitochondrial membrane are
quiz.why: The inner mitochondrial membrane folds into cristae, which increase the surface area for ATP production. Thylakoids and grana belong to chloroplasts.
Eukaryotic cytoplasmic ribosomes are 80S, made of 60S and 40S subunits. The 70S ribosomes are in prokaryotes (and also in mitochondria and chloroplasts).

quiz.q: Arrangement of microtubules in a cilium axoneme is
quiz.why: A cilium axoneme has nine doublets of microtubules around the edge and two single ones in the centre, the 9 + 2 arrangement. A centriole is different, with nine triplets and no centre pair.

quiz.q: Ribosomes were first observed under the electron microscope by
quiz.why: George Palade first saw ribosomes with the electron microscope in 1953. Robert Brown described the nucleus, and Golgi found the Golgi apparatus.
Thylakoids are flat sacs, and the stacks of thylakoids in a chloroplast are called grana. Stroma lamellae connect different grana. Cristae are in mitochondria.

sources: NCERT Class 11 Biology (Cell: The Unit of Life)

lessons.title: The nucleus and chromosomes

scenes.text: A cell without its nucleus, like a mature human RBC, cannot divide or make new proteins for long.
The nucleus holds the instructions; chromosomes package them.

steps.title: The nucleus
steps.body:
First described by **Robert Brown (1831)**; the material stained by basic dyes was named **chromatin** by **Flemming**.
- **Nuclear envelope:** two parallel membranes with a **perinuclear space** (10–50 nm); interrupted by **nuclear pores** for movement of RNA and proteins.
- **Nucleoplasm** contains the **nucleolus** (site of active rRNA synthesis; not membrane-bound) and chromatin.
- **Chromatin:** DNA + basic proteins (**histones**), some non-histone proteins and RNA. A single human cell has about **two metres** of DNA in 46 chromosomes.
- Most mammalian RBCs and sieve tube cells of vascular plants lack a nucleus.

steps.title: Chromosome structure and types
steps.body:
Each chromosome has a primary constriction — the **centromere** — with disc-shaped **kinetochores**.
- **Metacentric:** centromere in the middle — two equal arms.
- **Sub-metacentric:** slightly away from the middle — one shorter arm.
- **Acrocentric:** close to one end — one extremely short and one very long arm.
- **Telocentric:** terminal centromere.
Some chromosomes have a non-staining **secondary constriction**, giving a small fragment called the **satellite**.

steps.title: Solved question 1
steps.body: Where is rRNA synthesised? In the **nucleolus**; larger and more numerous nucleoli occur in cells actively making proteins.

steps.title: Solved question 2
steps.body: Which chromosome type has arms of very unequal length with the centromere near one end? **Acrocentric**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling the nucleolus membrane-bound.
- Confusing centromere (constriction) with centrosome (organelle with centrioles).
- Saying all eukaryotic cells have a nucleus at maturity (mammalian RBCs lack it).

activity.prompt: Classify by centromere position.

quiz.q: The nucleus was first described by
quiz.why: Robert Brown described the nucleus in 1831. Palade saw ribosomes, Flemming named chromatin and Virchow said new cells come from old ones.

quiz.q: The nucleolus is the site of
quiz.why: The nucleolus is where ribosomal RNA (rRNA) is made and ribosomal subunits are put together. It is a non-membranous structure in the nucleus.
