quiz.q: Disc-shaped structures on the centromere are
quiz.why: Kinetochores are disc-shaped protein structures on the centromere of each chromatid. Spindle fibres attach to them during cell division.

quiz.q: A chromosome with a terminal centromere is
quiz.why: A telocentric chromosome has its centromere at the very tip (terminal). Acrocentric has it near one end, metacentric in the middle and sub-metacentric slightly off the middle.

quiz.q: A cell lacking a nucleus at maturity is the
quiz.why: Mature mammalian red blood cells have no nucleus, which leaves more room for haemoglobin. Guard cells, liver cells and neurons keep their nuclei.

sources: NCERT Class 11 Biology (Cell: The Unit of Life)

questions.q: Cell theory was proposed by
questions.why: The cell theory was put forward by Schleiden (a botanist) and Schwann (a zoologist) in 1838–39. Hooke saw cells earlier, and Singer, Nicolson, Watson and Crick did other work.

questions.q: Power houses of the cell are
questions.why: Mitochondria are called power houses because they make most of the cell's ATP by respiration. Ribosomes make proteins and lysosomes digest materials.

questions.q: Prokaryotic genetic material is
options: naked circular DNA in a nucleoid
questions.why: Prokaryotes have naked (no histone covering), circular DNA lying in the cytoplasm in a region called the nucleoid, with no nuclear envelope around it.

questions.q: Suicide bags of the cell are
questions.why: Lysosomes contain digestive (hydrolytic) enzymes that can digest the cell itself if the membrane bursts, so they are called suicide bags.

questions.q: Middle lamella is made largely of
questions.why: The middle lamella cements neighbouring plant cell walls together and is made largely of calcium pectate. Cellulose, lignin and suberin are in other wall layers.

questions.q: Leucoplasts storing oil are
questions.why: Leucoplasts are colourless plastids that store food. Those that store oil are elaioplasts (elaio means oil), while amyloplasts store starch and aleuroplasts store proteins.

questions.q: Assertion: Mitochondria can make some of their own proteins. Reason: They contain DNA and 70S ribosomes.
options: Both true and R explains A
Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true and R explains A. Mitochondria have their own DNA and 70S ribosomes, so they can make some of their own proteins. This is why they are called semi-autonomous.

questions.q: Which organelle is not part of the endomembrane system?
questions.why: The endomembrane system includes ER, Golgi, lysosomes and vacuoles, which work together. Peroxisomes are not part of it because they work on their own.

questions.q: The 9 + 2 arrangement refers to
questions.why: The 9 + 2 pattern, nine doublets of microtubules around a central pair, is the axoneme of cilia and flagella. Centrioles have nine triplets with no central pair.

questions.q: Steroid hormone synthesis occurs mainly in
questions.why: Smooth ER (SER) makes lipids and steroid hormones such as those of the adrenal cortex and gonads. Rough ER makes proteins, because it has ribosomes.

questions.q: Case: An electron micrograph of a cell shows mesosomes, a nucleoid and 70S ribosomes but no mitochondria. The cell is
questions.why: Mesosomes, a nucleoid and 70S ribosomes, with no mitochondria, are prokaryotic features. So the cell is a bacterium. Animal, plant and fungal cells are eukaryotic with mitochondria.

questions.q: Case: A tomato turns from green to red as it ripens. The plastids involved change from
questions.why: When a tomato ripens, chloroplasts lose chlorophyll and change into chromoplasts, which hold red carotenoid pigments. This turns the fruit from green to red.

questions.q: The cis face of the Golgi is
options: attached to the nucleus by pores
questions.why: The cis (forming) face of the Golgi is convex and faces the ER, receiving vesicles from it. The trans (maturing) face is concave and sends out vesicles.

questions.q: In human RBC membranes, the approximate proportions are
questions.why: In the human red blood cell membrane the proportion is about 52% protein and 40% lipid, with the rest carbohydrate. Membranes differ in this ratio from cell to cell.

questions.q: The S in 70S stands for
questions.why: S stands for the Svedberg unit, a measure of how fast a particle sediments when spun. It depends on size, shape and density, so subunits do not add up simply.

questions.q: Each centriole is made of
questions.why: Each centriole is made of nine evenly spaced peripheral triplets of tubulin microtubules, arranged like a cartwheel, with no central microtubules. The 9 + 2 pattern belongs to cilia.

questions.q: Which statement is correct?
options: Nucleolus is not membrane-bound and is the site of rRNA synthesis
Golgi was discovered by Robert Brown
questions.why: The nucleolus has no membrane and is where rRNA is made. Prokaryotes have 70S, not 80S, ribosomes. Golgi found the Golgi apparatus, and lysosomes do not come from mitochondria.

questions.q: A chromosome with one extremely short and one very long arm is
questions.why: An acrocentric chromosome has its centromere very near one end, so one arm is extremely short and the other very long. A telocentric one would have no second arm.

courses.title: Ch 9 · Biomolecules
courses.summary: Chemical composition of living tissue, amino acids, lipids, nucleotides, primary and secondary metabolites, biomacromolecules — proteins, polysaccharides, nucleic acids — and enzymes with their properties and classification.
outcomes: Learners can describe how chemical analysis reveals biomolecules
Learners can describe amino acids, lipids, sugars and nucleotides
Learners can explain levels of protein structure and polysaccharide types
Learners can explain enzyme action, factors affecting activity, inhibition, classes and cofactors

lessons.title: Chemical analysis and small biomolecules

scenes.text: In the lab, a leaf is ground with trichloroacetic acid and filtered.
The filtrate (acid-soluble) holds small molecules; the residue (acid-insoluble) holds the giants — proteins, nucleic acids, polysaccharides.

steps.title: Chemical analysis
steps.body: Living tissue ground in **trichloroacetic acid (Cl₃CCOOH)** gives an **acid-soluble filtrate** (micromolecules, MW < 1000 Da: amino acids, sugars, nucleotides) and an **acid-insoluble retentate** (macromolecules: proteins, nucleic acids, polysaccharides; lipids appear here because membranes break into insoluble vesicles). Ash analysis shows inorganic elements (Ca, Mg, Na, K etc.).

steps.title: Amino acids, lipids, sugars, nucleotides
steps.body:
- **Amino acids:** α-carbon bearing H, carboxyl, amino and a variable **R group**. 20 types in proteins: glycine (R = H), alanine (CH₃), serine (CH₂OH). Acidic (glutamic acid), basic (lysine), neutral (valine); aromatic (tyrosine, phenylalanine, tryptophan). Ionisable groups → **zwitterion** at certain pH.
- **Lipids:** water-insoluble. Fatty acids: carboxyl + R group; e.g. **palmitic acid** has 16 C (including the carboxyl carbon), **arachidonic acid** 20 C; saturated (no double bonds) or unsaturated. **Glycerol** is trihydroxy propane. Esters: mono-, di-, **triglycerides** (fats and oils; oils have lower melting point). **Phospholipids** (e.g. **lecithin**) in membranes.
- **Sugars:** glucose, ribose etc.
- **Nucleotides:** nitrogen base (**adenine, guanine** = purines; **cytosine, uracil, thymine** = pyrimidines) + pentose sugar = **nucleoside**; + phosphate = **nucleotide**.

steps.title: Solved question 1
steps.body: Why do lipids appear in the acid-insoluble fraction though they are small? Grinding breaks membranes into vesicles that are insoluble — so they settle with macromolecules.

steps.title: Solved question 2
steps.body: Name the R group of serine. **–CH₂OH** (hydroxymethyl).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling lipids macromolecules (most have MW < 800 Da).
- Confusing nucleoside (base + sugar) with nucleotide (base + sugar + phosphate).
- Thinking uracil occurs in DNA (it occurs in RNA).

activity.prompt: Match the compound.

quiz.q: Acid used in chemical analysis of tissues is
quiz.why: Trichloroacetic acid (Cl₃CCOOH) is used to treat tissue and separate the acid-soluble pool from the insoluble part for analysis. The others are not the standard acid for this.
A nucleotide has three parts: a nitrogenous base, a pentose sugar and a phosphate group. Without the phosphate it would be a nucleoside.
Purines have a double ring: adenine and guanine. Pyrimidines have a single ring: cytosine, thymine and uracil.

quiz.q: Aromatic amino acid among these is
quiz.why: Tryptophan has an aromatic ring in its side chain. Glycine, lysine and valine do not have a ring.

quiz.q: Oils differ from fats in having
quiz.why: Oils have lower melting points than fats, so they stay liquid at room temperature. Both contain glycerol and fatty acids, and oils have more unsaturated fatty acids.

sources: NCERT Class 11 Biology (Biomolecules)

lessons.title: Metabolites and biomacromolecules

scenes.text: Turmeric's curcumin, the anti-cancer drug vinblastin, rubber and morphine all come from plants.
They are secondary metabolites — not needed for basic life processes, but valuable to us.

steps.title: Primary vs secondary metabolites
steps.body:
- **Primary metabolites:** amino acids, sugars, nucleotides etc. with identifiable roles in normal physiology.
- **Secondary metabolites** (mainly plants, fungi, microbes): **pigments** (carotenoids, anthocyanins), **alkaloids** (morphine, codeine), **terpenoids** (monoterpenes, diterpenes), **essential oils** (lemon grass oil), **toxins** (abrin, ricin), **lectins** (concanavalin A), **drugs** (vinblastin, curcumin), **polymeric substances** (rubber, gums, cellulose). Many are important for human welfare.

steps.title: Biomacromolecules
steps.body:
Molecules with MW > 10,000 Da in the acid-insoluble fraction: **proteins, nucleic acids, polysaccharides** (lipids are the exception noted earlier).

Approximate composition of a cell: water 70–90%, proteins 10–15%, carbohydrates 3%, lipids 2%, nucleic acids 5–7%, ions 1%.

steps.title: Solved question 1
steps.body: Classify concanavalin A. A **lectin** — a secondary metabolite that binds sugars.

steps.title: Solved question 2
steps.body: What is the most abundant chemical in living cells? **Water** (70–90%).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling every plant chemical 'primary'.
- Placing lipids among true macromolecules.
- Confusing alkaloids (morphine) with toxins (ricin).

activity.prompt: Classify the secondary metabolite.

quiz.why: Concanavalin A is a lectin, a protein that binds to specific sugars. It is not an alkaloid, a toxin or a pigment.
Ricin is a toxin, a poisonous protein obtained from castor seeds. It is a secondary metabolite and not a pigment, oil or drug.

quiz.q: The most abundant component of a cell is
quiz.why: Water is the most abundant compound in living cells, making up 70 to 90 percent. Proteins come next among the organic compounds.
Macromolecules have a high molecular weight, usually above about 10,000 Da (daltons), such as proteins, nucleic acids and polysaccharides. Small molecules are below about 1,000 Da.
Primary metabolites like glucose have a known role in normal growth and metabolism. Curcumin, morphine and rubber are secondary metabolites.

sources: NCERT Class 11 Biology (Biomolecules)

lessons.title: Proteins, polysaccharides and nucleic acids

scenes.text: A drop of iodine turns a potato slice blue-black, but cotton wool stays brown.
Starch forms helices that trap iodine; cellulose, a straight chain, does not.

steps.title: Proteins
steps.body:
- Polypeptides = heteropolymers of amino acids joined by **peptide bonds**.
- **Essential amino acids** must come from the diet; non-essential ones the body makes.
- Functions: transport (GLUT-4 glucose into cells), hormones (insulin), enzymes (trypsin), antibodies, receptors (sensory), intercellular ground substance (**collagen** — most abundant protein in the animal world). **RuBisCO** is the most abundant protein in the whole biosphere.
- **Structure:** **primary** (sequence; N-terminal left, C-terminal right), **secondary** (e.g. **right-handed** α-helix), **tertiary** (3D folding of the chain), **quaternary** (several subunits, e.g. adult haemoglobin: 2 α + 2 β chains).

steps.title: Polysaccharides and nucleic acids
steps.body:
- **Polysaccharides:** chains of monosaccharides joined by **glycosidic bonds**. **Cellulose** — homopolymer of glucose (plant walls; no complex helices, so no blue colour with iodine); **starch** — plant store, forms helices holding I₂ (blue); **glycogen** — animal store; **inulin** — polymer of fructose; **chitin** — complex polysaccharide in arthropod exoskeletons and fungal walls. Right end of a chain is reducing, left non-reducing.
- **Nucleic acids:** polynucleotides with **phosphodiester bonds** (phosphate links 3′-C of one sugar to 5′-C of the next). DNA: deoxyribose; RNA: ribose. **B-DNA** (Watson–Crick): double helix, antiparallel strands, A=T (two H-bonds), G≡C (three H-bonds), one turn ≈ **10 base pairs**, pitch **3.4 nm**, rise per base pair **0.34 nm**, right-handed.

steps.title: Solved question 1
steps.body: Why does cellulose not give blue colour with iodine? It lacks the complex helical structure needed to hold iodine.

steps.title: Solved question 2
steps.body: How many hydrogen bonds hold a G–C pair? **Three** (A–T has two).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying collagen is the most abundant protein in the biosphere (that is RuBisCO).
- Calling inulin a glucose polymer (it is fructose).
- Writing 3.4 nm as the distance between adjacent base pairs (that is 0.34 nm).

activity.prompt: Match the bond to the polymer.

quiz.q: Most abundant protein in the biosphere is
quiz.why: RuBisCO, the enzyme for carbon fixation in photosynthesis, is the most abundant protein in the whole biosphere. Collagen is the most abundant in the animal world.
Inulin is a polymer of fructose units (a fructan), found in plants such as dahlia and chicory. Starch and glycogen are polymers of glucose.
Adult haemoglobin has four subunits, two α chains and two β chains. This is a quaternary structure.

quiz.q: In B-DNA, one turn contains about
quiz.why: In B-DNA each turn of the double helix has about 10 base pairs. The pitch is 3.4 nm, and the base pairs are 0.34 nm apart.
Chitin is a complex polysaccharide with nitrogen. It forms the exoskeleton of arthropods and the cell walls of fungi. Plant cell walls have cellulose.

sources: NCERT Class 11 Biology (Biomolecules)

lessons.title: Enzymes

scenes.text: A very high fever can be life-threatening.
Most enzymes are proteins with a precise shape; heat can denature them, and metabolism slows or stops.

steps.title: Nature and action
steps.body:
- Almost all enzymes are proteins; some nucleic acids act as enzymes (**ribozymes**).
- Tertiary structure creates an **active site** (crevice) where the **substrate** fits.
- Enzymes lower the **activation energy**; e.g. carbonic anhydrase speeds CO₂ + H₂O → H₂CO₃ about 10 million times.
- **Catalytic cycle:** substrate binds active site → enzyme–substrate complex (ES) → enzyme shape changes, substrate bonds break/form → product released → enzyme free for another cycle.

steps.title: Factors, inhibition, classes, cofactors
steps.body:
- **Temperature and pH:** each enzyme has an **optimum**; activity falls on either side; high temperature **denatures**; low temperature preserves enzymes in an inactive state.
- **Substrate concentration:** velocity rises then reaches **Vmax** when all enzyme molecules are saturated.
- **Competitive inhibition:** inhibitor resembles the substrate and competes for the active site, e.g. **malonate** inhibits **succinic dehydrogenase** (substrate succinate); used to control bacterial pathogens.
- **Six classes:** **oxidoreductases/dehydrogenases**, **transferases**, **hydrolases**, **lyases** (remove groups forming double bonds), **isomerases**, **ligases** (join two compounds).
- **Cofactors:** the protein part is the **apoenzyme**. (i) **Prosthetic groups** — tightly bound organic compounds, e.g. **haem** in peroxidase and catalase; (ii) **coenzymes** — loosely bound organic compounds; many contain vitamins (NAD and NADP contain **niacin**); (iii) **metal ions**, e.g. **zinc** for carboxypeptidase. Removing the cofactor destroys activity.

steps.title: Solved question 1
steps.body: Why does malonate slow succinic dehydrogenase? Malonate looks like succinate and occupies the active site — competitive inhibition.

steps.title: Solved question 2
steps.body: Name the class of an enzyme that splits a peptide bond with water. **Hydrolases**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying enzymes are consumed in reactions.
- Thinking low temperature destroys enzymes (it only inactivates them temporarily).
- Mixing prosthetic groups (tightly bound) and coenzymes (transiently bound).

activity.label: Temperature for a typical human enzyme

bands.text: Too cold: the enzyme is inactive but not destroyed; activity returns on warming.
Activity rising as molecules move faster.
Above optimum: activity falls as the enzyme begins to denature.
High heat: the protein is denatured and activity is lost.

quiz.q: Nucleic acids that act as enzymes are
quiz.why: Ribozymes are RNA molecules with catalytic activity, so they work as enzymes. Isozymes, apoenzymes and coenzymes are all protein enzymes or parts of them.
Malonate looks like the substrate succinate, so it binds the active site of succinic dehydrogenase and blocks it. This is competitive inhibition, which can be reduced by more substrate.
Haem in peroxidase and catalase is tightly bound to the enzyme protein, so it is a prosthetic group. Coenzymes are loosely bound, and metal ions are different cofactors.
Zinc is a metal-ion cofactor required for the activity of carboxypeptidase. Catalase uses iron in its haem, and RuBisCO and amylase are not linked to zinc here.
NAD contains niacin (nicotinamide) as its vitamin part. Riboflavin is in FAD, and thiamine is in thiamine pyrophosphate.

quiz.q: Enzymes that join two compounds are
quiz.why: Ligases join two compounds together, usually using ATP. Hydrolases break bonds with water, isomerases rearrange atoms, and lyases remove groups to form double bonds.

sources: NCERT Class 11 Biology (Biomolecules)

questions.q: Proteins are polymers of
questions.why: Proteins are polymers of amino acids joined by peptide bonds. Polysaccharides are made of monosaccharides and nucleic acids of nucleotides.

questions.q: Cellulose is a polymer of
questions.why: Cellulose is a homopolymer made only of glucose units, joined by β-1,4 linkages. It is the main component of plant cell walls.

questions.q: Enzymes are mostly
questions.why: Most enzymes are proteins. A few, called ribozymes, are made of RNA. Vitamins, carbohydrates and lipids are not usually enzymes.

questions.q: A nucleoside lacks
questions.why: A nucleoside is a nitrogenous base joined to a sugar. A nucleotide is a nucleoside with a phosphate added, so a nucleoside lacks the phosphate.

questions.q: Most abundant protein of the animal world is
questions.why: Collagen is the most abundant protein in the animal world, found in connective tissue. RuBisCO is the most abundant in the whole biosphere.

questions.q: Starch gives blue colour with iodine because
questions.why: Starch forms helical coils that trap iodine molecules inside, which gives the blue colour. Cellulose does not form such helices, so it gives no blue.

questions.q: Assertion: Lipids appear in the acid-insoluble fraction. Reason: Lipids are true macromolecules with very high molecular weight.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
Both true and R explains A
questions.why: The assertion is true: lipids do appear in the acid-insoluble fraction, because broken membranes form insoluble vesicles. The reason is false, since lipids are not true macromolecules. So A is true and R is false.

questions.q: Number of H-bonds between A and T is
questions.why: Adenine and thymine pair with two hydrogen bonds. Guanine and cytosine pair with three, which is why G–C pairs are stronger.

questions.q: Distance between two consecutive base pairs in B-DNA is
questions.why: In B-DNA the rise per base pair is 0.34 nm. One full turn has 10 base pairs, so the pitch is 3.4 nm.

questions.q: Enzymes catalysing removal of groups to form double bonds are
questions.why: Lyases remove groups from substrates by means other than hydrolysis, forming double bonds. Transferases move groups, isomerases rearrange them, and ligases join molecules.

questions.q: Case: A student boils an enzyme solution and finds no activity even after cooling. The reason is
questions.why: Boiling destroys the three-dimensional structure of the enzyme protein, so it is denatured and the change is permanent. Cooling does not restore the shape, so there is no activity.

questions.q: Case: Adding more substrate does not increase the reaction rate beyond a point. This is because
questions.why: When all enzyme molecules are busy with substrate, adding more substrate cannot raise the rate. The enzyme is saturated and the rate stays at its maximum (Vmax).

questions.q: Which is a secondary metabolite used as a drug?
questions.why: Vinblastin is a secondary metabolite (an alkaloid) used as an anticancer drug. Glycine, ATP and glucose are primary metabolites.

questions.q: An enzyme with its cofactor removed is called
questions.why: An enzyme without its cofactor is an apoenzyme (only the protein part). With its cofactor it is a holoenzyme, which is the active form.

questions.q: The quaternary structure of a protein refers to
questions.why: Quaternary structure is how two or more polypeptide chains (subunits) are arranged together, as in haemoglobin. The amino acid sequence is the primary structure.

questions.q: Arachidonic acid has
questions.why: Arachidonic acid is a fatty acid with 20 carbon atoms, counting the carboxyl carbon. Palmitic acid has 16 carbons.

questions.q: Which pair is incorrectly matched?
questions.why: Inulin is a polymer of fructose, not glucose, so that pairing is wrong. Cellulose is in plant walls, chitin in the exoskeleton and glycogen is the animal storage polysaccharide.

questions.q: The 3′ → 5′ linkage between nucleotides in a chain is a
questions.why: In a nucleic acid chain the 3′ carbon of one sugar is joined to the 5′ carbon of the next sugar through a phosphate. This linkage is a phosphodiester bond.

courses.title: Ch 10 · Cell Cycle and Cell Division
courses.summary: Phases of the cell cycle, mitosis and cytokinesis with significance, the stages of meiosis I and II including crossing over, and the significance of meiosis.
outcomes: Learners can describe interphase (G1, S, G2) and G0
Learners can sequence and describe the stages of mitosis and cytokinesis
Learners can describe the five sub-stages of prophase I and crossing over
Learners can compare mitosis and meiosis and state their significance

lessons.title: The cell cycle

scenes.text: A scraped knee heals in a week as skin cells divide to fill the gap.
Each dividing cell follows a timed sequence — the cell cycle.

steps.title: Phases
steps.body:
The **cell cycle** is the sequence of events by which a cell duplicates its genome, synthesises other constituents and divides into two. A typical human cell in culture divides about once every **24 hours**; yeast in about **90 minutes**.
- **Interphase** (resting phase, but metabolically very active): > 95% of the cycle.
  - **G1:** cell grows and is metabolically active; no DNA replication.
  - **S (synthesis):** DNA replication; DNA per cell doubles **2C → 4C**, but **chromosome number stays the same** (2n). In animal cells the centriole duplicates in the cytoplasm.
  - **G2:** proteins made for mitosis; growth continues.
- **M phase** (mitosis): about **1 hour** in human cells; karyokinesis followed by cytokinesis.
- **G0 (quiescent stage):** cells that exit G1 and stop dividing (e.g. heart cells), but remain metabolically active and may divide on demand.

steps.title: Solved question 1
steps.body: A cell has 2C DNA in G1. How much in G2? **4C** (doubled in S phase), with the same chromosome number.

steps.title: Solved question 2
steps.body: Why is interphase not truly 'resting'? DNA replicates, organelles and proteins are synthesised and the cell grows in preparation for division.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying chromosome number doubles in S phase (only DNA amount doubles).
- Thinking G0 cells are dead or inactive.
- Placing centriole duplication in G2 (it occurs in S phase in animal cells).

activity.prompt: Order the phases of one cell cycle.

quiz.why: DNA replication takes place in the S (synthesis) phase of interphase. M phase is cell division, and G1 and G2 are gap phases for growth.

quiz.q: A typical human cell cycle lasts about
quiz.why: A typical human cell in culture divides about once every 24 hours. Yeast can divide in about 90 minutes.
Cells that stop dividing leave the cycle at G1 and enter the quiescent G0 stage. They stay metabolically active but do not divide unless signalled.

quiz.q: If G1 DNA content is 2C, after S phase it is
quiz.why: DNA doubles in the S phase. So a cell with 2C in G1 has 4C after S phase, though the chromosome number stays the same.
Interphase is the long period between divisions and takes more than 95 percent of the cycle. The M phase is only a small part.

sources: NCERT Class 11 Biology (Cell Cycle and Cell Division)

lessons.title: Mitosis and cytokinesis

scenes.text: In the practical, students squash a stained onion root tip and find cells caught in different stages of division.
Chromosomes lined up in the middle? That's metaphase — the best stage to count them.

steps.title: Stages of mitosis (equational division)
steps.body:
- **Prophase:** chromatin condenses into chromosomes (each with two chromatids joined at the centromere); centrosomes move to opposite poles and form the **mitotic apparatus** (asters + spindle); at the end Golgi, ER, nucleolus and nuclear envelope disappear.
- **Metaphase:** nuclear envelope gone; chromosomes fully condensed — **best stage to study morphology**; spindle fibres attach to **kinetochores**; chromosomes line up at the **metaphase plate**.
- **Anaphase:** centromeres split; sister chromatids (now daughter chromosomes) move to opposite poles, centromere leading, arms trailing.
- **Telophase:** chromosomes cluster at poles and decondense; nuclear envelope, nucleolus, Golgi and ER re-form.

steps.title: Cytokinesis and significance
steps.body:
- **Animal cells:** a **furrow** in the plasma membrane deepens and divides the cytoplasm.
- **Plant cells:** a **cell plate** forms from the centre outward (it becomes the **middle lamella**), because of the rigid wall.
- Karyokinesis without cytokinesis → multinucleate **syncytium** (e.g. liquid endosperm of coconut).
- **Significance:** produces genetically identical diploid daughter cells; growth of multicellular organisms; restores the nucleo-cytoplasmic ratio; cell repair (epidermis, gut lining, blood cells); meristems in plants grow continuously by mitosis.

steps.title: Solved question 1
steps.body: Why is metaphase best for counting chromosomes? Chromosomes are maximally condensed and arranged in one plane.

steps.title: Solved question 2
steps.body: How does cytokinesis differ in plants? Plants form a cell plate from the centre outward; animals form a furrow from the outside inward.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying centromeres split in metaphase (they split in anaphase).
- Calling mitosis a reductional division.
- Forgetting that the cell plate becomes the middle lamella.

activity.prompt: Arrange the events of mitosis in order.
items: Chromosomes align at the metaphase plate
Centromeres split and chromatids move to poles

quiz.q: The best stage to study chromosome morphology is
quiz.why: Metaphase is the best stage for studying chromosome shape. The chromosomes are most condensed and are lined up at the equator of the cell.
In anaphase the centromeres split and the sister chromatids separate, moving to opposite poles. In metaphase they are only lined up.

quiz.q: A multinucleate condition from karyokinesis without cytokinesis is a
quiz.why: If the nucleus divides but the cytoplasm does not (karyokinesis without cytokinesis), a multinucleate syncytium forms. The liquid endosperm of coconut is an example.

quiz.q: In plant cells cytokinesis occurs by
quiz.why: Plant cells have a rigid cell wall, so a furrow cannot form. Instead a cell plate forms in the centre and grows outward to divide the cell.

quiz.q: Mitosis is called equational division because
options: daughter cells have the same chromosome number as the parent
quiz.why: Mitosis is equational because the daughter cells have the same chromosome number as the parent (2n gives 2n). Meiosis I is the reductional division.

sources: NCERT Class 11 Biology (Cell Cycle and Cell Division)

lessons.title: Meiosis I

scenes.text: Two siblings have the same parents yet look quite different.
Crossing over during meiosis I shuffles genes, so every gamete is unique.

steps.title: Prophase I (five sub-stages)
steps.body:
Meiosis has **one DNA replication but two nuclear divisions**, producing four haploid cells.
- **Leptotene:** chromosomes gradually become visible and keep compacting.
- **Zygotene:** homologous chromosomes pair (**synapsis**) aided by the **synaptonemal complex**; the pair is a **bivalent** or **tetrad**.
- **Pachytene:** tetrads clearly visible; **recombination nodules** appear; **crossing over** (exchange between non-sister chromatids of homologues) by the enzyme **recombinase**; leads to recombination.
- **Diplotene:** synaptonemal complex dissolves; homologues separate except at **chiasmata** (X-shaped). In oocytes of some vertebrates diplotene can last months or years.
- **Diakinesis:** **terminalisation** of chiasmata; chromosomes fully condensed; spindle assembles; nucleolus and nuclear envelope disappear.

steps.title: Metaphase I to interkinesis
steps.body:
- **Metaphase I:** bivalents align on the equatorial plate; spindle fibres from opposite poles attach to kinetochores of homologues.
- **Anaphase I:** **homologous chromosomes separate**; sister chromatids stay together at their centromeres.
- **Telophase I:** nuclear membrane and nucleolus reappear; cytokinesis gives a **dyad of cells**.
- **Interkinesis:** short stage between the two divisions; **no DNA replication**.

steps.title: Solved question 1
steps.body: In which sub-stage does crossing over occur and which enzyme helps? **Pachytene**, enzyme **recombinase**.

steps.title: Solved question 2
steps.body: What separates in anaphase I versus anaphase II? Anaphase I: homologous chromosomes. Anaphase II: sister chromatids.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Placing synapsis in pachytene (it occurs in zygotene).
- Saying chiasmata form in zygotene (they become visible in diplotene).
- Saying DNA replicates in interkinesis.

activity.prompt: Arrange the sub-stages of prophase I.

quiz.why: Synapsis, the pairing of homologous chromosomes, occurs in zygotene of prophase I. Crossing over happens later in pachytene.
Crossing over is the exchange of segments between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes. It creates new combinations of genes.
Chiasmata, the X-shaped points where crossing over happened, are first seen in diplotene, when the homologous chromosomes begin to separate.
Terminalisation of chiasmata, where the chiasmata slide toward the ends of the chromosomes, takes place in diakinesis, the last sub-stage of prophase I.
Homologous chromosomes separate in anaphase I, which is why meiosis I is reductional. In anaphase II it is sister chromatids that separate.

sources: NCERT Class 11 Biology (Cell Cycle and Cell Division)

lessons.title: Meiosis II and significance

scenes.text: One diploid cell in the anther gives rise to four haploid pollen grains.
Meiosis II is like mitosis, but it starts with haploid cells.

steps.title: Meiosis II (resembles mitosis)
steps.body:
- **Prophase II:** begins right after cytokinesis, usually before chromosomes fully elongate; nuclear membrane disappears; chromosomes compact again.
- **Metaphase II:** chromosomes align at the equator; microtubules attach to kinetochores of sister chromatids.
- **Anaphase II:** centromeres split simultaneously; sister chromatids move to opposite poles.
- **Telophase II:** nuclear envelopes re-form; cytokinesis → **tetrad of four haploid cells**.

steps.title: Significance of meiosis
steps.body:
- **Conserves the chromosome number** across generations in sexually reproducing organisms (n gametes fuse → 2n zygote).
- Increases **genetic variability** (crossing over + independent assortment of homologues), which is important for evolution.

steps.title: Solved question 1
steps.body: A cell with 2n = 16 undergoes meiosis. Chromosome numbers? After meiosis I: 8 per cell (each with two chromatids). After meiosis II: four cells with 8 chromosomes each.

steps.title: Solved question 2
steps.body: Mitosis vs meiosis: mitosis — 1 division, 2 identical 2n cells, somatic; meiosis — 2 divisions, 4 genetically varied n cells, in reproductive cells; crossing over only in meiosis.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking DNA replicates before meiosis II.
- Saying meiosis II halves the chromosome number (meiosis I does).
- Forgetting that meiosis occurs during gamete or spore formation, depending on the organism.

activity.prompt: Mitosis or meiosis?

items.text: Repair of skin and gut lining

quiz.q: Meiosis II is most similar to
quiz.why: Meiosis II is like mitosis, because the sister chromatids separate and the chromosome number stays the same. Meiosis I is different, as homologues separate.

quiz.q: A cell with 2n = 20 after meiosis gives cells with
quiz.why: Meiosis halves the chromosome number. A cell with 2n = 20 gives cells with n = 10 chromosomes.
Crossing over in prophase I and independent assortment of homologous chromosomes in metaphase I and anaphase I shuffle genes, so meiosis creates variation. DNA replicates only once.
Meiosis I is the reductional division because it halves the chromosome number (2n to n). Meiosis II is equational and mitosis keeps the number the same.

quiz.q: At the end of meiosis we get
quiz.why: One meiotic division sequence of two divisions gives four haploid cells (a tetrad). In mitosis two diploid cells are formed.

sources: NCERT Class 11 Biology (Cell Cycle and Cell Division)

questions.q: DNA content doubles in
questions.why: DNA content doubles during the S phase, when DNA is copied. G1 and G2 are growth phases and metaphase is part of division.

questions.q: Spindle fibres attach to the
questions.why: Spindle fibres attach to the kinetochores, protein discs on the centromere of each chromosome. They then pull the chromatids apart.

questions.q: Number of cells formed at the end of meiosis is
questions.why: Meiosis has two divisions after one DNA replication, so one cell gives four cells, each haploid.

questions.q: Crossing over occurs during
questions.why: Crossing over takes place in pachytene of prophase I, where recombination nodules help the exchange between non-sister chromatids.

questions.q: Cytokinesis in plant cells begins with
options: cell plate formation in the centre
questions.why: In plants cytokinesis begins with a cell plate forming at the centre and growing outward (centrifugally) to meet the wall. Animal cells form a furrow from outside instead.

questions.q: Chromosome number in a cell at G2 compared to G1 is
questions.why: The chromosome number does not change from G1 to G2. Only the DNA content doubles in S phase, as each chromosome gets two chromatids, but it is still one chromosome.

questions.q: Assertion: Interphase is called the resting phase. Reason: The cell is metabolically inactive during interphase.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
Both true and R explains A
questions.why: Interphase is called the resting phase, so A is true, but the reason is false. The cell is very active in interphase, as it grows and copies its DNA. So R is false.

questions.q: The synaptonemal complex is formed during
questions.why: The synaptonemal complex forms during zygotene, and it holds the paired homologous chromosomes together. It stays through pachytene.

questions.q: Which stage involves splitting of centromeres in meiosis?
questions.why: In meiosis the centromeres split in anaphase II, so the sister chromatids separate. In anaphase I the centromeres stay intact and whole homologous chromosomes move apart.

questions.q: Liquid endosperm of coconut is an example of
questions.why: In coconut liquid endosperm the nucleus divides repeatedly without the cytoplasm dividing, which gives many free nuclei in one cell. This is a syncytium.

questions.q: Case: Onion root tip cells (2n = 16) are observed at anaphase of mitosis. The number of chromosomes moving to each pole is
questions.why: In mitosis anaphase the sister chromatids separate, and each pole receives one full diploid set. With 2n = 16, 16 chromosomes move to each pole.

questions.q: Case: A plant cell has 4C DNA and 2n chromosomes. It is in
questions.why: A cell with 4C DNA but 2n chromosomes has already copied its DNA but has not yet divided. That is G2 (after S, before M).

questions.q: In which stage can oocytes of some vertebrates remain for months or years?
questions.why: The oocytes of some vertebrates stop in diplotene of prophase I and stay there for months or years, until they are triggered to complete meiosis.

questions.q: If a meiocyte has 24 chromosomes, a cell at the end of meiosis I has
questions.why: Meiosis I halves the chromosome number, so 24 gives 12 chromosomes. Each still has two chromatids until meiosis II separates them.

questions.q: Human cells in culture take about 24 h per cycle; M phase lasts about
questions.why: The M phase is short, about one hour of the 24-hour cycle. Interphase takes the rest.

questions.q: Which statement is correct about G0?
options: Cells are metabolically active but do not proliferate unless called on
It occurs after M in all cells
questions.why: In G0 cells are alive and metabolically active, but they do not divide unless they are stimulated. Some cells, like neurons, stay in G0 for life.

questions.q: The amount of DNA in a meiocyte at G1 is 2C. At prophase I, metaphase II and after telophase II it is
questions.why: After S phase a meiocyte has 4C at prophase I. Meiosis I halves it to 2C, which is the amount at metaphase II. Meiosis II halves it again, giving 1C after telophase II.
